DCC recognises that international assistance is important in combating crime, but warns that it must not be misused to suppress political expression. OM: data not yet shared. The <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> in Amsterdam says in a written response to news agency ANP that the seizure was carried out on the basis of the treaty between the Netherlands and the US on mutual legal assistance in criminal matters. In this case there would have been no ground for refusal for the OM. The OM further states that the seized data have not yet been shared with the US. Anti-capitalist internet service provider A/I is a left-wing Italian internet provider that until recently, for about 25 years and for activist reasons, offered free email services and web hosting to around 20,000 organisations and activists worldwide who stand up for civil rights and equality. According to the US, the Italian provider is a terrorist organisation that provides services to "extreme left-wing organisations". Those organisations are said to include "Antifa cells", among others. Antifa is the international decentralised protest movement that combats fascism, without a clear structure or central leadership. A/I dissolved itself. After the US imposed sanctions at the end of August, A/I decided a good week later to dissolve as a precaution. The organisation said it wanted to prevent others from being put in danger, as stated in an online statement. Because of the US sanctions, A/I lost access to its domain name, among other things, its PayPal account was withdrawn and its regular bank account was blocked. In the days before the blockade, an unsolicited wave of donations came in from people who wanted to support A/I, NRC reported earlier. The Italian bank Banca Etica, where A/I had an account, decided to block it after the sanctions, out of fear that possible US secondary sanctions could also endanger services to 130,000 other customers and members. The bank did, however, condemn the conduct of the US government.

title: Missing 29-year-old woman found dead in Amsterdam, police assume a crime
lead: A 29-year-old woman was found dead in the water on the Amsteldijk in Amsterdam this morning. She died as a result of a crime, the police said. The woman had been missing since 4 October. Her family reported her missing to the police on 5 October. At 8.30 a.m. this morning the police were alerted to a suspicious situation on the Amsteldijk in the Amsterdam-Zuid district. This evening it was announced that the woman was found there. The police say they cannot yet provide information on exactly what happened to her. RAI The 29-year-old Hajar was last seen on 4 October near the RAI congress centre in Amsterdam-Zuid. She was then cycling together with an unknown man in the direction of the Buitenveldert neighbourhood, the police reported earlier this week. At that time the police and her family already said they were seriously worried about her well-being.

title: Thousands of insulin pens stolen from Novo Nordisk from a Dutch wholesaler
lead: Thousands of Novo Nordisk insulin pens were stolen from a Dutch wholesaler last week, the Danish medicine producer reports. The stolen pens could possibly be resold via illegal channels. Novo Nordisk warns of serious health risks if the pens are used incorrectly. According to the company, there is a chance the pens will be offered as weight-loss medication. The stolen pens do, however, contain insulin and not the active substance of weight-loss drugs, semaglutide. The company also produces the injectable weight-loss drug Wegovy. 'Do not buy it via illegal channels' Using insulin in people who do not have diabetes can lead to a blood sugar level that is too low. It can cause symptoms such as trembling, sweating and nausea. People may also become confused or even lose consciousness. This year someone was in a coma for several hours after using a so-called weight-loss pen that turned out to contain insulin. In the worst case, use can even lead to death. Novo Nordisk urges people to only use medicines if they have received a prescription for them from their doctor. "Medicines must under no circumstances be bought or traded via illegal channels, including social media, online marketplaces, gyms or informal networks." The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> is investigating the theft. According to Novo Nordisk, measures have been taken to prevent this from happening again.

title: Frustration and disappointment after announcement of cabinet infrastructure plans
lead: Frustration and disappointment can be heard from various corners of the country following the announcement of the cabinet's plans for maintenance and renewal of aging bridges, roads, locks and other infrastructure. Today <entity id="person:vincent-karremans">minister Karremans</entity> and <entity id="person:annet-bertram">staatssecretaris Bertram</entity> announced that a total of 18 billion euros will be set aside for this. A large part of that amount is being taken from planned projects, which will be postponed as a result. Among others, the widening of the Kornwerderzand lock complex in <entity id="org:provincie-fryslan">Friesland</entity> will not go ahead, and the accessibility of <entity id="org:gemeente-ameland">Ameland</entity> will also not be tackled for now. "Extremely disappointing," says acting mayor <entity id="person:tytsy-willemsma">Tytsy Willemsma</entity> of Ameland. She says it has been shown for "more than ten years" that this ferry connection is not sustainable. In 2008 the national government itself had urged the widening of the lock at Kornwerderzand, but that too will not go ahead for now. Sijbrand de Vries, director of De Vries Scheepsbouw, builds superyachts and has been waiting for years for a wider lock. He calls it "a hard blow." "This file has been on the table for so long." These are some of the projects for which money has (and has not) been allocated: Elsewhere in the country there is disappointment too. In Brabant, for example, improving the N65 between Den Bosch and <entity id="org:gemeente-tilburg">Tilburg</entity> has been pushed back indefinitely. "It is already the sixth time in barely three years," says deputy Stijn Smeulders to news agency ANP. 81 million euros had been reserved for the N65, "an important traffic artery in the heart of our province." The provinces <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity> and <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">Zuid-Holland</entity> and the Metropolitan Region <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> say they "had hoped for more vision for the future" from the cabinet in the choices that have been made. The provinces had hoped for more investment in widening motorways and public transport. "The cabinet assesses projects solely within the limited financial resources made available," reads a joint statement. The replacement of the HRMK railway bridge at <entity id="org:gemeente-leeuwarden">Leeuwarden</entity> will also not go ahead for now. Deputy Matthijs de Vries (ChristenUnie) tells news agency ANP that for Friesland this is "very painful." In <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> part of the long-running Zuidasdok project is being postponed. The project includes, among other things, the partial tunnelling of the A10 motorway at the Zuidas. For the northern section of the project there is, for the time being, no money. 175 projects renewed or maintained In total, the plans cover the renewal or maintenance of 175 roads, locks, bridges, viaducts and tunnels. Most of them were built in the 1950s, 1960s and 1970s, and in many places the steel and concrete, for example, have reached the end of their life. The cabinet is also allocating money for improvements to the rail network. For all projects that are not being carried out now, the cabinet stresses that they are "not off the radar." After the autumn recess <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> will debate the plans.

title: Dead woman in home in Beek en Donk, man (56) arrested
lead: In the Brabant village of Beek en Donk, near Helmond, a dead woman was found in a house at 02.00 hours. She is a 50-year-old woman who lived in Tilburg. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> assumes she died as a result of a crime. The police have arrested a 56-year-old man on suspicion of involvement in her death. The man is in custody and is being questioned, writes Omroep Brabant . Nothing has been made public yet about the relationship between the man and the woman. The police are conducting an investigation at the home: Images show that the glass panels of the front door are broken. According to the regional broadcaster, this was caused by the officers who entered the house overnight.

title: New setback for Ukraine: Trump puts sanctions against Russia on hold
lead: US President Trump is putting a sanctions package against Russia on hold for now. Those sanctions had already been adopted a month ago and signed by himself, but according to Trump it is in the interest of the United States to refrain from them now. It concerns the so-called Graham Act, named after the recently deceased senator Lindsey Graham. He campaigned for years for sanctions against Russia. The sanctions package included, among other things, that import duties of up to 100 percent could be imposed on the five largest importers of Russian oil or natural gas, such as China, India and Turkey. The sanctions also targeted Russian banks, officials and the shadow fleet. Trump signed it after a majority in Congress had also voted for the Graham package. It was seen as the largest form of support for Ukraine since Trump's return to the White House. In a decree, Trump now writes that the penalties will not come after all, at least for now. "I refrain from imposing the sanctions, restrictions and obligations laid down in the Graham Act." Although the act was already signed, the president claims entitlement to an exemption. That would be "in the national interest of the United States". Diesel deal Over the past week Trump has increasingly sought rapprochement with Russia. For example, last week he concluded a diesel deal with Russian President Putin. By his own account, this was to bring down global fuel prices. That drew global criticism from, among others, <entity id="person:rob-jetten">premier Jetten</entity>, who stated that Trump is thereby filling the Russian war chest. The US president also clashed with Ukrainian President Zelensky, who feels betrayed by the diesel agreement. Trump, for his part, stated that it was time for a new Ukrainian president. According to experts, the relationship between Trump and Zelensky has reached a new low. Trump is not doing well in the polls, with the midterm elections just around the corner. With his efforts to bring down fuel prices, he hopes to win voters over.

title: Podcast De Dag: train staff on suicide on the railway
lead: Talking about suicide in the media is extremely delicate, especially when it concerns suicide on the railway. The NS and ProRail are also very reticent in their communication about 'collisions on the railway'. Yet a large campaign has now been launched in cooperation with the foundation 113 Suicide Prevention, in which conductors, train drivers and ProRail staff, among others, talk about their experiences. Listening? You can hear this episode of De Dag via NPO Luister and all other podcast apps. Like it? Don't forget to subscribe. Nieuwsuur reporter Mitra Nazar spoke with railway workers about what happens when someone jumps in front of a train and what impact that has on them. Feedback? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation and editing: Elisabeth Steinz Editorial staff: Judith van de Hulsbeek Final editing: Rosanne Sies 113 Are you thinking of suicide or worried about someone? Talking about it helps and can be done anonymously via the chat at www.113.nl or by phone on 113 or 0800-0113.

title: Harry and Meghan back in the UK: questions about a quasi-royal life and state security
lead: It all looked rather 'royal', even though Harry and Meghan are officially no longer 'working royals'. A cheering crowd welcomed the couple on Thursday in Nottingham, where the two appeared together in public for the first time since their return to the United Kingdom . Selfies with the public, flowers and Meghan in burgundy, who said it is "wonderful to be back". It was just dull without her, concludes the tabloid Daily Mail. It has now been four years since 'Megxit': the dramatic departure of Harry and Meghan from the British royal family. What followed was an American celebrity life, with Netflix productions, podcasts and cooking programmes, a much-discussed interview with Oprah Winfrey and Harry's book Spare , in which he did not spare his family. Yet in August they returned to the English life they had received so much criticism for in recent years. Palace spokespeople stress that Harry and Meghan, now that they are back in the country too, are not working royals and will therefore not carry out any activities on behalf of the royal household. They are private individuals, it is said. Prince Harry will focus on his charity work and Meghan on her lifestyle products and acting career. Actually, nobody can really explain why they returned so suddenly. Even Harry's father, King Charles, reportedly was only informed a few days in advance. On second thought, does the couple want a half-in, half-out model, a kind of quasi-royal life? Do they want to reconcile with the royal family, or be closer to Charles, who is still being treated for cancer? Do they want to put their children in a British school, or were they inspired by their friends Beyoncé and Jay-Z, who also bought a house in the beautiful English Cotswolds? The questions about their intended lifestyle and 'non-royal' public appearances coincide with another prominent issue: their security. That matter is currently being reassessed by the RAVEC ( Royal and VIP Executive Committee ), a committee that falls under the British ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> and assesses who is entitled to security at the taxpayer's expense. It is a difficult file, with many complications and a high level of public attention. When Harry and Meghan were still working royals, their security was paid for by the state. After their departure from the royal household, that arrangement lapsed. Since then Harry has argued, including in court, for security for his family whenever they are on British soil. Harry is and remains the son of the king, and that was never a choice. And, like them or not, Harry and Meghan are world-famous and controversial ratings magnets who would be worth a lot of money if someone wanted to kidnap them. Their security would reportedly cost the state well over five million pounds, with daily operations in which all their routes must be checked for safety. The risks range from stalkers and dangerous individuals to even the Taliban, after Harry revealed in Spare that during his military service in Afghanistan he had killed 25 Taliban fighters. The other side of the argument is that state-funded police protection belongs to people with an official role and public responsibility, and as non-working royals Harry and Meghan currently do not have one. The couple runs commercial projects with which they earn their own fortune, so why should the taxpayer pay for their costly security? Against this, former prime ministers are entitled to state security after leaving office. That also applies to, for example, Liz Truss, who was prime minister for only 49 days. Why should she be, and prince Harry, who has been a prince his whole life, not? That is a difficult question. Harry offered to pay for his own police protection, but that was refused on the grounds that 'the police are not for sale'. According to experts, their situation calls for police protection rather than private security, partly because officers may carry weapons. According to a recent YouGov poll, a majority of Britons think the state should not pay for the security of Harry and Meghan. Their return to the United Kingdom is being received with some scepticism: 46 percent view it negatively. Older Britons in particular are critical of the couple, while Harry and Meghan are relatively more popular among young people.

title: From schoolchildren to yellow vests: France prepares for a day of mass protests
lead: Demonstrations, motorway blockades and actions at fuel depots: protests are taking place across France today. Schoolchildren and students, as in recent weeks, have again announced they will take to the streets, but this time they have company. Farmers, taxi drivers and, back after a long absence, the yellow vests are joining them. For <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> this is a decisive day: will the anger of the schoolchildren's protests spread further, and is France facing a new convergence des luttes in the coming months, in which different protest movements merge into one large mass protest? Half a million posts The date 17 October already circulated on social media in September, but it only really gained momentum with the rise of the schoolchildren's protests. Those are now entering their fourth week. According to data research commissioned by the newspaper Le Monde, more than 460,000 posts about '17 October' have been published on French social media. What makes this protest day especially remarkable is that diverse groups are joining forces: from young to old and from left to right. Actions have been announced by schoolchildren and students, but also by farmers' unions, firefighters, taxi drivers and nurses. Their reasons for taking to the streets vary, but they share one thing: growing discontent over rising costs of daily life and government policy. High fuel prices and falling purchasing power in particular are hitting French people hard in their wallets. Former leaders of the yellow vests have said they will join the protests. The government is watching this development with concern. In 2018 and 2019 the yellow vest movement, which at one point also spread to Belgium and the Netherlands, managed every Saturday to paralyse public life in France, among other things by blocking motorways and roundabouts. What began as a protest against high fuel prices grew into a broad popular movement. The protests regularly ended in large-scale riots. At the request of Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, Prime Minister Lecornu has therefore announced a crisis meeting for tomorrow with the ministries involved. They are taking into account that the protests could turn violent. Nuñez told French radio yesterday that he does not rule out the use of flashball grenades. Last week the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> stopped using one type of flashball grenade after a schoolchild lost his hand. He now appears to be backing away from that. "Officers must be able to use all the weapons at their disposal", Nuñez said. Although the government has tried in recent weeks to bring the schoolchildren's protests under control, including through heavy-handed policing and various concessions, this has so far achieved little. On Tuesday, once again hundreds of thousands of schoolchildren and students took to the streets. Government in a bind To meet the schoolchildren and the other demonstrators, the government has almost no financial room to manoeuvre. France structurally spends more than it takes in, so the national debt is sky-high and keeps rising. At the same time, investor confidence in the French economy is declining. This autumn the government therefore faces an almost impossible task: steering a budget with tens of billions in spending cuts through parliament. Cutting spending is urgently needed to get public finances back under some control, but it could fuel anger on the streets even further. The government is therefore in a bind. "On 17 October we are going to write history", a young person wrote on TikTok last week. Online, an interactive map is being shared on which people can register their protest action. The counter stands this morning at almost 1,800 actions. How many of those actions will actually get off the ground, and how massively people will turn up? That will become clear in the coming hours.

title: Wolf makes wild boar and deer on the Veluwe more alert: 'In the past there was little go in them'
lead: Wild boar, red deer and roe deer on the Veluwe have adjusted their behaviour in recent years to the presence of the wolf. That is the conclusion of the <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> Game Management Unit after monitoring. That organisation is responsible for counting wild animals and for any management through culling. Around a hundred wolves, spread across several packs, currently live on the Veluwe. Their presence makes prey animals more alert and affects how and when those animals move through the area, the research shows. Forest rangers and land managers recognise those changes. According to experts, wild boar show different, more natural behaviour. They move more often in larger groups, also called sounders, across the Veluwe. Sometimes they seek protection among large grazers, such as Highland cattle. It also happens that larger boars attack a wolf that tries to grab one of their young. Roe deer have also changed their behaviour. Before the wolf arrived, forest rangers could often predict fairly accurately where and when roe deer would graze in the forest. Now the animals move more through the area and are more often active in the evening and at night. The animals are monitored with cameras, and their changing behaviour can be seen there: Floris Leyssius, chair of the Vereniging Het Edelhert, sees that red deer have also become more cautious. In the first weeks after birth, hinds usually leave their calves alone in a sheltered spot. "When a red deer gives birth, since the wolf settled it is more often hidden at the edge of the area," says Leyssius. According to him, the calves are also suckled less often, so as not to give away the hiding place to the wolf. Forest ranger Frank Theunissen also sees risks for calves lying in a less sheltered spot. Red deer that leave their young in the centre of the wolf territory, according to him, have a greater chance that the calf falls prey to a wolf. Hunters still needed. On the Veluwe, wild animals are shot to limit the number of collisions and to give young trees the chance to grow. The wolf has an effect on wildlife populations, but according to the Game Management Unit that effect is not sufficient to reach the desired wildlife level without shooting animals. Wolves hunt, among other things, young animals such as calves of red deer and fallow deer. Although the wolf can slow the growth of wild boar populations, that does not mean it regulates the size of those populations to the numbers the province has set. On the Veluwe you see many positive effects from the arrival of the wolf, says Erik Koffeman of the Gelderland Game Management Unit, which coordinates hunting in the province. "For nature management the settlement of the wolf is very positive. For agricultural areas that is of course a very different story." Before it is clear how many animals must be shot, the animals on the Veluwe are counted. That has become more difficult because of the changed distribution and behaviour of the animals. The management of species also works differently. "Now that wild boar move in larger sounders, you can sometimes shoot only one boar in an evening. After the shot they are all gone," says Koffeman. More natural behaviour. Forest ranger Theunissen enjoys the changes brought by the arrival of the wolf. "Prey animals now behave much more naturally, before there was little go in them. Now that there is an enemy they are alert and sharp and more active."

title: 'Heeft u terug van 100?' Larger notes in cash machines seem to be catching on
lead: Shopkeepers have not been waiting for it for years, but the 100 euro note is making a comeback, for now. At 46 locations in the Netherlands, Geldmaat has placed the note in machines as a trial. It seems to be catching on. People withdrawing larger amounts often choose the green note. 57 percent of customers who are given the choice choose the 100 euro note. The more money is withdrawn, the more often this note is chosen. This suggests enthusiasm for the 100 note, and that is exactly what <entity id="org:zbo-de-nederlandsche-bank">De Nederlandsche Bank</entity> (DNB) together with Geldmaat is trying to investigate with this trial. Early next year a decision will be made on whether the notes stay in the machines. Prices have risen sharply. About one in five of all payments is made in cash. Before this trial, 50 euros was the highest note you could get from a cash machine. But is that still enough, now that inflation keeps making euros worth less? Since 2002, when the euro was introduced, prices have risen by about 70 percent. In other words, with a 50 euro note you can now buy much less than in 2002. Koen Thuis, head of cash policy at DNB, points out that in nearly all eurozone countries it is quite common to pay with 100 euros. "We want to see whether that need exists in the Netherlands too." Still, entrepreneurs are not always happy when you pull out a 100 note. "No, no, I get punished for that at the bank. Then they start asking questions, sorry", says, for example, a market trader in the Utrecht neighbourhood of Overvecht. Some fast food outlets also do not accept 100 euro notes. Change "Those shopkeepers are happy with the turnover, but a 100 note is not efficient", says Janwillem Burgering of the Nationale Winkelraad. "You soon run out of change if everyone pays with 100 euros." For that reason, De Nederlandsche Bank urges consumers mainly to pay for large purchases with the green notes. "Use them sensibly. Don't buy a pack of chewing gum with 100 euros." Next step: 200 euros? Notes of 200 and 500 euros also circulate in the eurozone. The latter are no longer issued by the central bank, but perhaps the 200 euro notes will come into view here too. "In other countries it is not unusual to pay with a 200 note", says Koen Thuis of DNB. "We are first doing research on the hundreds. You never know, it also has to do with how the euro's value develops. What the 50 euro note was, the 100 euro may become. If you then wait long enough, the 200 euro comes into view."

title: Albert Heijn had to report hack due to new cyber law: 'Responsibility reaches further'
lead: The hack at Albert Heijn is one of the first major incidents since the entry into force of a new law on cybersecurity. The law took effect in August and applies to thousands of important organisations. They are required to report high-impact cyberattacks, and directors can be held personally liable if companies do not have their cybersecurity in order. The law applies to government organisations and companies that are important for the Netherlands. Among others, healthcare, drinking water and banks fall under it. But also the food sector, with supermarkets for example. "It concerns sectors that are essential to keep the Netherlands running at all times", says Bart Scholten of advisory and inspection company Kiwa. "They must register with the <entity id="org:nationaal-cyber-security-centrum">Nationaal Cyber Security Centrum</entity> NCSC." Major incident must be reported The Cybersecurity Act ensures that the same rules apply to a range of sectors, says Joke Bodewits of law firm Hogan Lovells Cadwalader. "If all goes well, companies were already aware of cyber risks and the measures they had to take. This law brings new obligations." For example, companies are required to report (suspected) cyber incidents with major impact within 24 hours. This concerns, for example, situations with major financial damage. Or incidents that seriously disrupt services, such as what happened at Albert Heijn. The company shut down part of its IT systems when it became clear that something was wrong. Call for input Do you normally have your groceries delivered by Albert Heijn, but were unable to this week? And would you like to tell the NOS Journaal on Monday how you solved it? Send an email to economie@nos.nl with your experience, place of residence and telephone number. The consequences were significant: the Albert Heijn website and app became unreachable, and groceries ordered online could not be delivered. A number of distribution centres also came to a complete standstill, so Albert Heijn supermarkets had more difficulty being supplied for some time, said Albert Heijn chief executive Margaret Versteden-van Duijn on Monday: Reporting to the NCSC also means that an affected company can make use of the knowledge and expertise of the centre, says Bodewits. "There are very good and motivated people there, ready to help and think along with you. For example, to go through the signals that indicate you have been affected." After the initial report, companies must give the NCSC an update after 72 hours. "If you are hit by a cyber incident, a lot happens at the same time", says Bodewits. "It often turns out that something you thought was one way is actually different." Supervisor is informed The information received by the NCSC is also forwarded to supervisors who monitor compliance with the Cybersecurity Act. For supermarkets, this is the <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit</entity> (NVWA). "Supervisors check whether companies have taken the right measures", says Scholten of advisory firm Kiwa. "The Cybersecurity Act states that organisations must take 'appropriate' measures to prevent cyber incidents." What exactly is appropriate can vary from situation to situation. "You must at least try to prevent a cyberattack from happening, but also have a plan in case it does happen anyway." "That responsibility reaches further than the company itself", he says. "Around 8000 companies fall under the Cybersecurity Act, but many do not. These are, for example, smaller companies and the suppliers of large companies. If you do fall under the cyber law, you must map the risks of companies you do business with. That way you can, for example, set requirements for their cybersecurity." Directors are responsible If the supervisor suspects that cybersecurity was inadequate, it can impose penalties. Directors can even be held personally liable for this. This is probably only the case if they acted in a seriously culpable manner, or if there was intent, says lawyer Bodewits. "Directors are expected to try to prevent cyber incidents and to take the subject seriously." "The Cybersecurity Act makes cybersecurity a subject that must be handled at the highest level", says Scholten. "Companies and organisations can no longer say: this is something for the security or IT department. The subject must be discussed in the boardroom, with the aim of making the Netherlands more digitally resilient."

title: Prisoner has chicken nuggets, fries and drinks delivered by drone to Canadian prison
lead: A Canadian man managed to get chicken nuggets and fries from McDonald's, and alcohol, into his cell by drone. That is what the Canadian union for prison guards UCCO-SACC-CSN announced, reports broadcaster CBC . The drone was flown by unknown persons to the prisoner's window. The man is held in the prison complex near the city of Sainte-Anne-des-Plaines, on paper one of the most heavily secured prisons in the country. "The prisoner found it very funny when the guards found it in his cell", says a spokesperson for the union to CBC News. The union itself is extremely critical. The union has long warned about contraband. "We have reached a point where a prisoner has McDonald's delivered. What is the next step? A loaded gun? This scares us badly." In the extra secure section of the prison where the drone could reach, Canada's most serious criminals are locked up, comparable to the Extra Beveiligde Inrichting in the Netherlands. According to the union spokesperson, the motion detectors hanging at the prison did not go off. The news outlet TVA Nouvelles reports that one or more surveillance cameras were not working. The Canadian government has launched an investigation into the incident. Growing problem Drones are a growing problem for prisons worldwide, including in the Netherlands. This year in the Netherlands, for example, a man was convicted for dropping phones and drugs by drone at prison exercise yards. And in 2024, three men were arrested who had flown drones over Dutch prisons several times since 2021 and delivered items to order. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> announced in March that it wants prisons to be able to bring down smuggling drones themselves. To do so, the help of the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> still has to be called in. In the Netherlands, there have also been attempts to deliver a meal to a detainee. This week the Den Bosch police reported that the family of an arrestee had a meal delivered that was meant for their relative. "Although we thought the order looked very tasty, we cannot deliver it to the detainee", the police wrote on Instagram . "Besides posing a security risk, all detainees are well looked after by the colleagues at the cell complex with a morning, afternoon or evening meal. And of course this is simply not permitted."

title: Riots at protests in France, police deploy tear gas and water cannon
lead: After weeks of student protests, other groups also took to the streets in France today, including farmers, taxi drivers, nursing staff and the gilets jaunes movement. They protested against the rising cost of living. In several French cities the protests turned into riots. In Paris the police deployed tear gas and a water cannon. By around 15:00, a total of 272 people had been arrested across France. In Paris shops and a McDonald's were stormed, and in Lyon the tourist office was set on fire: people also forced their way into the town halls of Lille and Marseille. In Lille, among other things, glass doors were smashed. In Marseille, the second city of France, intruders painted an anarchist symbol on the wall of the town hall, destroyed televisions and threw a bust of Marianne (France's national symbol) to the ground. Mayor Payan of Marseille reacted furiously. "It is unacceptable to use this kind of protest to break in, commit vandalism and destroy this national symbol", Payan said. The damage in the town hall seems to be limited. The damage in the town hall of Marseille: in Marseille the windows of a police station were also smashed. Smoke bombs were thrown inside, the newspaper Le Figaro reports. No injuries are reported. 'Tragedy' in Lyon Besides Paris, the police also deployed tear gas in Bordeaux and Lyon. In Lyon masked rioters smashed the windows of the tourist office and set it on fire. Mayor Doucet is appalled. In his words it is an "iconic and recognisable monumental building. It is a tragedy that rioters have attacked this building and set it on fire." Despite the disturbances, the police in Paris say that "the vast majority of participants are demonstrating peacefully". Most rioters are gathering at the Place de la République, where a car was also set on fire. The French government had already anticipated riots. Anyone who looks like a demonstrator is being checked and must identify themselves. Around the Champs-Élysées a demonstration ban applies. Nevertheless, shopkeepers had placed boards in front of their shopfronts just in case. In advance, the French authorities expected 40,000 demonstrators in Paris, Le Monde writes. In the rest of France 150,000 protesters were expected. Around midday, 140 protests were counted in the French provinces, with almost 33,000 people taking part, the <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> ministry reports. Gilets jaunes movement The gilets jaunes movement was also present today. It arose in France in 2018 out of discontent over the announced increase in fuel prices and developed into a broader protest against the high cost of living and income inequality. For months, people in yellow vests took to the streets every weekend, and this was accompanied by a great deal of violence. The gilets jaunes movement was followed in Belgium and the Netherlands, among other places. For Salif and Jérémy, today was their first time in a yellow vest. They had come to Place de la République from outside Paris. "In the supermarket you now pay one and a half times as much as a few years ago, it is no longer manageable", they told NOS correspondent Saskia Houttuin. In Belgium there were also protests this afternoon. Pupils and students are opposed to the cuts in education. "I am protesting because my school's budget has been drastically reduced", says a student to the Flemish broadcaster VRT. In Brussels fireworks and stones were thrown at the police, and rioters damaged cars, including with road signs. Windows of a building were also smashed. Near Brussels-South station, shared bicycles and scooters were set on fire, just as last week. Officers deployed tear gas and a water cannon and cleared the Beursplein in the centre. Calm seems to have returned there. Ten people have been arrested. Rioters on a car in Brussels: the Belgian Minister of Internal Affairs, Quintin, has expressed his horror: "What is happening in Brussels has long ceased to be a protest", he wrote on social media. According to him it concerns organised and repeated violence, intended "to destabilise our society". In Liège demonstrators were also out. There too, the police deployed a water cannon after some time.

title: Man (81) dies after home robbery in Schagen, suspect arrested
lead: An 81-year-old man from Schagen (Noord-Holland) has died after he was robbed in his home. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has arrested a suspect. The suspect is a 36-year-old man with no fixed residence or place of stay. It is not yet clear what exactly happened in the house. The man was robbed at around 23.15 hours in the house on Groenling. He was seriously injured and died shortly afterwards in hospital, reports regional broadcaster NH . The suspect fled after the robbery. Officers blocked his car on an N-road between Heerhugowaard and Obdam. The suspect then fled on foot but was eventually arrested in Obdam.

title: Alberta goes to the polls: does Canada's richest province want to become independent?
lead: Canadian Prime Minister Carney once again addressed voters in the province of Alberta yesterday during a pro-Canada campaign rally. On Monday they go to the polls to vote on a secession from Canada. Carney's message to <entity id="org:kiesgerechtigden-nederland">het electoraat</entity> was clear: vote against secession. "This is no game. This is not poker. A vote against Canada is a dangerous bluff that will lead to years of uncertainty and missed opportunities for the people of Alberta and the rest of Canada," said Carney. He pointed out to his listeners that it is an open secret that US President Trump would very much like to annex Canada as the 51st state. "They are trying to break us" A vote for an independent Alberta would play into the hands of Trump, who is waging a trade war with Canada, reasoned Carney. "Some outside our borders are trying to break us so they can bring us under their control." According to Carney, this must "never" happen. Precisely because so much is at stake for Canada, the prime minister set out on a pro-Canada offensive to Edmonton, the capital of Alberta, where he grew up. Yet Monday's referendum does not yet give a definitive outcome. If a majority says "no" to the question of whether Alberta should remain part of Canada, then there will be yet another referendum in 2027. Only after that is the decision binding. As far as Carney is concerned, it will not come to that. As prime minister he wants to prevent Canada from falling apart, while Trump openly speculates about annexing the country. Over the past years Carney has therefore made a clear effort to strengthen ties with Alberta, after relations under his predecessor Trudeau had come under serious strain. For many separatists Trudeau was the face of the climate policy that they saw as pointless and that harmed Alberta's economic interests. Carney was therefore pleased that the federal government in Ottawa and the critical province of Alberta reached an agreement in 2025 on a more flexible energy policy for the large oil industry there and a new oil pipeline towards the west coast. Large economic interests are also at play. Alberta is rich in oil, natural gas and coal, among other things, and has a large agricultural sector. Alberta's oil reserves are among the largest in the world, which makes it by far the richest province in the country. A lot of oil and natural gas is exported to the US. That is precisely what makes separation from the rest of the country attractive to separatists. The vast province is home to only 5.1 million people, but because of its exports the province pays above-average taxes to the federal government in Ottawa. Criticism in Alberta has for years held that it sees little of these payments in return. The reasoning of supporters of a separate state is therefore simple: upon independence, no one in Alberta will have money worries anymore. In times of inflation, high fuel prices and a sluggish housing market, that is an attractive prospect for many. Additionally, the population of this agricultural province has traditionally had a soft spot for the US. Canadian media reported earlier this year that close ties exist between supporters of the split and the government of Trump and his MAGA movement. During the Forever Canadian gathering where Carney spoke, thousands of supporters of independence stood outside demonstrating. Banners were held up with texts such as: "Say no to Carney's new world order." A supporter said earlier to local media that he fears Carney will, in retaliation for the trade war with the US, additionally tax oil exports. Shoulder to shoulder Whether an independent Alberta will actually come about is very much in question. Polls consistently show that the vast majority of voters in Alberta want the province to stay in Canada. Only 30 percent of the electorate would support the separatists. Danielle Smith, the premier of Alberta, is not one of them. Although she and Carney sometimes have a tense relationship, she said during the pro-Canada campaign rally: "For the first time in a long time, Alberta and Canada stand shoulder to shoulder."

title: Police arrest suspect for explosion at hair salon in Vlaardingen
lead: The police have arrested a 27-year-old man from Vlaardingen on suspicion of involvement in an explosion at a hair salon. It was also a restless week in Vlaardingen, but the arrested man is suspected of involvement in an attack from just over two months ago. On 6 August, the windows of a hair salon in the city centre along the Rotterdam harbour were badly damaged after an explosive went off in the early morning hours. No one was injured, regional broadcaster Rijnmond reported. Last night things also went wrong at a hair salon. According to the police, shots were fired at a business at the Liesveld shopping centre after midnight. No one was injured then either. The police would not say, after questions from NOS, whether it concerns the same hair salon. There are several hair salons on Liesveld. Last weekend it also happened. An explosion damaged the facade of a hair salon on Westhavenkade and blew out a shop window. That business had already been a target of vandalism before. 'Unfair competition' It is not clear what the motive for the attacks is, but it is being speculated about. AD previously wrote that hairdressers with prices below the usual rates are targets. There would be unfair competition. The police and the <entity id="org:openbaar-ministerie">Openbaar Ministerie</entity> are still investigating the explosions. The 27-year-old man was arrested yesterday. They do not rule out further arrests.

title: French government says it will not be intimidated by violence on protest day
lead: French Prime Minister Lecornu says his government "will not be intimidated" by the violence at today's demonstrations. "No one will impose their political agenda through violence", the prime minister writes on X. President Macron says there is no place for violence in France and that those who misbehaved will be prosecuted and punished. According to Prime Minister Lecornu, peaceful demonstrations are permitted, but arson, looting and attacks do not belong to them. He expresses his support for the police, who in his view faced extreme violence. Across France, 1200 people were arrested. Also, 150 police officers were injured. Hundreds of thousands of French people took to the streets today out of discontent with the poor state of education, rising costs and government policy in general: Most demonstrators protested peacefully, but in a number of cities, such as Paris, Marseille, Toulouse, Angers, Lyon and Bordeaux, it turned into violence. Tonight the mood is still tense in several cities, including Paris, Toulouse and Bordeaux. Early in the evening, the historic city hall in Limoges was set on fire. The fire spread through one wing and the building is largely considered lost. The fire also reached the roof, after which the city hall tower collapsed: According to Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 550.000 people turned out at 110 demonstrations across France. The organizing action groups put the number at 800.000 participants. 'Organised by the far left' Many demonstrators indicate that rioters were deliberately out to cause damage and to confront the police. The rioters often targeted government buildings, such as town halls and police stations. In cities such as Strasbourg, Rouen, Nantes, Pau and Valence, shops were also looted, says Minister Nuñez. Lecornu and Nuñez accuse far-left groups of organising the violence. "And criminals took part in looting and vandalism", Lecornu writes. According to the prime minister, this is related to the French presidential elections, which are to be held next April. 'Vandals will pay' In his post on X he addressed himself explicitly "against those who want to use this violence as a 'warm-up' for the presidential elections". He promises the French that the vandals will pay. "Public money is scarce", he writes. "We must not endlessly repair the damage vandals cause. They must bear the costs." The mayor of Paris has also strongly condemned the violence in France. In an interview with France-Ouest, Mayor Emmanuel Grégoire says the protest has now overshot its goal. "The vast majority of demonstrators want to protest peacefully. These destructive acts distract attention", says Grégoire. "Vandalism is not a solution." It is not clear how many demonstrators were injured. The French news agency AFP reports that in the southern French city of Saint-Étienne a demonstrator lost a hand to a police grenade. Earlier this month a 15-year-old schoolboy suffered the same, which led to great criticism of the police's harsh conduct at the education demonstrations. The French police then stopped using flash-ball grenades. Nevertheless, Minister Nuñez of Home Affairs said yesterday on French radio that he did not rule out their use: "Officers must be able to use all the weapons at their disposal", he said.

title: Limoges city hall set on fire during French protests, tower collapses
lead: In the aftermath of large-scale protests in France, the tower of the city hall in Limoges has collapsed. The historic building had earlier in the day been set on fire by rioters. As in many other French cities, many people in Limoges took to the streets out of dissatisfaction with education, the cost of living and government policy. According to French media, several masked individuals in Limoges managed to enter the city hall by smashing a window. The building, dating from 1883, was then set on fire. That fire raged until late in the evening. Besides the tower, the roof of the city hall was also destroyed. According to the regional administrator, the building must be considered "largely lost". Mayor Guérin of Limoges addressed the perpetrators in a statement. "You will be arrested. You came here to kill. Everything is on camera." Earlier, police cars were also set on fire in the city and shops were looted. Monument The city hall of Limoges is on the French list of monuments and has great historical value for the Limousin region. During the Second World War, it served as a refuge for Belgian parliamentarians in exile, after Belgium had surrendered to the Nazis. Most French demonstrators protested peacefully, but in a number of cities, such as Paris, Marseille, Toulouse, Angers, Lyon and Bordeaux, it turned into violence. French Prime Minister Lecornu says his government "does not allow itself to be intimidated" by the violence at the demonstrations. According to Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 550.000 people took part in 110 demonstrations across France. The activist groups involved put the number at 800.000 participants. According to the authorities, more than 1200 people have been arrested and 150 officers were injured.

title: Eleven people unwell after tour of Grolsch factory in Enschede
lead: Eleven people became unwell after a tour of the Grolsch factory in Enschede. They have been taken to hospital for a check-up. According to RTV Oost, the people had tasted brewing water used to brew beer. The caustic substance sodium hydroxide may have been in it. The victims may have suffered internal chemical burns in their stomach, oesophagus and throat. Several ambulances were on site. A German trauma team was also called in, but that call was later cancelled. Investigation The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has started a forensic investigation to determine whether it really is sodium hydroxide. The <entity id="org:nederlandse-arbeidsinspectie">Nederlandse Arbeidsinspectie</entity> will also investigate the incident. According to Grolsch, it is unclear how this could have happened. The brewer says it is very shocked by the incident.

title: Four dead and dozens injured after explosion and fire at Canadian army base
lead: An explosion and subsequent fire at a Canadian army base in the province of Alberta have killed four soldiers, says Prime Minister Carney. Dozens of people have also been injured. The Canadian medium Global News earlier spoke of seven dead. According to Global News, live fire was being used during a military training exercise on the grounds in Wainwright when a gas pipeline or gas well was hit. The explosion caused a fire. The first report of it came in around 16.00 local time (just after midnight in the Netherlands). Earlier, Canadian Minister of Defence McGuinty spoke of a "very serious incident" in which "multiple dead and injured" have fallen. He did not give details. In a spoken statement he said he could not recall a recent comparable incident. 'A disaster' A doctor from Edmonton, which lies about 200 kilometres from the military base, told the Canadian broadcaster CBC that the medical facilities in Wainwright were "completely overwhelmed". He said the hospital in Edmonton where he works is also receiving victims. "There are more patients than we want to count at this moment," said emergency physician Warren Thirsk. "It is a disaster. A disaster that happens once every 15 to 25 years." He said an emergency protocol has been activated and extra medical personnel have been called in. According to Defence Minister McGuinty, the authorities of Alberta are working together with those of other provinces. Premier Moe of the neighbouring province of Saskatchewan wrote in a Facebook post that people have been sent to Alberta. Fire spread beyond the base The Wainwright military base lies about 200 kilometres southeast of Edmonton. It is one of the largest military training grounds in Canada. Due to the strong wind, the fire spread outside the complex, where the flames quickly spread before the fire brigade got it under control. Prime Minister Carney said his thoughts go out to "all the brave women and men who have been affected". Premier Smith of Alberta called the incident "serious and tragic" and said many soldiers have become victims. Moe said his thoughts go out to those affected, but also to "the first responders and those on the front line of this tragic incident".

title: Wake-up call 18/10: Pope prays again after surgery • Amsterdam Marathon
lead: Good morning! Pope Leo XIV is back at work and reads the Sunday Angelus prayer. And in Amsterdam the annual marathon is run. First the weather: this morning there is a lot of cloud and for some time rain falls, especially in the west and north. During the day it becomes drier and the sun occasionally shows itself in the south. It reaches a maximum of 11 to 13 degrees. Are you going out today? Here you can find the overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here everything about the situation on the railways. What can you expect today? What did you miss? During the large-scale protests in France, the town hall in Limoges, in the centre of the country, was set on fire by rioters. The tower of the historic building subsequently collapsed. As in many other French cities, many people in Limoges took to the streets to demonstrate for better education and out of dissatisfaction with rising living costs and government policy in general. According to French media, several masked people managed to force their way into the town hall by smashing a window. The building, dating from 1883, was then reduced to ashes. The fire raged until late in the evening. Other news from the night: And one more thing: Actor and presenter Maarten Spanjer has died at the age of 73. He had been suffering from bladder and prostate cancer for some time. As an actor he appeared in, among others, the cult film Spetters (1980) by Paul Verhoeven. He also became well known through the TV programme Taxi. In it, in the 1990s, he went out onto the streets. In the car he struck up conversations with passengers while a hidden camera was rolling. The best-known fragment dates from 1995, when he was driving back with Rijk de Gooyer after the Gouden Kalveren Gala and threw De Gooyer's freshly won Gouden Kalf out of the window onto the motorway. Have a nice day!

title: One dead in house fire in Terneuzen, several apartments uninhabitable
lead: A resident died in a fire in an apartment complex in Terneuzen last night. The victim is a 50-year-old man from Terneuzen, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. The fire on the Diepenbrockstraat was reported around 22.30 hours. Emergency services turned out in large numbers. A trauma helicopter was also called in, Omroep <entity id="org:provincie-zeeland">Zeeland</entity> reports. The fire was in an apartment on the second floor. Because of the scale of the fire, all residents of the apartment block had to leave their homes as a precaution. They were taken in at a sports hall. Uninhabitable Around 23.00 hours the fire brigade had the flames under control. A large part of the residents could then return to their homes. That does not apply to everyone, as a number of homes are temporarily uninhabitable. Replacement housing has been arranged for those residents. Mayor Weerwind visited the location last night to encourage the affected residents. Nothing has been made public about the cause of the fire.

title: After half a year of the Iran war, calm has returned to the Gulf states, but certainty has not yet
lead: After months of fighting in the Middle East, a certain calm has returned to the cities on the Persian Gulf. In Dubai, Doha and Abu Dhabi, schools, restaurants and offices are largely operating as before. Residents still feel safe there. Still, there is uncertainty about the future. Above all, the question of what happens between America and Iran after the American midterm elections of 3 November is keeping the Gulf region busy. In Dubai you would almost forget there was a recent war. The terraces and restaurants are full, there are traffic jams on the motorways, and new migrant workers are settling in the city again. Daily life is also continuing in Doha and Abu Dhabi. The rocket and drone attacks that hit the cities earlier this year have faded into the background. "With all the planned events, such as the World Investment Forum, Formula 1 and the Doha Forum, it seems we are 'back to normal' again," says a Dutch diplomatic source in the region to the NOS. Dark clouds Still, the calm is relative. The war with Iran is not over, but seems to have entered an intermediate phase. President Trump has said he does not intend to attack Iran again before the midterm elections. But what happens after that is uncertain. That recent escalation in Saudi Arabia underlines how fragile the calm is. During Houthi attacks from Yemen on Riyadh airport last week, at least 17 people were killed and more than 300 injured. The airport was closed and air traffic was seriously disrupted. In the article below you can read more about the tensions between both parties: That has turned the tables. Whereas Riyadh was earlier in the war still a refuge for residents of the Gulf states, residents of the Saudi capital are now moving to cities on the Persian Gulf to fly from there. Notably, the public warning system in Riyadh stayed silent for almost two weeks despite repeated attacks. Only on Monday did residents receive an air raid alert on their phones again. According to news agency Reuters, the constant warnings during the first attacks caused irritation, and the authorities feared they would disrupt daily life. Qatar too is taking dark economic clouds into account. Emir Tamim bin Hamad al-Thani warned that everyone, from government to citizens, must be prepared for "the worst conceivable scenarios". His words, together with the recent escalation in Riyadh, illustrate the dilemma of the Gulf states. After all, how do you keep the trust of residents and investors while the threat of new attacks persists? Safety as a selling point The Gulf states have invested billions over the past decades to attract foreign companies, wealthy migrants and tourists. Dubai grew into an international financial centre, Qatar invested in aviation, education and international events, and Saudi Arabia is trying with mega projects to make its economy less dependent on oil. Safety was the key asset in this. While wars raged elsewhere in the Middle East, residents of the Gulf states could count on stability. That image has taken a hit, but has not disappeared. When the first missiles and drones reached the Gulf in February, the shock was great. Meanwhile the sense of safety has returned and daily life is largely going on as usual. But especially among tourists and people outside the region, reluctance remains great. So the war seems to be not only a security problem for the Gulf, but also an image problem. Economic uncertainty For Dutch entrepreneurs in the region, the uncertainty is palpable. Disruptions to air traffic and shipping drive up costs, while tourism in particular is stalling. "Some small entrepreneurs have indeed packed up their things because there is simply no work here for the moment," says a Dutch consultant in Dubai, on condition of anonymity. Larger companies are also becoming more cautious, he notices. "I wouldn't call it panic, but people have become a bit more realistic about the situation here." According to him, concern about the consequences grows if the uncertainty lasts for months. For now normal life goes on and the cities on the Persian Gulf are "open for business". Children go to school, companies organise events and most foreigners see no reason to leave. But behind that normality lies the realisation that the future of the region is strongly influenced by what happens in Washington, Tehran and Tel Aviv.

title: France shocked after protest day with 'unprecedented violence' and 2,000 arrests
lead: "Uprising", "chaos", "the republic in flames", the French press headlines this morning. France wakes up to devastation after a day of large-scale riots. Streets are strewn with glass, fences, tear gas grenades, burned belongings and all kinds of other rubbish. Clean-up crews are trying to make the cities presentable again, shopkeepers are sweeping their own pavements. The total extent of the damage is not yet known, but that it is enormous is clear. On Saturday, hundreds of thousands of people took to the streets at at least 110 locations across the country to protest against government policy, the state of education and the rising cost of living. Looting The protests were largely peaceful, but in many cities the demonstrations attracted groups of rioters. In Paris, Marseille, Toulouse, Lille, Angers, Lyon and Bordeaux among others, the protests escalated into riots, vandalism and violence. Cars and bins were set on fire, countless shops were looted, from small supermarkets to upmarket stores. Demonstrators threw fireworks, stones and other objects at the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, which intervened with tear gas and water cannons. Security services in Paris report that there were 1,500 fires in public spaces. Sixty buildings have been on fire. Images of the damage on Sunday morning: According to Minister Nuñez of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>, 2,000 people have been arrested. The number of injured emergency workers now stands at 600. According to Nuñez these are still provisional figures. The police are still identifying more perpetrators. In Paris, 111 injured demonstrators have been reported. A demonstrator in Saint-Étienne, in central France, lost a hand to a grenade. 'Only the flag is left' Mayors, shopkeepers, politicians and people on the street are reacting with disbelief and horror to Saturday's riots. People are in shock at the "unprecedented level of violence", or are ashamed of what has happened in their country. In Limoges the last smouldering remains of the town hall are being extinguished this morning. The fire in the historic town hall, set by rioters, is under control, but the building dating from 1883 has largely been lost. The fire brigade rescued the French flag from the building and handed it to the mayor of the city. "This may be the only thing left of the town hall," he said. In daylight the damage to the building is clearly visible: Mayors of various cities are responding sharply to the events. They speak of a "wild horde", "violent groups that are only out for destruction" and "systematic looting". In several places it appeared that the groups were acting very methodically, authorities report. The French judiciary has started an investigation into the degree of organisation behind these groups. The mayors of the three largest cities - Paris, Marseille and Lyon - call what happened in their cities yesterday unacceptable. They want a conversation with Prime Minister Lecornu as soon as possible. Shopkeepers' associations demand financial support from the state. And a request for a parliamentary inquiry committee has also already been submitted. President Macron gives a speech this evening at 8 p.m. Police deployment The police too are reacting dismayed this morning. "We have been through hell," the police union tells Le Parisien. In some places the police seemed totally overwhelmed by the rioters. "Nobody came to help us." He points to the major staff shortage in the police. The deputy mayor of Paris speaks of a lack of resources for the police to stop this kind of scenes. At the same time, voices are also rising that disapprove of the heavy police intervention. "We have the right to fight for decent conditions at school without being hit by a grenade," says the mayor of Marseille this morning. Meanwhile, peaceful demonstrators are also fed up that their protest has been overshadowed by violence. "All those men in black with masks have no placards, they have no demands, and that makes everything we have to say invisible," says a demonstrator to FranceInfo. "I have a placard. One for the environment and also for a fairer distribution of prosperity." Some say to French media that they hope the demonstrations will continue despite the violence. In France, a day after the major riots, the damage is being assessed:

title: 'Fryslân's oldest communist' and longest-serving councillor Rinze Visser (87) has died
lead: The Frisian politician Rinze Visser has died at the age of 87, the Communist Party of the Netherlands (CPN) reports. Visser was the longest-serving municipal councillor in the Netherlands and at the same time one of the last communist elected representatives. Visser was elected as a councillor for the communist party in the municipality of Lemsterland in 1970, which later merged into <entity id="org:gemeente-de-fryske-marren">De Fryske Marren</entity>. He remained a councillor for more than 55 years, but in March of this year he did not stand for re-election due to his deteriorating health. In the 1970s Visser was also a member of the <entity id="org:provincie-fryslan">Friesland</entity> Provincial Council. Visser grew up in Lemmer. Through his father he came into contact with communist ideals at an early age. At home De Waarheid, the party newspaper of the CPN, was read. At the age of 21 he became a member of the party, writes Omrop Fryslân. "A better world and a better distribution of wealth", was how he described his motivation at the time. "And putting an end to the powerlessness of a large group in the community." Change of course In the 1980s the CPN wanted to merge into a broad progressive movement. Because Visser disagreed with this change of course, he switched in 1985 to the Verbond van Communisten in Nederland (VCN). After various regroupings, Visser returned to the CPN. Because Visser could count on a lot of support in Lemmer and surrounding areas, he was re-elected fourteen times in a row. In the municipal elections of 2022 he ran for the last time as lead candidate for a new four-year term. "The voice we make heard is more relevant than ever. Income differences have never been this large", he said at his fourteenth installation. No successor With Visser's decision not to stand for re-election in the elections this spring, communism disappeared from Frisian politics. The party could not find a successor. "Rinze remained loyal to his ideals and principles throughout his life, also in the difficult years of the counter-revolutions in the socialist countries or when his health made the work difficult", the CPN writes. "Rinze continued to fight steadfastly from the conviction that a better, socialist future is necessary and possible."

title: Danish cleaner trapped for more than three days in underground cell
lead: A Danish cleaner was locked in an underground cell for more than three days last month. The Danish newspaper Ekstra Bladet reports this. The woman was cleaning in the former Supreme Court building in Copenhagen when a cell door in the basement accidentally slammed shut behind her. These doors cannot be opened from the inside. No phone on her The woman, whose age has not been disclosed, did not have a phone with her and therefore could not call for help, the newspaper writes. Knocking on the door was also pointless, because the building is only used sporadically. The Supreme Court was previously located in the historic building, but a few years ago it moved to another part of the city. The building in the city centre is sometimes still used today by the Copenhagen District Court. The building is near Amalienborg Palace, where Danish King Frederik lives with his wife Mary and their four children. The world-famous statue of the Little Mermaid is also within walking distance. Man alerts police The incident with the cleaner happened just over a month ago, on Wednesday 16 September at 18.00. The woman's husband had been away for a few days and discovered upon returning home that she was missing. He then began a search and found her bicycle at the historic building in the city centre. He then alerted the police. After her release, the woman was taken to hospital. After the incident, all cell doors were checked and the locks replaced, the newspaper writes. From now on, cell doors can only be locked from the outside. The cleaning company the woman works for says the employee has received psychological support. "The employee is doing well under the circumstances and has returned to work at their own request", the company wrote in a response to the newspaper. Belgian politician stuck on toilet for thirteen hours The story of the Danish woman recalls an incident in Belgium that happened at about the same time. Belgian politician Frédéric Erens was stuck on the toilet for thirteen hours last month because the lock turned out to be jammed. He also did not have his phone with him. Erens could not sleep because, in his view, the space was too small. Early in the morning, the man was discovered by a cleaner. "There is no point in getting annoyed. It could have happened to anyone."

title: Trump's new voting law was already tested in Kansas in 2014 and it turned into chaos
lead: The American president Trump wants voters to present proof of citizenship and their passport before they may cast their vote in the midterm congressional elections at the start of November. In the state of Kansas this was already tried. It was a dismal failure, and tens of thousands of eligible voters fell victim to it. When Steven Fish from Ottawa, Kansas, wanted to register as a voter in 2014, he had to show his birth certificate. He had no idea where to look for it. The document could be with his stepfather, but he had fallen out with him. And where should he request the original? The military base where he was born had already closed in the 1990s. It may sound strange to the Dutch, but many Americans do not have their birth certificate on hand. Even more: half do not even have a passport. In Kansas there are even fewer. Voters who did have their documents in order also ran into problems. "Women also had to show a marriage certificate to explain why their name differed from the one on their birth certificate," recalls Micah Kubic of civil rights organisation American Civil Liberties Union (ACLU). The ACLU stands up for fundamental rights and civil liberties. Tad Stricker did have all the required documents when he applied for a driver's license in Kansas City, and was immediately registered as a voter. But nobody asked for them. When he reported to the polling station, it turned out he was not on the electoral roll. He was allowed to fill in a provisional ballot, but it was not counted: his vote was lost. Fish and Stricker were not the only ones affected by the rule: research showed that the registration of 30.000 residents of Kansas had been wrongly blocked. And the remedy proved worse than the disease: only a few dozen non-citizens had registered, often through misunderstandings. A handful of them had actually cast a vote. "It was certainly not worth losing tens of thousands of votes for that," says Kubic of the ACLU. The figures match the national picture. Even the conservative think tank Heritage Foundation found, over a quarter century and more than a billion votes cast, no more than ninety examples. "The consequence for such fraud is prison or deportation, and almost nobody takes that risk," says Lana Nott of the Campaign Legal Center in Washington D.C. So it usually does not seem to be malicious intent. For example, a mayor in Kansas voted for Trump several times while not being a citizen. Joe Ceballos is of Mexican descent and, as a permanent resident of the US, does have a 'green card'. He says he was not aware that he was not allowed to vote. Ceballos resigned as mayor and was sentenced to a year of suspended imprisonment and a fine. Shortly afterwards he was nonetheless arrested by the immigration service ICE. He has since been released on bail, pending his hearing. Republicans, however, point to a recent scandal in the Democratic state of New Jersey. There, due to a software error, 6600 residents were wrongly registered as eligible to vote. 400 of them actually cast their vote as well. Two million dollars to repay: Steven Fish and Tad Stricker therefore could not cast their votes after all. With the help of the ACLU they sued the state of Kansas. With success: in 2018 the judge declared the rules unconstitutional. Kansas had to repay the plaintiffs almost two million dollars in legal costs. The state appealed, but the higher courts also reached the same conclusion. That meant the end of the 'SAFE Act', as the law in Kansas was called. But through President Trump the law is getting a new life, under an almost identical name: the SAVE Act. Trump is trying to get it through Congress with all his weight, after his presidential decree with similar requirements had run aground in court. This spring Trump even refused to sign other legislation as long as his own party did not rally behind the SAVE Act. Still, there is so far no majority for it in <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>, although a dozen Republican states have already introduced similar rules. In half of those states the rules already take effect at the upcoming midterms. For Steven Fish it feels like déjà vu. "It is shocking that our voting rights are being undermined again, with the same rhetoric." For Tad Stricker too it feels like a repeat of the same moves. "We have seen this film, and its ending, already," he says. According to Stricker, voters are being deprived of the right to vote for political motives. He fears it will become harder, especially for immigrant Americans, to register as voters. "If I, as a middle-aged white man, am already a victim, how will it turn out for naturalised immigrants?" But even if the rules are not introduced, Trump can use this politically. If Republicans suffer defeat, he can again claim there was election fraud.

title: Macron lashes out at rioters in TV speech as riots continue in Paris
lead: One day after the demonstrations that completely got out of hand in Paris and other French cities, French President Macron lashed out at the rioters in a televised speech. He said that those who caused damage "must pay". "We will not compromise", he added. He also said he wants the damage caused to be recovered from the perpetrators of violence. "Whoever caused damage must pay. Whoever looted must compensate the damage", he said. He explicitly pointed to far-left groups in the country. "Whoever wanted to bring down the Republic will be held accountable." Macron clearly distinguished between the demonstrators who protested peacefully yesterday, and the looters and arsonists. "We must never confuse demonstrators with legitimate demands with those who caused damage. Their voice must be heard without prejudice and without trivialising the problems." 'Firmly uphold order' He further called the violence "unbridled" and "not justifiable". Besides in Paris, yesterday, after weeks of pupil protests, people also took to the streets in at least 110 other places in the country to protest government policy, the state of education and rising costs of living. In many places this went orderly and calmly, also in Paris, but where it went wrong, it also went badly wrong. In Limoges the 19th-century town hall was set on fire, after which the tower collapsed. In Marseille the bust of Marianne, the symbol of the French Republic, was destroyed in the town hall. Also, many cars and buildings were set on fire across the country and there was widespread looting. According to the French Ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> 2397 people have been arrested. In his TV speech Macron said he understood the demonstrators' problems. "Our responsibility is therefore twofold: listen to the anger and address its causes, and firmly uphold republican order." However, he did not announce concrete measures to curb the ever-rising cost of living in France. Excerpt from Macron's TV speech: He did point to the conflict in the Middle East as the main cause of price increases in French supermarkets and at the pump. Tomorrow his three-day tour of the Gulf states begins, he then emphasised. He promised the French people that he is continuing his efforts to secure France's fuel and gas supply. Finally, he called on all political parties and social organisations to unequivocally condemn all violence. "The country needs order and reconciliation, not escalation." It remains to be seen whether that will happen. Centre-right presidential candidate Bruno Retailleau finds Macron's speech "very disturbing", he writes on X. According to him, Macron should have declared a state of emergency to "protect the French people". Paris senator Yannick Jadot calls the performance a "terrible demonstration of powerlessness". "Our country is like a drunken ship without a captain taking water from all sides." Unrest again in Paris While Macron addressed the rioters, it was again restless in the streets of Paris. As early as the afternoon, the public order police had to intervene at Place de la République. They deployed tear gas to disperse dozens of masked participants in a demonstration not registered with the city council. A message had circulated on social media calling to "continue the movement". Several French media reported that it then quickly got out of hand again. In the centre of the French capital shops were looted, and many large fires were set. Footage shows dozens of young people destroying the stone fountain around the Monument to the Republic and then throwing debris at the police. After the Paris police, as yesterday, deployed the CRS 8, an elite unit of the French police specifically trained in combating urban violence, the rioters spread into surrounding streets. Especially on the busy Faubourg du Temple street, which runs from Place de la République to the northeast of the city, it got out of hand between youths who tried to make themselves unrecognisable with hoods and the law enforcement services. French newspaper Le Monde reports that rubbish bins are still being set on fire and the rioters are using electric bicycles to build burning barricades. Shops close Also the paper writes that at the start of the evening youths entered a tobacco shop and looted it. Yesterday this shop was also a victim. The owner was in her shop at the time to protect it against the rioters. Eventually she had to be taken to hospital with a head wound. The district mayor of central Paris calls on X for shopkeepers to close their shops. He speaks of vandalism and arson that have flared up again.

title: More than three hundred new arrests for looting in Paris
lead: In Paris yesterday and overnight another 351 people were arrested. The French police report this. According to the police, the group consists of young people who tried to vandalise and loot shops. According to the French news site 20minutes, demonstrators also threw glass bottles at officers.
