The weather forecast for the area is highly uncertain because the signal from the <entity id="org:koninklijk-nederlands-meteorologisch-instituut">KNMI</entity> radar in the Betuwe is disrupted by a row of poplars. For now, it is not allowed to prune or fell those trees. First it must be investigated whether there are bats, reports Omroep Gelderland . The Netherlands has two precipitation radars, one of which is in the Betuwe, specifically in Herwijnen. The KNMI uses the data from those radars for the weather forecast in apps such as Buienradar. But the fast-growing tall poplars near the radar turn out to affect precipitation forecasts in part of Gelderland: much more or much less rain falls than the radar indicates. Pulses blocked: That is because the trees block the pulses sent out by the radar. It concerns a strip from Herwijnen towards Germany, running between <entity id="org:gemeente-arnhem">Arnhem</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-nijmegen">Nijmegen</entity> and across <entity id="org:gemeente-doetinchem">Doetinchem</entity>. The problem has been going on for some time. At the end of last year the KNMI asked the <entity id="org:gemeente-west-betuwe">gemeente West Betuwe</entity> for permission to prune the trees. But the municipality has not yet granted permission. "We cannot intervene directly," says a spokesperson for the West Betuwe municipality. He points to nature protection legislation. The poplars may be part of a foraging area or flight route of bats. "These areas and routes are protected," says the spokesperson. Next steps: Ecological research has in the meantime been carried out into what role the trees play precisely for bats and what consequences a possible "intervention" would have. The results are expected soon. Based on the outcome, the next steps will be determined, says the municipal spokesperson. Meanwhile the KNMI is applying corrections to compensate for disturbances in the radar image. To do so, the weather institute uses radar scans at greater height, which as it were look over the trees. Data from other radars in the Netherlands, Belgium and Germany are also used. In the corrections, the radar scans of the area behind the row of trees are not included in the forecasts, says a KNMI spokesperson. "But it remains desirable to have as few disturbances as possible."

title: Porn on hacked billboards along highway in Egypt
lead: Hackers this week showed pornographic footage on digital billboards along a major highway in the Egyptian city of Giza, a suburb of Cairo. The footage has since been taken offline. The billboards originally displayed advertisements for an international company, writes the Egyptian ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> . However, the website of that international company was hacked, allowing the hackers to broadcast the pornographic footage. The company was able to restore the website and has also taken the footage offline. The authorities say they have taken legal steps in response to the incident. Footage of the incident is circulating on social media. Drivers on the highway in question are filming from their cars or from the side of the road. The pornographic footage carried the text "Leaked by: Ch, 19ylegal never and nivex" and the name of the Telegram account Leakersgov . That channel shares, among other things, photos of the billboards and articles about the hack. 'Dictatorship' "Egypt is still a dictatorship", the hacker group writes on the channel. "The government maintains its power through repression, while the country struggles to move forward." The group calls on the government to "change its priorities and commit to the population". In 2013 army chief Sisi seized power through a military coup. Under him the country has become an authoritarian state, according to Freedom House among others. There is almost no room for opposition or criticism of the government. Demonstrating is also almost impossible. Although the Egyptian constitution guarantees press freedom in the country, this is far from reality. This week the critical, independent news site Mada Masr was banned by a judge. 'Digital security is a joke' Little is known about the hacker group. The group says it created the Telegram channel to show that digital security is "a total joke worldwide". "The media want to portray this attack as a very sophisticated, state-sponsored cyberattack", the group writes. "But the truth is that your digital infrastructure is shameful, wherever you are." The group says it will share more footage of hacks worldwide, and the reactions to them, in the group. It is unclear what exactly is meant by this. "Welcome, the show is international."

title: Dozens of arrests in The Hague, no major demonstrations in the Netherlands
lead: The Hague is quiet again after a turbulent day. Although the looting that was feared has not materialised, 34 arrests were made on and around the Malieveld. People were arrested for wearing face coverings or for possessing illegal fireworks, a police spokesperson said. <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> was out in force in the city because of possible youth protests. In various places people were searched and had to show identification. This happened on and around the Malieveld, near Centraal Station, at the Spui and on the Grote Marktstraat, among other places. An emergency order is in force in that area, which earlier in the day applied only to the shopping district. 'Manageable' The police urged people not to come to the city centre. According to the police, the number of people in the city did increase during the day. Earlier in the day the municipality had described the situation as "manageable". It mainly concerned small groups of young people, reporter Edwin van den Berg observed: Dozens of people had gathered on the Plein to protest. Some demonstrators carried a Prinsenvlag. The orange-white-blue flag was used by the NSB among others and is now a symbol of the far right. The hard core of football club ADO Den Haag was also present on the Plein. Yesterday it announced that it would protect the city and local businesses. On social media, supporters wrote: "We are not against violence; in fact, it is our hobby. What we do not tolerate, however, is the looting of our city, the destruction of cultural heritage or any other form of vandalism." Shops boarded up As a precaution, many shopkeepers boarded up their façades and kept their shops closed. Although it remained fairly quiet in a large part of the city centre, businesspeople in The Hague estimate the damage will likely run into the many thousands of euros, mainly due to lost income. On the Korte Voorhout it was briefly tense: On the Korte Voorhout the Mobiele Eenheid intervened to prevent a confrontation between ADO supporters and a group of young people. The supporters were sent back to the Plein by the ME. Good-natured in <entity id="org:gemeente-maastricht">Maastricht</entity> In Maastricht too, account was taken of violent demonstrations and there was a large police presence. There too, a number of shopkeepers had boarded up their façades as a precaution. The day passed in Maastricht without incident, a police spokesperson said. No arrests were made and the atmosphere on the Vrijthof was good-natured. In <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity> demonstrations were also expected. No large groups of people have gathered there either.

title: Mexico challenges Panama Canal with railway across narrowest part of Mexico
lead: A new overland trade route in Mexico is nearly finished. A railway line in the south of the country is meant to serve as an alternative to the Panama Canal, the most popular trade route through Latin America. Like a huge brown snake, a train stands along a quay in the south of Mexico, while a strong sea wind from the Pacific Ocean relentlessly lashes against the carriages. In the background, an enormous hangar is being built from the ground up. Next to the train stand machines operated by men in white helmets and orange vests, pouring concrete over a large sandy plain. Today the train is not running, but it stands on the construction site as if to remind everyone of the reason this port is being expanded. Corredor Interoceánico The Mexican city of Salina Cruz is the starting point of this train, which every day will carry goods from container ships coming from Asia to the other side of Mexico, to the port city of Coatzacoalcos on the Atlantic Ocean. From there, container ships can take the goods to the east coast of the United States or even further, to Europe. The project is called the Corredor Interoceánico. Over the coming years it is meant to grow into a trade route of global scale. It should also serve as a solution to logistical problems that transport companies between Asia and Europe, among others, are facing. The narrowest part of Mexico The route crosses the narrowest part of Mexico, an isthmus of 200 kilometers, in the economically less developed southeast of the country. A first test already showed the speed and efficiency of the project: 900 cars from Hyundai's South Korean car factory were transported by train to the Atlantic Ocean within a day last month. Had the ship moored off the coast of Panama to take the Panama Canal, it would have taken much longer. That canal is still the most popular trade route through Latin America, but its locks are struggling to handle the huge numbers of container ships. 'Dry canal' In addition, the Panama Canal has been hit by drought in recent years. The water level fell so low that fewer container ships could pass and shipments faced delays of several weeks. The authorities in Mexico call their alternative trade route a 'dry canal', which offers transport companies the same passage through Latin America, from one ocean to the other, but without the vulnerability of the Panama Canal. European interest There is already interest from Europe. "We have already concluded an agreement with Portugal for the use of this route, and we want to extend that to the rest of the European Union," says Pascual Rosario Sepúlveda Soto, one of the coordinators of the project. A benefit for Dutch companies too? The Dutch trade organization Evofenedex calls the railway in Mexico an interesting alternative to the Panama Canal. In addition to the drought, the American president's wish to control the canal also plays a role. "That creates uncertainty," says policy adviser Elmar Otten. An alternative is therefore "certainly welcome". Whether Dutch entrepreneurs will actually use the Mexican railway depends on factors such as price, reliability, capacity and the suitability of the seaports. "If all of that is in order, it is an attractive alternative," said Otten. Apart from the train and the ports at both ends, the <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> wants villages and towns along the route to benefit as well. Ten industrial parks are to be established so that companies can load and unload goods along the way, for example to get closer to the sales market in the United States. It is a huge economic boost for a region that is much less developed than northern Mexico. Investments needed Although the train is running and the ports are being expanded quickly, the remaining infrastructure still needs to be improved, emphasizes Daniel Méndez Sosa, mayor of Salina Cruz. He points out that the federal government mainly puts its money into the ports and shows little concern for the towns. "This project can only work if all authorities cooperate. As a municipality, we do not have the money for large investments, for example in roads. If those investments do not come, the project will not get very far," says the critical mayor from his office on the square of Salina Cruz. Nevertheless, he has no doubt about the enormous potential of the project for his city. "Salina Cruz will become one of the most important cities in Mexico and the whole world with this project," he says confidently. "With this route we save time and offer companies economic benefits, also close to the US. And one of the poorest regions of Mexico can benefit from the industry that will grow here."

title: Rotterdam builds unusual bridge, of value to cancer patients
lead: A new pedestrian bridge was installed today at the Erasmus MC in Rotterdam. It is a striking bridge about one hundred meters long, partly clad in wood, which is of great value to cancer patients. The bridge directly connects the Daniel den Hoed Family House with the cancer ward of the Erasmus hospital. This means cancer patients and their families will no longer have to cross a busy road. "This has been long awaited," says Heidi Leeuwangh of the family house, enthusiastically, to broadcaster Rijnmond. "It's hugely important. Our guests are very involved with it." 'Faster and more comfortable' Construction of the bridge began last September. "Family members can get from one side of the road to the other much faster and more comfortably," said alderman Pascal Lansink (VVD) at the time. "Imagine your loved one is in hospital and is very ill. Then you really want to be there in time, for example to say goodbye." The family house offers a temporary 'second home' for family members of cancer patients. This way they can be close to each other during treatments. Patients can also stay overnight in the house. Like the family house, the bridge is named after Daniël den Hoed, the doctor who was one of the pioneers of radiotherapy in the Netherlands in the late 1930s. In use in December The bridge has been partly financed by KWF Kankerbestrijding. The foundation has donated 1.1 million euros. A large part of that amount was raised during the Rotterdam Marathon in 2023. The municipality, together with the Daniel den Hoed foundation and the Erasmus MC, is paying the rest. The bridge cannot be used immediately. Over the coming weeks the bridge will be fitted out. "The expectation is that the bridge will open in mid-December," the municipality reports.

title: Protests in dozens of French and German cities, riots in Paris and Frankfurt
lead: In dozens of French cities there was a demonstration for the third weekend in a row. By far the largest rally was in Paris, with around 70,000 participants according to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>. In various cities, riots broke out in the course of the afternoon and early evening. The police deployed tear gas and arrested people. In addition, there were youth protest marches in at least thirty German cities. Across Germany there were tens of thousands of participants. In Berlin and Cologne around 5,000 demonstrators, says the German police. 'Infiltrated by extremists' After the demonstrations ended, rioters took over in several cities. They reportedly deliberately mingled with the demonstrators, writes the German Tagesschau. Things got out of hand especially in Frankfurt. There, shop windows were smashed, shops were looted and officers were injured. Around midnight the police reported having made thirty arrests. Officers were present in large numbers in the city centre until deep into the night. In Cologne too, officers intervened after the demonstration, when riots broke out around the cathedral and the central station in the evening. The Cologne police chief called it "sad and very distressing that young people who wanted to demonstrate peacefully for their future were today infiltrated by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". See here how the protest day unfolded in a number of French and German cities: At least 290 people have been arrested across France, the ministry of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> reports. At the height of the day the demonstrations drew over 300,000 participants according to the national authorities. That is somewhat fewer than at the mass protests of the past two weekends. According to the organisers, there were now nearly half a million participants in the protests across the whole country. Protest marches largely peaceful The official protest marches were mostly peaceful. Halfway through the afternoon, dozens of arrests had been reported in France, and later in the day the mood turned. In parts of Paris, masked people dressed in black took action, reports the news site Franceinfo. Video footage from broadcaster BFM shows officers being pelted and police using tear gas, not only in Paris but also in cities such as Lyon and Marseille. Out of fear of a repeat of the large-scale unrest on 17 October, tens of thousands of officers were deployed. A protest march through the centre of the French capital had been banned in advance. Instead, demonstrators had to follow an alternative route through the suburbs of Paris. Dozens of metro stations were closed as a precaution. Halloween costumes and masks Across the country, around 150 Halloween demonstrations had been announced in advance. The protest actions by pupils, students and yellow vests coincided with the Halloween festivities. Participants played along with Halloween by dressing up, as here in Paris: Minister Nuñez of the interior warned in advance that wearing masks is prohibited. Rioters trying to hide behind a face disguise risked a fine of 150 euros. The demonstrators have for weeks been expressing their discontent over various themes. Campaigns are being waged against rising living costs, police violence and for better facilities in schools, among other things. At the same time, there is also protest against racism. The immediate cause for this is the racially motivated attack recently in a Paris suburb. Some arrests in the Netherlands Calls for demonstrations have also been made in other European countries in solidarity with the protesters in France, but also calls for looting and violence. The call found the most response in Germany. On and around the Malieveld in The Hague, dozens of young people were arrested this afternoon. They were wearing face coverings or carried fireworks, but in the Netherlands there were no large-scale protests.

title: Police apologise for passing on identities of activists to wholesaler
lead: The police have apologised for passing on the personal data of seven animal rights activists to catering wholesaler Hanos. "It has been established that there was no adequate legal basis for this disclosure," a police spokesperson told RTV Utrecht. In other words, the law does not allow the name and address of the activists to be shared with the store. The police have asked Hanos to delete the data and all copies of it. On 15 July the activists entered the wholesaler in Nieuwegein with protest signs and a megaphone to loudly demonstrate against the sale of foie gras. Foie gras is made by force-feeding geese. Because this involves animal cruelty, production is banned in the Netherlands. Import and sale are however permitted. Hanos employees intervened and forcibly removed the activists from the store. One of the demonstrators later filed a report with the police, because she allegedly had been assaulted. Still a store ban: When the activists discussed the action in a car park nearby afterwards, police officers asked the group to identify themselves. Seven of them did so, but said they did not consent to sharing their data with Hanos. The eighth person refused and was taken to the station. After the incident the police informed the activists in writing that the data had not been shared with Hanos. But when the seven activists who had shown their ID cards received a two-year store ban from Hanos, it became clear that it had. "How does Hanos get that data?" activist Kelly asked aloud afterwards in a video on Instagram. According to the police spokesperson, it is still unclear why the police passed on the data. He points out that what went wrong is being examined internally.

title: No deal with opposition on tax plan, debate in House of Representatives on Wednesday
lead: The minority cabinet-Jetten has not been able to reach a deal on support for the tax plan. <entity id="org:kabinet">Het kabinet</entity> spoke again today with seven opposition parties, but this did not lead to any agreements. Meanwhile, time is running out. A House of Representatives debate on the package of measures is on the agenda for Wednesday. "It is exciting. The homework is not finished, the time pressure is great and there is still no majority," 50Plus leader Jan Struijs summed up the situation. He was at the Catshuis this afternoon with Mirjam Bikker of the ChristenUnie to talk about their possible support. "That we are standing here on Saturday afternoon, that elaboration still has to follow, and that it is clear that majorities still need to be found on a number of points, worries me," Bikker added. The ChristenUnie and 50Plus are working together in the talks with the cabinet. They cannot help it reach a majority, but with the support of, for example, the Groep Markuszower, it adds up enough. Bikker and Struijs do, incidentally, think that the cabinet has listened well to them regarding their wishes for the elderly, chronically ill and ordinary, hardworking families. They say that steps in their direction have been taken in this respect. Pro leader Jesse Klaver came out very differently. He said that the cabinet is increasingly drifting away from Pro and Volt, which together could help the cabinet reach a majority in the House of Representatives and the <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity>. "The political will to work together with us is not there," he stated today. Volt leader Laurens Dassen also stated that it will no longer be possible to find a majority by Wednesday and that it now comes down to the debate. According to him, "people who see the bill mounting at the end of the month" are not being accommodated sufficiently. The opposition parties that came to the Catshuis today point out that the tax plan must be sent to the House of Representatives by Tuesday at the latest, so that the parliamentary groups can prepare for the debate on Wednesday. It will be voted on on 12 November, a week later. After that, the plan still has to pass through the Eerste Kamer. And then the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity> still needs to have sufficient time to prepare the tax measures, which take effect on 1 January. Besides Pro and Volt and the ChristenUnie and 50Plus, the cabinet also spoke this afternoon with the new 'bondje' of JA21, SGP and BBB. These three parties said this week that they want to support the tax plan if a number of hard demands are met. Among other things, they want commitments on asylum, nitrogen, abortion and surrogacy. The coalition parties D66 and CDA quickly said they were not interested in this. The three opposition parties are disappointed about this and did not come to the Catshuis today. They did, however, consult digitally with the cabinet and were much more positive afterwards: "We are not there yet, but we do see points of contact to continue talking." According to them, the "route to a majority with the right-wing parties" still remains open. They themselves speak of "a realistic option with a chance of success", but behind the scenes of the consultation it is said that there was little movement.

title: Red or blue? Republicans walk a tightrope to keep voters
lead: From Alaska and Texas to large parts of the American Midwest, Donald Trump won there three times in a row without much effort. Yet deep-red Republican states now seem able to turn Democratic blue. In the final days before the congressional elections, Republicans have to pull out all the stops. "These are the most crucial elections of our lives," says Ashley Hinson, a Republican congresswoman. She hopes to claim a vacant Senate seat for Iowa. There is no certainty: in the polls she is neck and neck with her Democratic challenger. "Who has already voted?" Hinson asks the people in a motel meeting room in Coralville. Most of the fifty people present raise their hands. She can count on most of the people here. The motel is located on the I-80, the highway that connects the west and east coasts of the US. New York and San Francisco, the start and end points of the highway, are blue: there people always vote Democratic. In between, certainly in states like Iowa, Kansas and Nebraska, the red of the Republicans is dominant. This year the Republicans are having a hard time, in an election that seems mainly to become a referendum on Trump's policies. Hinson brushes aside concerns about that. "I think we are going to win," she says. "Many people feel that the American dream is unaffordable. We will bring prices down." But with prices at the pump staying high, voters no longer accept that message. "At first it was supposed to be a six-week war, and now it has been going on for six months," someone sighs. "Iran is one of my biggest frustrations." But that is no reason not to vote Republican: "No, I'm not that worried." Tricky tightrope act That frustration puts Republican candidates in a dilemma. In a tricky tightrope act, they increasingly try to distance themselves somewhat from Trump, but not so much that they let 'their' president down. "I want the war to end immediately, with a good outcome," says Hinson. Her voting record does not reflect that: as a congresswoman she has already voted six times against ending the war with Iran. She did not want to limit Trump's power, she said at the time. Now she does not want to go into that. "We must focus on measures that provide relief." Petrol prices Under pressure from voters, congressman Mariannette Miller-Meeks recently did vote for ending the war. The Republican is not doing well in the polls. She is working on her third term in the House of Representatives for Iowa, but risks losing her seat to a Democrat. "Are petrol prices somewhat higher than I would like? Yes," says Miller-Meeks. "But are we better off than two years ago? Absolutely. We don't want to go back to open borders." She does not mention that inflation is now higher than before the war with Iran. When Trump visited Iowa this year, he saw prices of less than 2 dollars at the pump, he proudly said. Now the average is more than 4 dollars on the signs. "Your petrol and oil prices will drop again," Trump said recently. Costs many millions Together with the other 'battleground states' Alaska, Kansas, Maine, Michigan, Ohio and Texas, Iowa plays a key role when it comes to <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>. That is why enormous sums are being spent. For the federal races, candidates in Iowa themselves already raised over 80 million dollars. Analyses by the federal election commission show that in addition, 240 million was spent by outside organisations. The big money behind the American election battle In this special we explain how much money is pumped into election campaigns and where all those millions end up. Texas, which is much larger, stands head and shoulders above the rest, from the hundreds of millions that billionaire Elon Musk put on the table alone. Calculated per voter, Iowa, like the sparsely populated states Alaska and Maine, is far above Texas. Persuading voters So much money is not spent in neighbouring Nebraska, but it is also tense there. In Fremont, campaign volunteer Kim Stabbe goes door to door with her sister to persuade voters to vote for Dan Osborn, a former union member. "People in Nebraska are worried about high costs. Petrol and diesel prices, especially for farmers, because it is harvest time," says Stabbe. Asking committed Republicans to vote for a Democrat is difficult, but as an independent candidate Osborn is still considered to have good chances. "There are many people here who belong to the MAGA cult, it is extremely hard to get someone out of that," says Stabbe. In most places the door stays shut, at most someone peeks through the window. "Everyone is fed up, they are being overwhelmed with ads. We walk for two hours through the neighbourhood and are glad if two people open the door," she laughs. "But every vote counts." By the end of the afternoon they seem to have success. "I am a committed Republican, but I am fed up with it," says an older woman in her garden. "I cannot rule out that I might still vote for him." Listen to our podcasts about the US midterms Ahead of the midterms on 3 November, NOS colleagues from the Washington Bureau are making new episodes of the podcast Amerika Kiest. Listen to them via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Or listen via another audio platform

title: Mostly minors arrested in The Hague, no major incidents
lead: In The Hague, 34 people were arrested today for, among other things, disturbing public order, wearing face coverings and possessing illegal fireworks, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. According to the police, mainly minors aged between 15 and 18 were arrested, from among others <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>, Beerta, Lemele, <entity id="org:gemeente-zwijndrecht">Zwijndrecht</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-zwolle">Zwolle</entity>. An officer was injured when illegal fireworks were thrown at the police. The officer was taken to hospital with possible hearing damage. Several groups of young people had called on social media in recent days to come to The Hague for demonstrations and looting. It mainly involved small groups of young people, reporter Edwin van den Berg saw. According to the police, no major incidents occurred. However, around 15.00 hours "the atmosphere became grim for a moment" when demonstrators and the hardcore of football club ADO Den Haag faced each other. Then "we acted decisively and prevented The Hague from being looted or vandalised", according to the Hague police. In the city centre many officers were on the streets all day. Various measures had also been taken, such as an emergency order in the city centre. This was later extended to the Malieveld and the station area. 'Worrying' <entity id="person:jan-van-zanen">Burgemeester Van Zanen</entity> says the situation has remained controllable thanks to the heavy police deployment. However, he considers it worrying that this was necessary. He also expressed his thanks to the police and the ME for their deployment.

title: Soviet Ereveld in Leusden defaced again, slogans against communists
lead: The Soviet Ereveld in Leusden has been defaced again. The war memorial and the memorial wall have been smeared with paint, the Stichting Sovjet Ereveld reports on its website. The texts on the memorial wall are in red paint, and the texts on the monument, an obelisk, are in black. They include "Not against Russians, but against commies", "Dutch government = commies" and "Fuck refugees". The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> does not yet know who is behind the defacing. In July, the cemetery was also defaced. At that time, besides the memorial wall and the obelisk, 150 graves were also smeared with paint. The paint had soaked into the porous stones, and it took the greatest effort to remove it. "Tragic and sad. We are in consultation with the authorities involved", says Remco Reiding, director of Stichting Sovjet Ereveld. "We hope a solution will be found that prevents this from happening again." Respectful commemoration 865 victims of the Second World War are buried at the war cemetery. They are soldiers of the Red Army, prisoners of war, forced labourers and deserters who died in various ways across Europe. Some died of hunger, disease or exhaustion, others were executed by firing squad. "We remain committed to respectful commemoration of these war victims and to telling their stories", says Reiding.

title: Ethiopian Prime Minister Abiy sends ministers to military training
lead: For <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> of Ethiopia, today was not about meetings but push-ups. Prime Minister Abiy Ahmed had sent his <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> to military training. He took part himself too, as seen in photos the prime minister shared on social media. Leadership requires iron discipline, said the prime minister of the East African country. Ministers and state secretaries must therefore undergo "intensive military training". He did not say how long the exercise will last. This is an unusual decision by Abiy, the BBC writes. It is rare in Ethiopia for senior government officials to undergo military training. It is unknown how the prime minister came up with the idea. Ethiopia has 130 million inhabitants and the country is plagued by military conflicts. Various armed groups are fighting for greater autonomy or independence against the government army. Fighting is taking place, among other places, in the northern region of Tigray, where a bloody civil war already raged between 2020 and 2022. Tensions with Eritrea. Tensions between Ethiopia and neighbouring Eritrea have also risen sharply. The two countries recently severed diplomatic ties and a new war is feared. Abiy concluded a peace agreement with President Afwerki of Eritrea in 2018. A year later, the Ethiopian leader was awarded the Nobel Peace Prize. After the civil war in Tigray, which led to a hundred thousand deaths, there was strong criticism of the awarding of the peace prize to Abiy. His government was accused by UN human rights experts of committing war crimes. The Ethiopian government rejected these accusations.

title: FBI: North Korea behind billion-dollar theft from crypto platform Binance
lead: The FBI holds North Korea responsible for the theft of more than 6 billion dollars in cryptocurrency from trading platform Binance. According to the US security service, a hacker unit directed by North Korea converted the stolen bitcoins into ethereum, another cryptocurrency, and "further laundering stages" may follow to erase traces. Early last year the FBI also named a North Korean hacker group as the perpetrator after a hack at the popular crypto exchange ByBit. In that attack, 1.5 billion dollars in digital money was stolen. That heist was then considered the largest ever in the crypto world. The FBI describes this new form of cybercrime with the term "TraderTraitor". According to the security service, these hackers act quickly and spread their stolen cryptocurrencies across thousands of addresses to make them harder to trace. '90 percent reimbursed' The FBI's statement follows a day after the news about the latest largest crypto theft ever. In the digital theft at Binance, the world's largest crypto platform, hackers reportedly made off with an estimated 6.3 billion dollars in cryptocurrencies, equivalent to just over 5.6 billion euros. In a new update, Binance states that it has reimbursed 90 percent of the stolen crypto to users by buying new crypto with its own funds. The company says it also wants to compensate the remaining 10 percent, but is taking more time for that. "Users will not suffer any financial harm from this incident", co-owner Richard Teng said in the statement. Binance, the global market leader, is keen to retain users' trust. Reports of the historic hack led to sharp drops in cryptocurrency prices, although the decline of the largest cryptocurrency, bitcoin, ultimately remained limited to a few percent. No license in the Netherlands Crypto experts who spoke to NOS do not expect many Dutch people to trade on the Binance platform, because it did not receive a license a few years ago from regulator <entity id="org:zbo-de-nederlandsche-bank">DNB</entity>. Binance then withdrew from the Dutch market in 2023.

title: The Hague becomes a marathon city as running craze grows
lead: In The Hague a marathon is being held today for the first time in years. Nearly 10,000 participants are at the start this morning, making it the third-largest marathon in the Netherlands, right after Rotterdam and Amsterdam. Like many other marathons, the one in The Hague sold out within a few days. This fits a broader trend that has been going on for longer: running the 42.195 kilometres in a competitive setting is in vogue. The marathon calendar in the Netherlands keeps expanding. The growing popularity also raises the question of whether this leads to extra pressure on medical aid posts. The Red Cross supports the medical aid posts at large marathons such as The Hague's. According to the aid organisation, demand for assistance has increased in recent years. Mainly more people are being treated for heat illness. Too many layers. Overheating doesn't only occur on extremely hot days, warns first aid guidelines specialist Cees van Romburgh of the Red Cross. "Heat illness, or in serious cases heatstroke, can also occur during the Midwinter Marathon in Apeldoorn in February, for example," he says. "When it gets colder, you see athletes wearing more layers, but that isn't always better." He gives pure nylon as an example, a synthetic fabric that doesn't breathe. As a result, sweat evaporates less well and the body has more difficulty losing heat. This way a runner can overheat. Wall of heat. Also high humidity, little wind, strong sunshine, poor preparation or too high race pace can cause a person's body temperature to rise too high. "Keep drinking enough. Your body needs fluid to shed heat and cool down," he says. And: "Listen to your body and step in if it doesn't feel right. Finishing a race should matter more than setting a personal record." Some marathons, such as those in Leiden and Utrecht, run partly through rural areas and partly through the city. As soon as runners return to built-up areas they sometimes hit a "wall of heat," says Van Romburgh. "The body then doesn't get the chance to gradually adjust to the higher temperature. Even well-trained people can then get heatstroke." To be better prepared for heat illness, the Red Cross has extra equipped its volunteers. Think of cooling baths and cooling with towels soaked in ice water. Today 120 Red Cross responders are present at the Hague marathon. Also so-called bikers, responders on bicycles, talk with runners to check whether they are doing okay. They transport ice and towels. In The Hague twenty are riding around today. Ambulance rides. The ambulance is usually only called in when transport to hospital is needed and there is a serious medical situation. The Rotterdam-Rijnmond Safety Region reports that the number of ambulance rides for participants in the Rotterdam marathon is not recorded. During the Eindhoven marathon, the deployment of ambulances fluctuated between 2021 and 2026 between forty and fifty times, with an outlier of 75 in 2025. That does not only concern marathon runners. Bystanders and other people who needed medical help in the city centre during the marathon weekend are also included, says the GGD Brabant-Zuidoost. So that does not give a good picture of the number of serious incidents. Van Romburgh also says it is difficult to say whether a growing number of participants also leads to more medical incidents. "But in general more people take part, so the number of people for whom something can go wrong also increases." A positive development is that spectators increasingly recognise when a runner is not doing well, for example when they start to stagger. According to Van Romburgh, the public is better informed. "They ask, for example: are you okay?" Because the alarm is raised sooner, responders can also intervene faster. "We are glad about these extra feelers." More events in The Hague. The Hague has had a running classic, the City-Pier-City Loop, since 1975, with the half marathon as its main distance. In 1998 there was a city marathon to mark The Hague's 750th anniversary. In 2013, 2014 and 2015 marathons were also held, but on a smaller scale than today. The sports weekend in The Hague began yesterday with walks, runs of 5 and 10 kilometres and a kids' run. In total around 21,000 people take part in the various events, says spokesperson Michel Butter. "That is nothing but good news, because events like this bring people together."

title: Night of looting and fires in Frankfurt after day of peaceful protests
lead: In several German cities large-scale peaceful protests yesterday turned violent at the end of the day. Especially in Frankfurt things got badly out of hand. Windows were smashed, shops looted and fires set. According to Die Welt, even a gun shop was cleaned out. Officers were also pelted, including with Molotov cocktails. More than 100 officers have been injured, the German news agency DPA reports. The Zeil shopping street, just over a kilometre long and one of the busiest in Germany, was completely closed off. Until deep into the night a special police unit was active to keep rioters in check. 54 people have been arrested, says DPA. Earlier, 100 arrests had been reported. The demonstrations in Germany were aimed, among other things, at better education and affordable housing. In Frankfurt the rioters reportedly deliberately mingled with the demonstrators during the day, writes the ARD. According to a reporter they presumably did not take part in the protest marches. He saw several small groups running amok, which made it difficult for the police to get the situation under control. Earlier in the day there had also been clashes between police and demonstrators in the city, according to the police. Officers were pelted with fireworks, stones and bottles, and people were injured too. Minister-president Rhein of the state of Hesse, where Frankfurt is located, is shocked by the violent scenes. He says the perpetrators will be punished. "Anyone who behaves like the attackers in the centre of Frankfurt places themselves outside our society." State minister Poseck of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> also says he will deal hard with the rioters. "We have seen images we did not want to see. We need swift and decisive action against those who ignore our rules and attack our entire society." He says far-left extremists and violent youths joined forces and took to the streets. Cologne, Berlin and Hamburg Peaceful protests also got out of hand in other cities. In Cologne, police intervened after the demonstration, when riots broke out in the evening around the Cathedral and the central station. The Cologne police chief called it "sad and very distressing that young people who wanted to demonstrate peacefully for their future were infiltrated today by extremists who had nothing but violence in mind". In Berlin and Stuttgart stones and fireworks were thrown at the police. Incidents were also reported in Hamburg, Bremen and Karlsruhe. The organisers of the demonstrations had in fact called for a non-violent protest. Many tens of thousands of people marched in various German cities. There were also protests in France again, as in recent weeks. In Switzerland there was unrest as well. The police in Zurich say a crowd attacked officers with fireworks, stones and bottles. People piled up barricades from rubbish bins and electric scooters, which they set on fire. Officers responded with water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets. In Basel public transport came to a standstill in the evening because a group of people walked through the centre and set things on fire there.

title: Hundreds of thousands of cars on the road despite possible defects, here is what it means for your car
lead: Hundreds of thousands of passenger cars are driving around in the Netherlands even though they should actually be checked or repaired by a garage. These are cars subject to recalls that the <entity id="org:zbo-rdw">RDW</entity> classifies as "ernstig". Occupants run a risk of more serious consequences in accidents, for example due to problems with the airbags. For one in five affected cars, the problem can by itself cause an accident, for example because the battery catches fire. Car owners sometimes keep driving for years despite an open recall. For example, Daihatsu Materias are still on the road whose bolts around the steering wheel may not be properly secured, a recall that started nineteen years ago. Repair is free. <entity id="person:vincent-karremans">Minister Karremans</entity> of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-infrastructuur-en-waterstaat">Infrastructuur en Waterstaat</entity> is considering a law to oblige motorists to cooperate with recalls. "Het gaat om je veiligheid en om die van je gezin, het is echt belangrijk dat dit gebeurt." Improving registration. Continuing to drive may have consequences for insurance coverage, warns the Verbond van Verzekeraars, although that depends on the circumstances. Check here whether your car has an open recall. The data is delayed, so recent repairs may be missing. According to the RDW, it concerns just over 400,000 cars, although the exact number is not certain, the agency itself notes. Both repaired cars and affected cars may be missing from that count, because there is no obligation to supply that data correctly. As far as Karremans is concerned, that registration must first be improved, as must communication with car owners. "We hebben nu geen goede grip op dit probleem en over hoeveel auto's het precies gaat", he says. If that does not work, the minister is considering an obligation for consumers to cooperate. Of the open recalls, in seven out of ten cases the problem is protective equipment. This concerns, for example, seatbelts, airbags, the so-called Isofix attachment for child seats, or head restraints. Most recalls for protective equipment now come from airbags of the Japanese company Takata, which supplied airbags to various car manufacturers that turned out to be able to explode. As a result, deaths have occurred abroad. An estimated 160,000 cars in the Netherlands are driving around with such a vulnerable airbag. Other recent examples are the hybrid Ford Kuga, with a battery that can catch fire, and the Volvo EX30, whose head restraints can come loose. Owners of the latter recall will be informed next week. Other countries are stricter. The problem with recalls has been known for some time; back in 2019 <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>-Rutte III promised improvement. At that time it was also investigated whether vehicle owners could be obliged to have their cars repaired and whether manufacturers could be obliged to provide better information. In other countries stricter rules apply: for example, in Norway, Denmark and Germany manufacturers can face sanctions if they do not meet the conditions for recalls. In Denmark, Germany and Finland car owners can receive fines if they do not have defects repaired. The car trade organisation Bovag supports an obligation for vehicle owners, just like the RDW and the Inspectorate for Living Environment and Transport. The number of recalls of affected cars fluctuates, but there is no clear rise or fall: people could then be banned from driving on public roads with an unresolved problem, just as happens with an expired <entity id="org:zbo-erkenninghouders-algemene-periodieke-keuring">APK</entity>. The registration with the RDW does need to be better than it is now, Bovag also believes, because otherwise people could wrongly be given a driving ban. Consequences for insurance. Continuing to drive with an open recall can cause problems for your insurance coverage, warns the Verbond van Verzekeraars. An open recall is not enough on its own, but depending on the circumstances it can be. That could be the case, for example, if someone knowingly keeps driving with a warning light on the dashboard caused by a known problem. In such a case, the car owner would have to pay for the damage in an accident themselves. The most important thing is that people get the chance to have a problem repaired, the insurers also emphasise, and that this actually happens. And if not, then "vinden wij het goed dat aanvullende maatregelen worden onderzocht om dit te verbeteren". Methodology. For this article we used publicly accessible data from the RDW. Specifically for the estimate of the number of cars with still vulnerable Takata airbags, we used an AI model to estimate whether or not a recall was related to Takata. This concerns the so-called Jev classification model. We verified that estimate with several large language models, such as models from Claude and OpenAI, and by hand.

title: Democrats benefit from concerns about corruption: 'We must stop greed'
lead: Government corruption has quickly grown into one of the most important themes in next Tuesday's US congressional elections. Voters are worried about politicians who enrich themselves at the expense of the public. In some polls, corruption even ranks above the high cost of groceries and fuel. Democratic candidates are now trying to win votes by linking economic dissatisfaction to government corruption. "I call it treason," says Democratic candidate Shannon Taylor to a room full of voters. With an outspoken anti-corruption message, she is trying to win a Republican congressional district for the House of Representatives. It earns Taylor loud applause in the library of Yorktown, Virginia. She hopes to spark a new revolution here. The district has been represented for almost twenty years by Republican Rob Wittman, but Taylor has managed to create a neck-and-neck race. 'The swamp is getting deeper' Democrat Taylor accuses her opponent of corruption. She claims, for example, that he voted for tax breaks from which his own companies profited. "The corruption in Washington D.C. lets politicians like Rob Wittman enrich themselves instead of putting your interests first." She points to Wittman's shares, which have become considerably more valuable during his time in office, documents show. Wittman disputes the accusations. Still, Taylor's promise to tackle corruption firmly appeals to the audience. "The government promised to drain the swamp," a visitor says, referring to President Trump's well-known slogan Drain the Swamp. "But the swamp just keeps getting deeper." Another adds: "We must stop the corruption and the disgusting greed and culture of grabbing." Corruption at the top of the list of concerns Concerns about corruption and misuse of government money are not exclusively a theme for Democrats. But because of the role of billionaires like Elon Musk, who spent nearly half a billion dollars in these elections to get certain Republican candidates elected, Democrats can use the theme well to their advantage. In addition, nearly two-thirds of Americans believe that Trump is using his presidency to enrich himself. According to Forbes, Trump has become more than 2.7 billion dollars richer since the start of his second term, partly thanks to crypto and stock trading. "The scale of the corruption and conflicts of interest is staggering," says Virginia Canter. She advised the Obama and Clinton administrations on ethical issues and now sees how Trump has blurred the norms around conflicts of interest. "He has tried to normalise it, and he doesn't hide it." She points to the "gifts" Trump received: the plane worth 400 million dollars from the Qatari royal family, and the hundreds of millions in donations from companies with interests in the federal government for the construction of Trump's ballroom. In the library, Taylor is by no means the only one using corruption as an election theme. "I have never seen such shameless corruption in America," sighs senator Mark Warner. The Democrat has represented Virginia for seventeen years in <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and is campaigning together with Shannon Taylor. "I have tried to regulate cryptocurrency. That is difficult when the president uses it to enrich himself." In a campaign ad, Warner stresses that Trump alone earned 636 million dollars from his crypto memecoin. "That is not governing but money grabbing!" Who fights corruption best? The political battle is not only about who is guilty of corruption, but also about who can fight it best. According to a CNBC poll, voters have more trust in the Democrats than in the Republicans on this, although the difference is small: 35 percent versus 31 percent. And so in the final weeks, both parties are trying to capitalise on the theme. For example, the Trump administration opened a reporting point before the elections where people can report suspected fraud with government money. Anyone who files a report can receive up to 30,000 dollars in tip money. In the library in Virginia, Taylor also tries to reach Republican voters. With some, it seems to work. "I think there is corruption in both parties, but there is almost no accountability," says a conservative visitor.

title: Injured in fight and stabbing on bus in Breda, 17-year-old boy arrested
lead: In Breda, two groups of young people came to blows late last night. One boy suffered a stab or cut wound during this, and another was beaten up. One suspect has been arrested, a 17-year-old boy. A number of young people wanted to take the bus in the west of the municipality, in Prinsenbeek. They passed another group, from which remarks were made. The atmosphere turned grim and when the young people boarded the bus, one of them was pulled outside by his clothing. A scuffle then broke out in the doorway of the bus with someone who came to help his friend. At one point the driver closed the doors and drove off. The 18-year-old who wanted to help his friend noticed in the bus that he had a bleeding wound. He had presumably been stabbed or cut. Transferring money The victim who was pulled off the bus was beaten up by the group. He was also forced to transfer money to the bank account of one of the attackers. The father of this attacker reported to the police station with his son a little later to turn him in. The 17-year-old boy has been arrested and the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> does not rule out further arrests.

title: The Hague wants to recover financial damage to shopkeepers from instigators
lead: The Hague alderman Richard de Mos (City Centre and Economy) wants to look into whether people who called for violence in The Hague this week can be held liable for the damage suffered by entrepreneurs. Out of fear of riots and looting, shopkeepers boarded up their shops before the weekend. This was done following posts on social media. Via platforms such as Snapchat, Telegram and Instagram, young people were urged to take to the streets in Dutch cities on Saturday and protest. Calls to protest were also made in The Hague. Shopkeepers in the city centre expected severe riots. Many entrepreneurs therefore had their shopfronts boarded up as a precaution and remained closed yesterday. On Friday evening carpenters were hard at work on the emergency request. Although it was restless in the city yesterday, the situation remained manageable. Many officers were on duty and 34 people were arrested in and around the Malieveld. All arrestees are free again, according to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>.  'Not over yet' "It is a huge relief that the feared looting did not happen," says De Mos. "But that is not the end of it. Is it not absurd that hardworking entrepreneurs have to barricade their shops because people on the internet call on others to smash everything to pieces?" Entrepreneurs in the city centre speak of many thousands of euros in damage. Not only because of the costs of boarding up windows and doors, but also because of lost turnover since the shop was closed. Shops that were open lacked customers. The police yesterday urged people not to come to the city centre. "Why should the bill be left with the entrepreneurs?" said De Mos. The alderman wants to examine, together with entrepreneurs' organisations and lawyers, which options exist to recover the damage, writes Omroep West. It is so far unclear who posted the calls for the so-called Gen Z protests.  Boy from Middelburg The police have arrested at least one minor from Middelburg on suspicion of calling for violence. The boy was picked up at home on Thursday by the Dienst Speciale Interventies (DSI). Plainclothes DSI officers led him away blindfolded. The suspect was found because he called for violence under his own name. Violent demonstrations were also taken into account in <entity id="org:gemeente-maastricht">Maastricht</entity>. The day passed without incident, says a municipal spokesperson. Demonstrations were also expected in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity>. No large groups gathered there.  Looting in Germany In German cities there were demonstrations yesterday. That started peacefully but at the end of the day turned into violence. Especially in Frankfurt things got out of hand: windows were smashed, shops looted and fires set. In Switzerland too there was unrest. There, according to a spokesperson, a crowd attacked police in Zurich with fireworks, bottles and stones. And in France demonstrations took place for the third weekend in a row. Around 290 people were arrested across the country.

title: Hundreds more people arrested at Palestine Action protest in UK
lead: British police arrested 325 people at a Palestine Action protest in London yesterday. The action group has been designated a terrorist organisation by the British government and has been banned since July last year. People are regularly arrested at protests. That also happened yesterday in southwest London, in front of the American embassy. Demonstrators carried signs there with texts such as "I am against genocide, I support Palestine Action" and "We are demonstrators, not terrorists". The vast majority of arrests were made for "expressions of support for a proscribed organisation under terrorism legislation", according to the police. Ban back before the courts On Wednesday the British High Court will consider whether the ban on Palestine Action is justified. The case came before a lower court in June this year, which upheld the ban. The court said that although the ban was "highly controversial", Palestine Action "openly promotes unlawful violence amounting to terrorism". Activists of Palestine Action were previously sentenced to prison terms for a raid on an arms factory and for hitting a police officer with a hammer. Members also reportedly splattered military aircraft with paint. The group had not distanced itself from those acts, which weighed in the court's verdict. The Palestine Action issue continues to occupy minds in the United Kingdom. At the end of September, more than 160 people were still arrested at a protest outside the building where the Labour party conference was being held in Liverpool. Dutch nationals were also arrested there. In total, according to the organisation Defend Our Juries, more than 4000 demonstrators have been arrested since the ban came into force. Recently, the books of Irish bestselling author Sally Rooney were removed from sale in the United Kingdom because of her support for the group. Because she can therefore no longer receive royalties, her publisher has decided not to print any new editions of her books.

title: Wolf Bram stuffed at Naturalis, not everyone is happy about it: 'Take me instead, not him'
lead: Problem wolf GW3237m, shot dead last year on the <entity id="org:gemeente-utrechtse-heuvelrug">Utrechtse Heuvelrug</entity>, can be viewed from today at the museum Naturalis in <entity id="org:gemeente-leiden">Leiden</entity>. Visitors could see up close today how the wolf, known colloquially as Bram, was stuffed. Wolf Bram was shot dead on 1 December last year. That happened after the province, on the advice of experts, had given permission, after the animal had bitten a walking woman in the spring. Bram was involved in several more incidents. He knocked over a child in August 2024, and in summer 2025 he bit a child in the woods near the Pyramide van Austerlitz. 'Cosy family day out' Today Naturalis is organising a theme day about wolves. Children could make their own wolf mask, attend lectures about the wolf and see up close how wolf Bram was prepared. This is how the preparation went: Activists from the protest group Animal Rebellion think that Naturalis is turning the killing of Bram into "a cosy family day out". Today they marched in a protest from Leiden station to Naturalis. There they were stopped by the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, RTV <entity id="org:gemeente-utrecht">Utrecht</entity> reports. Brief protest In the lobby, several groups of demonstrators had also gathered. During one of the lectures about the craftsmanship behind the preparation, a man bared his upper body. With his arms spread, he sat down in front of the wolf. "Take me", he said repeatedly. "Let me take Bram's place, so that Bram can be left in peace." The demonstrator placed in front of him a sign reading 'Problem human': The man spoke for a few minutes, then stood up and thanked the audience and staff for the opportunity to tell his story. According to him, Naturalis should continue its "useful work" to emphasise the importance of biodiversity. "The story of Bram belongs in Naturalis, but Bram himself does not", the demonstrator said. General director Marcel Beukeboom of Naturalis does not agree. According to him, displaying the stuffed animal helps start conversations and provide information about the return of the wolf to the Netherlands. "We spoke beforehand with the people from the action group and we aim for the same thing", he says. "We want to protect nature and get people to love nature. We only differ in opinion about how to do that." Domino sparrow Possibly the stuffed wolf will later be lent to the Natural History Museum in <entity id="org:gemeente-rotterdam">Rotterdam</entity>. That museum has a collection of dead animals that became known for their special stories and their confrontation with humans. Bram will then be placed, among others, alongside the Domino sparrow, the house sparrow shot dead in 2005 in an event hall in <entity id="org:gemeente-leeuwarden">Leeuwarden</entity>. In that hall 4 million domino stones had been set up for the TV programme 'Domino Day'. The sparrow had knocked over 23,000 of them and was shot dead to prevent more from falling.

title: Six occupants of rubber boat off Zeeland coast were minors
lead: On the rubber boat with migrants picked up yesterday off the Zeeland coast were, among others, six minors. They have been transferred to the registration center in Ter Apel. Of the 38 people on board, one has applied for asylum. The Royal Netherlands Marechaussee announced this. Two Sudanese men from the group have been arrested on suspicion of people smuggling. The two are being held and may only have contact with their lawyer. "They must first be prevented, so we cannot yet say where they came from and where they wanted to go," says a spokesperson for the Marechaussee. The emergency services received an alert early Saturday morning that a boat had been seen off the coast of Zeeuws-Vlaanderen. A rescue operation was started and the rubber boat was towed to the marina of Cadzand. Wet feet: The migrants were packed together on board. People at the sides got wet feet from the waves, as could be seen in video footage. The occupants were medically examined for signs of hypothermia. According to the Marechaussee, they were doing well given the circumstances. The group consisted of 36 Afghan migrants and the two suspected people smugglers from Sudan. Apart from the one person who applied for asylum, all adults are going through the so-called foreigner procedure. That includes checking their nationality and residence status, among other things. It seems the Netherlands was not the intended final destination of the migrants. Rubber boats with migrants on board regularly sail from France toward the United Kingdom, sometimes also from Belgium. It is possible that such a boat strayed off course on the North Sea and ended up off the Zeeland coast.

title: Suriname expels group of Mennonites after illegal deforestation
lead: A group of 63 Mennonites, a religious community, was expelled from Suriname this weekend. They are mainly from Bolivia and Mexico and were engaged in illegal deforestation. The expulsion follows a protracted legal dispute. The ultraconservative Christian farmers had been staying in Suriname since 2024 without a residence permit. They cut down forests with the aim of setting up large-scale agricultural projects. President Jennifer Simons is strongly opposed to this. "The point is that we must not cut down the most important Amazon rainforest for large-scale agriculture," she repeatedly said in Surinamese media. Since mid-July the Mennonites, with their families including babies and young children, had already been served a summons by a bailiff to leave. They were in the so-called Masonia area, deep in the Surinamese interior. Search by <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> and army. When the Mennonites ignored the warnings, environmental organizations raised the alarm, after which a new ultimatum followed. There too there was no response. Eventually the police, with help from the army, entered the area at the end of October. The Mennonites had meanwhile fled and were hiding a few kilometres further away. After a search they were nevertheless found and taken out of the area by bus. Representatives of the Mennonites had meanwhile filed a summary injunction to prevent deportation. When they lost that, their lawyer filed a second summary injunction, but the Surinamese authorities did not wait for it and went ahead with deportation this weekend. The Mennonites are a current within the Anabaptists, also called 'rebaptizers', and originally followed the 16th-century priest and church reformer Menno Simons from Friesland. Living apart. Because Simons and his community were persecuted in the Netherlands, they moved to Germany. His followers spread over various places in the world in the following centuries, including Latin America. There, Mennonite colonies were founded in nine countries. Among other places in Bolivia and Peru they practise large-scale agriculture, such as soy cultivation. They prefer to live as isolated as possible. They separate themselves from the outside world and mix as little as possible with residents of the countries where they settle, in order to continue their traditional way of life. In their households they use no telephone, electricity or television. Watch this report by Nina Jurna from last year for Nieuwsuur about Mennonites in Latin America: According to international environmental organizations such as WWF and Greenpeace, the growing presence and expansion of Mennonite colonies in Latin America is one of the increasing causes of deforestation of the Amazon. Their presence also poses a threat to indigenous communities. Pilot project under the <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity>-Santokhi. Since 2022 Mennonites from Bolivia, Belize and Mexico have been focusing their attention on Suriname, in a search for more land and space to found colonies. Their affairs are handled by local parties and private intermediaries, including a number of Dutch entrepreneurs in Suriname. Under the Santokhi government (2020-2025), fifty Mennonite families were given permission to come to Suriname for three years for a pilot project on about 35,000 hectares of land. The plans to clear large tracts of land in the interior for large-scale agriculture leaked out and seemed to have been made outside parliament. This caused great public outrage, particularly among environmental organizations, indigenous groups and maroon communities. They feared large-scale deforestation and loss of their habitats. After public pressure and a lawsuit against the state and the Mennonites' representatives, Santokhi ultimately pulled the plug on the pilot project. Some of the Mennonites were already in Suriname by then. Tougher action. The Surinamese government of President Jennifer Simons is taking a stricter approach to illegal logging and the lack of permits. The president has indicated that land in the coastal plain is available for large-scale agricultural development. No tropical forest needs to be destroyed for this. It is estimated that several hundred Mennonites are still in Suriname, even after the expulsion of the group of 63. Their status is unclear. Surinamese environmental organizations, such as Probios, are continuously working to trace Mennonite colonies and draw attention to deforestation of Suriname's interior.

title: 800-year-old churches in Groningen crack under summer drought
lead: Besides earthquake damage, medieval churches in Groningen may also be suffering from drought damage. That is what climate and soil experts state in an exploratory study commissioned by the <entity id="org:provincie-groningen">provincie Groningen</entity> and the Stichting Oude Groninger Kerken. They examined the influence of drought on the wierden (mounds) on which churches stand in Oostum and Den Ham, northwest of the city of Groningen. The reason for the study is damage to the church in Oostum. It was discovered in 2018, while suspected earthquake damage had been repaired just two years earlier. Since then there have been no major earthquakes there, but the damage still appears to be increasing. The researchers therefore think soil movements caused by drought play a role. They warn that more heritage faces this problem. The nave of the small church in Oostum has stood for 800 years, say caretakers Hesther le Grand and Niels Smit Duyzentkunst. They love their church. Le Grand: "I always think it sounds a bit corny, but it does something to the energy that it is already so old. Somehow you feel it." Age That long history is easy to see for a trained eye. "It was a barrel-vaulted church, but after two centuries they were fed up with it and put a beamed ceiling in," says Smit Duyzentkunst, pointing at the roof. "Two centuries later the pulpit came in, and the family pews. The whole history can be seen here." It makes for a lovely picture of the times, but in recent years more and more cracks have appeared in the walls. Where there are cracks, water seeps in and age takes hold of the centuries-old house of God, which as a result is falling into decay. The cracks in the building are clearly visible: "It is not a given that the church will still be standing here in 800 years, because the aging is now going very fast," says lecturer in climate adaptation Floris Boogaard of the Hanze University of Applied Sciences. "Groningen pride," he calls this kind of small church, of which, according to him, more than the two buildings studied struggle with this problem. "We have looked at the movement of the building and also at the wierden. You can see that the church in Oostum is moving," he explains. The research runs for two years, and longer-term research is needed before definitive conclusions can be drawn. Boogaard is already certain that the ground under the church is sensitive to shrinking and swelling. That can have far-reaching effects during prolonged drought. Longer dry periods "You can see the groundwater levels dropping," says Boogaard, who mapped the soil. "Peat is known to oxidise and can become more compact. And then there is clay. We sampled that in the laboratory and it turns out to be 'shrink-swell clay'. That means it swells when water is added, and that the ground sinks during drought." The scientist stresses that all kinds of factors play a role in crack formation in churches; besides drought, for example, heavier traffic, changes in the surroundings and earthquakes. Apart from the drought, none of these factors has changed significantly in this region in recent years, while the cracks have become much worse. Boogaard: "The climate is changing. The drought periods are significantly longer: in 2018 it was dry for two months, and that simply has a real effect." This year also saw exceptionally long dry periods. "The intensity can be seen in the structural condition of this building." Digging pits Solutions are still being investigated, but what the researchers consider necessary in any case is a stable water management system at the old churches. At Oostum, for example, some pits could be dug around the church so that water collects there and slowly sinks into the ground. Such measures could offer relief in more places, they think. The caretakers in Oostum are pleased with the study. "I think it is wonderful that people are now looking into what it is and what we can do about it," says Smit Duyzentkunst. "For the whole community it would be lovely if places like this could continue to exist." Le Grand: "Even in 800 years' time."

title: Dutch foundation tries to prevent Swedish wolf hunt
lead: Stichting Wolven Belangen has lodged an appeal in Sweden against the shooting of 72 wolves. The Dutch foundation also demands that, pending a ruling by the court, no wolves are hunted. This year five Swedish district boards decided to shoot 72 wolves jointly in 2027. That number is higher than in other years, because the Swedish government has decided that the wolf population must decrease from 355 to 220 animals. Stichting Wolven Belangen lodged appeals in those five districts. The reason for this was "the exceptional scale of the Swedish hunting decisions", the foundation writes in a press release. Protected status The animal welfare organisation asks for a careful assessment of the consequences of the planned culling for the wolf population. The wolf has a protected status under European nature conservation rules. According to Stichting Wolven Belangen, the justification for the Swedish hunting decisions and the consequences for the conservation of the wolf must be critically assessed. The administrative court in Luleå will handle the appeal, but first that court will consider whether a Dutch organisation can start a legal case in Sweden on this matter and whether the demand to suspend the wolf hunt will be granted.

title: Fair elections? American voters fear most what comes after
lead: Requesting voter data, collecting ballots, redrawing electoral districts and filing lawsuits. These are just a few of the actions President Trump has taken in the run-up to the midterm elections. He also added last week that he would only accept the outcome of the elections "if they are fair". On Tuesday American voters will vote for Congress, their parliament. The elections will determine how much support Trump can count on in the last two years of his term in the House of Representatives and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>. For months the president has been trying to sow doubt about the fairness of the results. Listen to our podcasts about the midterms in the US In the run-up to the midterms on 3 November, our correspondents in Washington are making new episodes of the podcast Amerika Kiest. Listen to them via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister or via another audio platform A president is actually not supposed to meddle in elections. "The organisation of elections in the US lies primarily with the states", explains Lou Errens, an expert on American law affiliated with the UvA. "The president cannot independently decide how elections are organised. That is established in the American constitution." That does not mean the Trump administration abides by it. "They are simply pulling out all the stops to see whether they can get something done anywhere", says Errens. Invalid blockades For example, Trump tried to have 20,000 votes of registered voters in California declared invalid. He claimed that these were people who are not American citizens. Trump also wanted to block the results in Alaska in advance, should the sitting Republican senator lose. A judge rejected both actions. As recently as Thursday, the US Department of Justice sent letters to election officials in all fifty states, threatening a prison sentence of up to one year and a fine of a thousand dollars if they do not preserve election documents. In response, a judge prohibited the Department of Justice from threatening or pressuring election staff. Election officials trained The fact that these actions have little legal chance of success does not mean they have no consequences. "We have never before witnessed such a large degree of interference", says Kim Wehle, an American legal scholar and expert on democracy. Across the country, election officials are being prepared and trained in various scenarios. They learn what to do when immigration agents show up at a polling station and what federal observers may and may not do on election day. The threats could lead officials to no longer dare to do their work, says Wehle, because they fear prosecution. "There is a hundred percent chance the government will try something", she expects. Most Americans appear to share Wehle's concerns: seven in ten have no confidence that Trump will accept the election results if the Republicans lose; half of them even have "no confidence at all", according to a poll by ABC News/Washington Post/Ipsos. Despite Trump's actions, most Americans do have confidence in the results themselves. What could Trump do? What will happen should the Republicans lose will become clear next week. "I think we can at least expect a lot more chaos", says Errens. The problems may not be limited to election day. For example, The New Republic sketches a scenario for afterwards, if the Democrats have won in the House of Representatives. House Speaker Mike Johnson could replace the clerk in January, when the new members of the House are sworn in. He could appoint a partisan clerk who does not carry through the installation of the Democratic candidates. Ultimately that situation could end up with the Supreme Court, some of whose justices were appointed by Trump. In an interview with Time magazine, the American president also left open the possibility of declaring a national emergency. "I rule nothing out or in", he said. "We will see." Some people think these scenarios go too far, but Wehle does not. "In 2020 we saw more than sixty lawsuits in which Trump tried to overturn the election results. When that failed, we saw the storming of the Capitol on 6 January. Those are scenarios that are more likely than the quiet elections we used to have."

title: UN withdraws peacekeeping mission from Western Sahara, conflict not yet over
lead: There will be an end to the Minurso peacekeeping mission in Western Sahara. That is what the United Nations has announced. The UN troops and equipment will return in the coming weeks to the countries that took part in the mission. On Friday Russia vetoed an American proposal to extend the mandate of Minurso. As a result, after 35 years the peacekeeping operation will end, without the conflict having been resolved. The struggle over Western Sahara is one of the longest-running and most complex conflicts in the world. The area on the Atlantic Ocean is six times the size of the Netherlands and is rich in the valuable raw material phosphate. Morocco says it has always belonged to the kingdom, long before the former Spanish colonizer incorporated the area in 1884. Struggle since 1975 On the other side is the independence movement Polisario, which fights for an independent state. The diplomatic and sometimes armed struggle over the area has been raging since 1975. Morocco controls most of Western Sahara. Polisario, supported by neighbouring Algeria, controls areas east of the Moroccan military sand wall. In 1991 the United Nations set up the Minurso peacekeeping mission.
