Bystanders also hindered the emergency workers. According to the mayor, the risk of new violent incidents is too great and the venue must therefore remain closed. The shooting in September took place at night. During a party a man was shot on the dance floor. He was taken to hospital. A few dozen people stood outside the party venue, but the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> could not arrest a perpetrator. Aggressive guests At the end of October a woman was seriously assaulted at a party in the venue. She had had an argument with another woman early in the morning, a man got involved and struck the woman on the head with a heavy object. AT5 reported that there were many aggressive guests at that party. According to the police, the officers who rushed to the scene had to keep them at a distance with batons. In the chaos the suspect man was able to flee. Background At the party venue on Rhôneweg in Amsterdam, the 26-year-old rapper Bigidagoe was already shot dead in 2024. He was there with a group of friends at a festival and got into an argument with someone. That person later returned and fired four bullets at the rapper. The rapper did not survive this. The mayor fears further violence and danger to bystanders. "The short time between the shooting incident and the assault, combined with the history of incidents, makes a risk of recurrence real", she writes in the order to close the premises. Measures have already been taken to improve the situation, but these have not helped, Halsema writes. The safety of the public therefore now weighs more heavily than the interests of the operator, is the mayor's conclusion.

title: World reacts to Republican defeat: optimism in Europe, Moscow shrugs
lead: Many foreign leaders have responded positively to the Democrats' victory in the US midterm elections, in which the party gained control of both the House of Representatives and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>. Russia and China responded with restraint. Spanish Social Democratic Prime Minister Pedro Sánchez stated on X that American voters have spoken out "against policies that only make people poorer". He also described the result as a rejection of hatred, machismo, climate denial and privileges for the elite. According to Sánchez, the result fits into a broader international trend. "We saw that earlier in Brazil. Now it has also happened in the United States. And soon the same will happen in Spain", he wrote, pointing to (radical) right-wing politicians campaigning for the upcoming Spanish parliamentary elections. Iran reacts positively. South African President Ramaphosa said he saw in the election result "a new era in international relations". According to him, Americans have clearly spoken by giving power in Congress to the Democrats. German Defence Minister Pistorius spoke of a "historic victory" for the Democrats. At the same time, he stressed that Germany will continue cooperating with Washington and will remain in contact with both Democrats and Republicans. The result was also welcomed with approval in Iran. Parliament Speaker Ghalibaf stated on X that American voters "have said no to war". Incidentally, President Trump also told American media that he thought the war with Iran may have contributed to the heavy defeat of his Republican party. Musk and Texas. Tech billionaire Elon Musk, who spent hundreds of millions of dollars on the campaign of Republican Senate candidate Ken Paxton in Texas, also responded to the result. On his platform X he wrote sarcastically, with a shrugging emoji: "Apparently my election-influencing space lasers didn't work this time." The Senate seat went to Democrat James Talarico. In his victory speech he also referred back to Musk's financial support for his political opponent. "We have sent a message to mega-donor billionaires: in this state and in this country, power belongs to the people." Talarico's speech: In France, various politicians seized on the result to draw parallels with domestic politics. Party leader Marine Tondelier of the Greens called Trump's defeat a reckoning with, among other things, racism, misogyny and climate denial. Social Democrat Raphaël Glucksmann spoke of "a victory for democracy and decency". French Minister of Economy Lescure took a more nuanced tone. In conversation with the French news channel BFMTV, he acknowledged that Trump had been weakened domestically by the result. But internationally, he said, Trump "still holds the strings", and Lescure also pointed to Trump's "unpredictable character". Ukraine and Russia. European Parliament Vice-President Christel Schaldemose said on X that she was cautiously optimistic about the election result. "Not because everything will suddenly change for the better, but because this could benefit support for Ukraine, the green transition and relations with the rest of the world." "But the European Union must continue on the path it has taken to become stronger and stand on its own feet. That is not negotiable", she wrote. A different message came from Russia. Deputy Foreign Minister Ryabkov of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> said, quoted by the state news agency RIA, that the attitude of the Democratic Party leadership towards Russia is "clearly negative". "There is nothing new about that." Ryabkov also said that the "course" of foreign policy does not depend on "the fluctuations of the political barometer in other countries." China. China responded with restraint to the result. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Foreign Affairs called the elections "an internal American affair" and said that Beijing remains willing to cooperate with Washington, strengthen communication and manage differences.

title: Epstein files, tackling corruption, what will Democrats do with their power?
lead: A blue wave has swept across America. The Democrats have won both the majority in <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and in the House of Representatives. In January the new members will be sworn in, and the Democrats have big plans to thwart Trump in the last two years of his presidency. What can the Democrats actually do once they dominate Congress? First, a step back: what exactly does Congress do? Congress consists of the House of Representatives and the Senate. The 435 members of the House vote on legislation, can start investigations and request documents. The House also holds the power of the purse. Everything taken out of the treasury must pass through the House. Then the Senate, which confirms the appointment of cabinet members, ambassadors and judges, including those of the Supreme Court. A majority in the Senate can block Trump's nominees. Reversing spending cuts Democratic leader Hakeem Jeffries announced big plans today, including reversing the cuts to healthcare made by the Big Beautiful Bill . The Democrats also want to lower the cost of living by introducing new laws. That falls within their powers, and with a Democratic majority they could easily pass new laws. Even so, that does not mean the proposals will immediately become reality. The American president has a veto, with which he can strike down certain plans. President Trump said overnight in an interview with The New York Times that he would gladly work with the Democrats. Shortly afterward, however, he also posted an image of a red cap with the word 'VETO' on it on his platform Truth Social. The veto can be reversed, but that requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. The Democratic Party does not have that, but Republicans could vote with the Democrats. That is not unrealistic, explains American affairs expert Casper Thomas, because Republicans are now starting to think about how they want to position themselves ahead of the 2028 presidential election. "Republicans will have to think about which choices will be popular with voters toward 2028," says Thomas. If they do not vote to reverse the healthcare spending cuts, that could come back to haunt the Republicans. Money flows of the Trump family. Where the Democrats will probably get to work fastest, says Thomas, is on anti-corruption investigations. "Lawyer up", a Democratic congressmember already wrote on Instagram today. In other words: "go get lawyers." According to Thomas these investigations are not only the most feasible but also the most visible. Government corruption was an important theme in these elections. Democrats frequently pointed to the 2.7 billion dollars Trump has earned since the start of his second term, partly thanks to crypto and stock trading. Trump's son-in-law Jared Kushner's international business deals may also be on the agenda. Kushner was involved in negotiations on peace in Ukraine, Gaza and Iran, but also has business interests there. The Epstein files. The Democrats may also want to investigate the government's handling of the Epstein files in the House, and legislation could be introduced that makes all Epstein files public. Democrats have said they want to focus on Trump's ties to the deceased sex offender. One report claims that Trump "actively participated in the sexual abuse of young women by Jeffrey Epstein". Trump denies this. Third impeachment? The Democrats could also start a new impeachment procedure against President Trump. They did so already in 2018, and again in 2021, over his role in the violent storming of the Capitol on January 6. Both times the impeachment procedure failed in the Senate. Thomas does not see the Democrats launching another impeachment procedure. "Such a procedure takes a lot of time, and Trump is already on his way out," says Thomas. American media also raise the possibility of an impeachment procedure against Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth. That requires a majority in the House. Conviction and removal from office requires a two-thirds majority in the Senate. But those procedures also take long, says Thomas. He sees Trump himself more likely to kick Hegseth out. "Some heads always have to roll when things go wrong," says Thomas. "Hegseth is the face of unpopular foreign policy." Trump so far denies that he would want to dismiss cabinet members.

title: Residents file claim against Chemours over PFAS damage
lead: Residents of the region <entity id="org:gemeente-dordrecht">Dordrecht</entity> have jointly started a lawsuit against Chemours. They want to hold the company legally liable through the courts for PFAS pollution in the area. The foundation PFAS Vrij Green Claim wants to stop further PFAS emissions by the company on behalf of more than half a million residents and demands compensation for damage said to have been caused by PFAS emissions, according to regional broadcaster Rijnmond. PFAS is the collective name for thousands of non-degradable toxic chemicals. They accumulate in the food chain and damage the immune system. With long-term exposure, some types are carcinogenic. The chemical plant Chemours has been emitting PFAS for decades, although the amount has fallen considerably. Until 2012 the company used the PFAS substance PFOA, which ended up in the air and in surface water. Research has shown that people who lived close to the plant for a long time had higher PFOA concentrations in their blood than average. Nearly all people in the Netherlands have PFAS in their blood, research shows. Written response from Chemours: "Chemours has received the summons from Stichting PFAS Vrij Green Claim. We will study it carefully. We understand that there are questions and concerns in the area about PFAS and our activities. We take those seriously. In recent years we have taken major steps to further reduce emissions and we continue to invest in technology and measures to reduce them further and to produce responsibly. In Dordrecht we make essential materials for important applications, including in medical technology, semiconductors, green energy supply, transport and defense. Our aim is to produce these materials safely and responsibly, with ongoing attention to further emission reduction. We think it is important to carefully assess the content and the specific claims in the summons before responding substantively. Therefore we are not getting ahead of the individual legal claims at this time." According to the foundation, many residents are worried about their health. "This case is not only about environmental pollution but above all about the consequences for hundreds of thousands of people who lived for years without knowing which substances they were exposed to", says lawyer Michael Bacon, who is assisting the foundation. "As residents, we deserve recognition, redress and a safe and healthy living environment", says board member Anneke van Veen. Research: This is not the first time the company has had to answer in court. Earlier, the municipalities of Dordrecht, <entity id="org:gemeente-papendrecht">Papendrecht</entity>, <entity id="org:gemeente-sliedrecht">Sliedrecht</entity> and <entity id="org:gemeente-molenlanden">Molenlanden</entity> brought a case against the company and its predecessor DuPont. In an interim ruling in 2023, the court partly agreed with the municipalities about damage suffered from PFAS emissions. Last year the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> also raided the company as part of an extensive criminal investigation into the pollution. According to the OM, that investigation is at an advanced stage but is still ongoing.

title: Danish actor deceived for months about dream project and secretly filmed
lead: Danish actor and comedian Rasmus Wallbridge was thrilled that he was allowed to make a film. His dream came true, he thought. But after months of working on the 'film', Wallbridge was told that he had been duped. He had unknowingly been the main player in a hidden TV show. The TV programme Alle elsker Rasmus (Everyone Loves Rasmus) has led to a storm of criticism in Denmark. The six episodes have been taken offline and the makers have apologised to Wallbridge. The comedian performed again for the first time last night and received a standing ovation from the audience upon entering. "It was moving and wonderful to see", a spectator said afterwards to Danish media. They described it as "a hug from a distance" for the man who had unexpectedly ended up in a media storm. Truman Show-like The situation is reminiscent of the American film The Truman Show. In that 1998 film, lead actor Jim Carrey discovers that his life has been entirely staged. His loved ones turn out to be actors in a kind of reality soap. The main character Truman Burbank spends his life on a large film set. Around 150 friends, actors, celebrities and fellow actors of the Danish thirty-year-old were part of the plot in Alle elsker Rasmus. They knew that Rasmus could not really make a film, but played along. In some cases he was also secretly filmed by them for the programme of broadcaster TV2, a public broadcaster. Reaction manipulated In the final episode of the programme, Wallbridge is told in an empty cinema hall that the film project was staged. This is told to him by his friend and the show's initiator, Martin Johannes Larsen. Sound experts have established that the main character's reaction to the revelation was manipulated by the programme makers. Wallbridge's harsh laugh turned out to be a copy of an earlier laugh, with cut-and-paste work edited in. This discovery further fuelled the outrage over the team's methods. Larsen expressed regret to his friend on Instagram. "This is bullying of the worst kind", wrote the editor-in-chief of the newspaper Politiken in an opinion piece about the programme. Culture minister Zenia Stampe called the TV show scandalous and unethical. Prime Minister Mette Frederiksen expressed the hope that this "unfortunate affair" would make programme makers and media think. Never make something like this again Wallbridge has not responded publicly. Via social media, he has called on TV2 never to make this kind of programme again. "I have decided to focus fully on my upcoming show", he wrote last Sunday in a statement. That performance took place last night in Hanstholm. The stand-up comedian therefore received a warm welcome there. Wallbridge said nothing on stage about the row surrounding Alle elsker Rasmus. "I don't think you should bother him by constantly asking how he is doing. If he feels bad, he feels bad", someone said to journalists before the performance.

title: Over 1.7 million fake Pokémon cards intercepted in Rotterdam port
lead: The <entity id="org:douane">douane</entity> has seized more than 1.7 million counterfeit Pokémon cards in the port of Rotterdam. During an inspection of a sea container, a customs officer came across the cards and doubted their authenticity. After further investigation, it turned out they were forgeries. The container was inspected last May at the Maasvlakte. Although the customs officer who first found the cards quickly doubted their authenticity, the judgement of a specialist in counterfeit goods was needed to establish this with certainty. That specialist saw that the colours on the cards from the container were different from usual. It also stood out that there was no copyright on the cards, and that the paper used was different too. Finally, trademark holder Nintendo confirmed that the cards were not genuine. They were then destroyed. The cards were spread over 142,800 packs and packed in 9,300 boxes. In a statement, customs reports that these boxes, stacked, would be 515 metres high, almost three times the Euromast. Millionaire from Pokémon cards in the attic Rare Pokémon cards can represent enormous financial value. Last month it became known that a Brit, a retired house painter, became a millionaire from the cards that had lain in his attic for years. After an auction, his collection brought in 1.8 million euros. And when a special set of cards was released in September to mark Pokémon's thirtieth anniversary, a true rush ensued. Hundreds of people queued up for it in the Netherlands. The most expensive Pokémon card ever sold for 14 million euros at the start of this year. This was a version with a drawing of the character Pikachu, issued in 1998. Only forty of these were made, and the card was in perfect condition.

title: Tensions over 'open marriage' coalition parties D66, VVD and CDA
lead: The minority cabinet is already an experiment, but in the coming days the government parties are going a step further with experimenting: in the worst case they may abandon each other in votes on the tax plan, as the coalition parties D66, VVD and CDA have agreed. They may look for majorities separately with the opposition and may even vote in favour of important financial plans that the other opposes. In The Hague, no one is sure whether that will work politically and which plans will roll out for the country as a result. Follow the debate live. The debate on the tax plan in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> can be followed in a livestream on NOS.nl and <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Politiek en Nieuws. The debate can also be followed in a liveblog on NOS.nl. "A unique situation", is what a minister of the minority cabinet-Jetten calls it behind the scenes. The Tweede Kamer debates the tax plan of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> this afternoon, and then it will become clear what that release of ties might look like in practice. That could get very exciting, say people involved in The Hague. This afternoon the mutual bond of the coalition parties will be tested directly. Casino politics The cabinet has once again adjusted the financial plans for next year. That latest adjustment was made in the hope that enough parties will vote for them, because there is something nice in it for everyone, but reliable support in the Senate and especially in the <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">Eerste Kamer</entity> is still not arranged. Government party CDA is therefore frustrated and critical of the cabinet. That party wants certainty that the important financial plans will pass the Eerste Kamer. It frustrates CDA <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">leider Bontenbal</entity> that within the coalition it is not succeeding in jointly putting forward an offer that would guarantee that majority in the Senate. Bontenbal was referring to the VVD, he made clear on the TV programme Eva. "The VVD does not want to move a bit on wealth", said the CDA leader. And by taxing the very wealthiest more, the cabinet could win the support of Pro. That the cabinet instead chose to wait and see which parties would dare to vote against, Bontenbal even called "casino politics". 'Choosing chaos' That the CDA leader is so fiercely critical that the coalition is achieving too little and is pursuing his own plan is interpreted in part of the cabinet as choosing chaos. People do not know what will come of it. But Bontenbal says he is doing exactly this to prevent chaos. The CDA leader is not operating entirely alone. In the coalition they have agreed that it is now up to the House to reach majorities for the financial plans. And it has also been agreed that the government parties may vote differently on them. Certain rules have been agreed within this 'open marriage', they must not surprise each other, and it can be heard that agreements from the coalition agreement stand. The room for manoeuvre therefore lies mainly in what they have not yet agreed with each other. First test with the Pro plan Today in the tax debate, Pro and Volt are putting forward a plan to tax the wealthy more nonetheless. It promises to be the first test of this loose approach in the coalition. The CDA is also involved in talks about that proposal from Pro and Volt, although that would only be at the level of main outlines. According to those involved, it will be very exciting to see what happens with it. The VVD has so far blocked deals at the negotiating table to tax the wealthy more. "What if the CDA is going to support amendments that the VVD previously could not bear", asks one person involved. Are they really allowed to go that far? And can the mutual bond in the coalition withstand that? People in The Hague do not yet know, because this is a new experiment within the minority cabinet experiment. According to a cabinet source, it was necessary to try to 'force' it this way, because things were also 'stuck'. At today's debate not everything needs to become clear yet, because the votes on it have not yet taken place. And in the meantime, for example, a right-wing majority for other plans could also be arranged. There are more possibilities now that the government parties no longer necessarily act together on the major financial plans. So behind the scenes parties are now busily sounding out what is all possible. But plans on the left or right almost always need the CDA. Arrows at <entity id="org:ministerie-van-financien">Financiën</entity> In today's tax plan debate the arrows will also be aimed at the Ministry of Finance, and not only because there are still no certain majorities. Several parties are angry that Financiën did not cover the overhaul of the Box 3 system, the wealth tax. Against the bill of more than 17 billion there is no plan for how it is to be paid. "This is the biggest tax fraud ever by a <entity id="pos:minister-van-financien">minister van Financiën</entity>", says ChristenUnie MP Grinwis even, remarkably because the cabinet looks to his party for many financial plans. Pro wants the wealthy to pay that bill, but they feel that with Heinen's plan all Dutch people must now pay for a "billion-euro gift to the largest fortunes". And where Financiën hoped, for example, to reassure BBB and Mona Keijzer with a postponement of the higher VAT on ornamental horticulture, that is flowers, in practice this has not succeeded. They are disappointed that the cabinet has only set aside money to postpone the measure by three months.

title: More second hearing implants reimbursed: 'Not for nothing did we get two ears'
lead: Adults who are deaf or severely hard of hearing in both ears can now also qualify for reimbursement of a second hearing implant. <entity id="org:zbo-zorginstituut-nederland">Zorginstituut Nederland</entity> announced this yesterday. Children were already reimbursed for a so-called cochlear implant in both ears. But adults were only entitled to this if they were deaf due to meningitis, or if they were both deaf and blind. Other adults who are severely hard of hearing or deaf could only get one device reimbursed. For their other ear they therefore often wear a hearing aid. But for some people this does not work well enough. The Zorginstituut reviewed various scientific studies and concludes that a second device is of added value. For example, people can better distinguish sounds in a noisy room. This in turn makes them more self-reliant and less quickly tired, the Zorginstituut states. The reimbursement has applied since 27 October 2026. However, each case is assessed individually to see whether someone qualifies, says professor Hearing & Implants Wendy van Huinck of Radboudumc in Nijmegen. For this, the so-called "residual hearing" in the ear that does not yet have an implant must be "bad enough", Huinck says. The Zorginstituut expects sixty to one hundred patients per year. The Oorfonds is pleased that more people can get a second implant. "This has been a point of discussion for years", says Eddy de Ridder. "Whereas one implant is much more awkward than two, because with one you only hear on one side." Hearing rapidly deteriorating Alonda van Toor (59) is hard of hearing, already has one implant and wants "very much a second". Van Toor carries the DFNA9 gene. People with this condition hear well until about the age of forty, after which their hearing suddenly deteriorates sharply. In 2021 she received her first implant because hearing aids no longer helped enough. "I hardly heard anything anymore." The implant has changed her life. "Now I can have a one-on-one conversation well again." Electronic beeps A cochlear implant is fitted through an operation, says professor Huinck. "Electrodes are placed in the cochlea of the ear. These stimulate the nerve endings of the auditory nerve." Depending on where the electrode is placed, the person then hears a high or low tone. This sound is electronic and therefore sounds different from what people without hearing problems are used to. Patients with an implant often have to practise for months before they understand the sound, says Huinck. "Your brain has to learn to understand again. At first the sound may seem like beeps. Slowly you start to recognise sounds again. For some people this goes quickly, for others more slowly." Van Toor is now completely used to her first implant. But she still runs into things. On the left she still has a hearing aid and hears almost nothing. "If someone to my left says something, I have to turn my head. Socially that is difficult." And on the street she cannot tell well which direction a car is coming from. "I am very watchful about that." She expects that a second implant will further improve her life. That is also only logical, says Van Toor. "I did not get two ears for nothing."

title: HEMA 100 years: how does a store stay standing for a century?
lead: From a few guilders for a bag of chicken broth, to contactless card payment for a robot soft toy. After exactly 100 years, HEMA is still part of the shopping street scene. How has it managed that? On 4 November 1926 the doors opened of the first Hollandsche Eenheidsprijzen Maatschappij Amsterdam . For 25 or 50 cents you could buy 'everyday household items'. Because of those low prices, HEMA quickly became known as a 'poor people's shop'. Wealthy Dutch people did not want to be seen there. Over 100 years the retail chain has gone through many changes. The smoked sausage and the tompouce came into view, the store shed its old image and grew to more than 500 stores in the Netherlands, around 200 stores abroad and a webshop. Challenging market It is not often that a Dutch store turns 100. De Bijenkorf, Peek & Cloppenburg and Blokker, among others, went before HEMA as jubilee department store chains, but those stores have not always had it easy either. For example, Blokker made a restart, the Peek & Cloppenburg branch on Dam square in Amsterdam will soon close after 110 years, and De Bijenkorf also admits it is in a ' challenging market '. Ronald van Zetten, CEO of HEMA from 2003 to 2015, who now advises other retail chains, also sees that it is not a given for a store to reach 100. Many other chains, of which V&D is perhaps the best-known example, did not hold on. HEMA also has employees who have worked for the retail chain for a long time, such as Rob, who has been there for 43 years: Van Zetten was later himself involved in relaunching V&D as a webshop. "You have to stay attractive as a store, but building a reputation is at least as important," he says. According to Van Zetten, stores must keep adapting to modern times, but remain faithful to the basics of the store concept. Corine Noordhoff, special professor of Retail Marketing at the University of Groningen, agrees. That V&D did not make it, and HEMA did, is partly because, in her view, the store stopped making choices. "The store wanted to be everything to everyone. That was a bit far from their core. It is not the main reason they did not make it, but it certainly has something to do with it," she says. For HEMA too, reaching this jubilee looked anything but a given a few years ago. For a time the department store was in the hands of private equity investors with high debts. Later it came into the hands of investors who took over the chain with borrowed money, so HEMA paid high interest costs. The result was years of losses, so stores were not renovated and investments in the brand lagged. After many changes of ownership, the company now, under the Van Eerd family, which also owns Jumbo, is booking more turnover and more profit. Former CEO Ronald van Zetten calls the period a turbulent time with many faces. "The stores had to endure a lot of knocks in that time. Now they have really got back on their feet." Modern times Not only internally, but also outside, the store faced many challenges. Retail expert Rupert Parker Brady says that it is important for a retail chain to prove itself every day in a time when online shopping, fast fashion and budget stores such as Action are growing fast. "Competition does not stand still. You have to strive for people to keep having a reason to come to the store," says Parker Brady. Besides being a special professor, Corine Noordhoff is head of data at AS Watson, the parent company of Kruidvat. She sees the importance of data in the way stores operate. "The world is now very different from before, competition is very different and through all the data you now know so much more about your customer. You really need to think about how to smartly use that to bind the customer to you." According to Noordhoff, the fact that HEMA is now 100 years old is no guarantee that it can simply continue to exist for another 100 years. "Retailers like Hema must also adapt in a time when artificial intelligence plays an increasingly large role in our lives. We now select products based on a conversation with artificial intelligence instead of a typed search. It is important to keep up with that and adapt as a store."

title: Philippine police confirm: child pornography on devices of Meghan Markle's father
lead: There is indeed child pornography on the devices of Thomas Markle, the father of Meghan Markle. The Philippine police confirmed this after an investigation, according to the South China Morning Post. Last month the British newspaper The Sun wrote that Meghan's brother was searching for a phone in the house of their father, in the Philippines. During that search, Thomas Markle junior found a phone with a 15-minute video showing images of naked young girls. Later he found more shocking material. Markle junior went to the Philippine police and handed over three memory cards and a mobile phone there. The police then launched an investigation. The 82-year-old Thomas Markle senior is currently not in the Philippines. He is staying in a care home in the United States, where he is recovering from a stroke. Investigation in Mexico The investigation is still in full swing, emphasised the Philippine police chief. It still has to be investigated where the images come from, "who is responsible for them and whether any Philippine laws have been broken". An investigation into Markle senior is also under way in Mexico. Yesterday a storage unit where Markle had belongings was searched. The owner of the storage unit had reported that Markle stopped paying the rent two years ago but had not yet collected his belongings. Heartbroken Meghan Markle responded last month that she was "deeply heartbroken" about the news that her father was said to possess child pornography. "My thoughts go out to all the children who may have been harmed," she told a spokesperson. She also said she hopes people now understand why she has not been in contact with her father for a long time. In 2018 she had reportedly been informed of "disturbing and shocking allegations against my father".

title: Hormone-disrupting pesticide to be banned
lead: A widely used pesticide containing a hormone-disrupting substance may no longer be used. The College for the Authorisation of Plant Protection Products and Biocides (Ctgb) has decided this. It concerns the fungicide Pitcher from manufacturer Adama, which is widely used in agriculture and horticulture. This product contains the substance fludioxonil, which is harmful to people, animals and nature. 21.000 kilo Fludioxonil is hormone-disrupting, the European Food Safety Authority (EFSA) concluded in a 2024 study. Hormone-disrupting pesticides have not been permitted in the European Union since 2009. Ctgb's withdrawal of the plant protection product follows a court ruling last summer. The judge ruled that Pitcher should not have been authorised and that the product must therefore be removed from the market as soon as possible. A Ctgb spokesperson says that with current knowledge the product would not have been authorised. "It rarely happens that the authorisation of products is withdrawn after a reassessment." The case was brought by environmental organisation Pesticide Action Network (PAN). Sjoerd van de Wouw, a researcher at PAN, believes the withdrawal has taken "bizarrely long". "Only since 2018 has it been assessed whether substances are hormone-disrupting or not. But by then fludioxonil was already authorised on the market, and a substantive assessment only came in 2024." The organisation points out that in addition to Pitcher, 23 other pesticides containing fludioxonil are used in the Netherlands. "It is a widely used product," says Van de Wouw. A Ctgb spokesperson states that hormone disruption has been part of the assessment of products since last year. This procedure focused on Pitcher, the spokesperson says. Therefore the withdrawal applies to that specific product. "It is being studied what this ruling means for the authorisation of other products." Each year around 21.000 kilos of fludioxonil are used in the Netherlands. For example, in dip treatment of bulbs and tubers and in the cultivation of perennials and floricultural crops. "Farmers and residents near agricultural areas in particular are heavily exposed to this product," says Van de Wouw. 300 products. But residues have also been found on all kinds of vegetables and fruit. In an analysis by the <entity id="org:nederlandse-voedsel-en-warenautoriteit">Nederlandse Voedsel- en Warenautoriteit</entity> (NVWA), fludioxonil was found on more than 300 of the just over 2200 products tested, from potatoes and strawberries to tomatoes and grapes. "Of the hormone-disrupting substances, fludioxonil is the one most often found as a residue on vegetables and fruit," says Van de Wouw. "When consumed, it mainly poses a risk to pregnant women and young children," says Van de Wouw. He points to a broad range of risks. "All kinds of cancers, Parkinson's, asthma, allergies and cardiovascular diseases," says Van de Wouw. The manufacturer of Pitcher has been asked for a response. "We were not directly involved in the lawsuit between PAN and Ctbg. So we are taking note of the ruling and will accept it," says Jan-Willem van der Klugt, bulb manager at Adama. The use of Pitcher will be prohibited from May 2027.

title: Podcast De Dag: Trump's problems
lead: US President Trump has been hit hard in the midterm elections. Thanks to the blue tsunami, the Democrats now have both a majority in the House and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity>. What does this huge Democratic victory mean for Donald Trump? Listen here: you can listen to this episode of De Dag via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Luister and all other podcast apps. Enjoying it? Be sure to subscribe. American expert and lawyer Kenneth Manusama explains in the podcast De Dag what the Democrats can do with that majority. Because the demands are clear: America must become more affordable, the Iran war must stop, and the deployment of ICE agents must change. President Trump immediately threatened to use his veto if, in his view, things go in the wrong direction. But Trump also has to make sure that the Republican party continues to stand behind him. Respond? Email dedag@nos.nl Presentation & editing: Marco Geijtenbeek Editors: Rosanne Sies Final editing: Judith van de Hulsbeek

title: French blood banks escape damage after cyberattack on cooling installations
lead: Earlier this week, three French blood banks were targeted in a cyberattack that tried to raise the temperature of their cooling installations. It happened on the same day that cooling installations of shops in four European countries were hacked, from Carrefour in Belgium to Coop in Sweden. The attack on the blood banks was however thwarted before damage could occur, so no blood was lost. Whether there is a link between the two hacks is now being investigated by the French authorities. Raising the alarm The French blood supplier Établissement français du sang (EFS) confirms that on Monday, at three storage locations for blood plasma, the set temperature and thawing thresholds were raised to extremely high temperatures. Which places in France were broken into is not clear. "No health consequences have been identified and no blood products have been lost", the organisation says. The attack was aimed at a supplier of cooling equipment used at the locations. Monitoring and alarm systems raised the alarm in time, allowing staff to intervene. The supplier of cooling equipment states in a statement that it is aware of the incident. "The vulnerability reported in the media relates to a component of an external supplier and was beyond our direct control." Bags of plasma The French weekly Le Canard Enchaîné was the first to report the cyberattack. The satirical investigative paper reports that the temperature of the storage rooms, normally set at minus 30 degrees Celsius, rose to 110 degrees Celsius. EFS does not confirm the exact temperature to French media, but did say it concerned "very high temperatures." The stored bags of plasma were intended for transfusions and for the production of medicines. The plasma bags were moved or secured in time, EFS writes. In 2024 the organisation had 127 fixed donor centres spread across France. In addition, EFS collects blood and plasma through thousands of temporary collection points. The organisation says the work of the blood banks has not been disrupted. Patient services in hospitals and other care institutions can therefore continue as normal. The French national agency for cybersecurity and the ministry of Health are investigating the matter. The incident follows reports from supermarkets in several European countries whose fridges and freezers were taken over remotely. According to reports, the temperature in the installations rose to as high as 70 degrees. As a result, tons of food spoiled. The damage runs into millions of euros. Three weeks ago, fridges and freezers in hundreds of supermarkets and independent shops in France, Belgium and the Netherlands were targeted by a hack, including Albert Heijn. Hackers had disrupted the cooling systems, raising concerns about food security as a result. Some systems were set to 50 degrees. In France it concerned hundreds of shops of, among others, Intermarché, E.Leclerc, Netto and Coopérative U. At the time it seemed to mainly involve cooling installations from the Danish manufacturer Danfoss.

title: Censorship or badly needed protection? Australian court tests social media ban
lead: Australia's social media ban for children under 16 is "censorship", "poorly thought out" and a "serious restriction of political debate". Although this criticism has been known for a year since the ban was introduced, these arguments are now being presented for the first time to the highest court in Australia. The Australian government is being sued by the social media platform Reddit and the local interest group Digital Freedom Project, which want the ban to be declared unconstitutional. The groundbreaking Australian ban was introduced in December last year. It applies to Reddit, Facebook, Instagram, Kick, Snapchat, Threads, TikTok, X, YouTube and Twitch. Australia was the first country in the world to restrict social media companies in this way. Since then, more and more countries have introduced a minimum age for using the powerful platforms. But ever since its introduction there has been debate about whether the law conflicts with the Australian constitution. According to the plaintiffs in this case, the law conflicts with freedom of political expression. "If I had been born twenty or thirty years ago, it would not be a problem to live without social media", says 15-year-old Noah Jones. "But now social media is our modern village square. Information is shared here, everyone uses it. Those who are not on it are disadvantaged", he states in the Australian television program '60 Minutes'. He was one of the plaintiffs on behalf of the Digital Freedom Project, but withdrew because of the concern of being held personally liable if they lost the case. High Court For the past two days, seven judges of the Australian High Court have looked into the case. It may take months before there is a ruling, and until then the ban remains in force. During the court case, Reddit's lawyers pointed out that even the head of Australia's internet watchdog, Julie Inman Grant, said in 2021 that a ban was a "blunt instrument". The lawyer for the Australian government, Stephen Lloyd, responded forcefully to this. "This is precisely the most direct way to address the addictive features that cause harm to young people under 16", he said during the hearing. The ban targets the specific design features that make users addicted to social media, such as 'infinite scrolling', 'likes' and the personalised algorithm that tries to keep users engaged for as long as possible. According to the government, it poses a "real risk" of, among other things, sleep and concentration problems, depression, feelings of anxiety and suicidal thoughts. Australian Communications Minister Anika Wells was combative outside the court. "We are here to defend a fundamental principle of Australian democracy: the right of every Australian, and in particular of every Australian child, to be protected", she said after the hearing in Canberra. "We will defend ourselves against a sustained ideological attack." 'Digital duty of care' The case is being heard while parliament is debating a new law that is to restrict social media companies even further. A vote on the law for a 'digital duty of care' will take place soon. The government wants to once again take on a global pioneering role by restricting personalised algorithms. Users must be given the option to switch them off. Social media companies will also be required to remove harmful content and to protect children against cyberbullying, the glorification of eating disorders and violence. Criticism of the government's far-reaching measures is not only about the possible restriction of freedom of expression. It is also questionable whether these laws will achieve their goal at all. Almost a year after the ban was introduced, little has changed for Australian children. According to research, more than 85 percent of young people under sixteen are still on social media. Although more than five million accounts have been removed or restricted since the ban took effect, it is clear that affected users can create a new account without much difficulty. Lying about age is usually enough to get past the facial scans and checks. The government recently raised the maximum fine from 45 million Australian dollars to 99 million Australian dollars, roughly 60 million euros. The internet watchdog, the so-called eSafety Commissioner, may also force tech companies to provide evidence of measures they have taken to prevent teenagers under 16 from creating an account. No fines have been issued yet.

title: Suspects Tarwekamp: plan went from stealing bridal gowns to arson
lead: Greater clarity about what exactly preceded the devastating explosion in a flat on Tarwekamp two years ago. That is what the court in The Hague tried to obtain this afternoon from the four suspects who were heard on the first day of the hearing. Six people did not survive that explosion. This morning the main suspect Moshtag B. was already heard by the judges. B. was questioned about statements from himself, the three other suspects and those of his ex-girlfriend. It was her bridal fashion shop that the attack with heavy fireworks and about 175 litres of petrol was aimed at. Possessive and jealous: In the interrogation of the main suspect and the statements of his ex-girlfriend, it emerges that she initially felt pampered in the relationship. He often took her out to eat, gave her many gifts and a monthly allowance. Later in the relationship Moshtag B. became possessive and jealous because he thought his girlfriend was cheating. So he regularly hung around her home and her bridal shop, and Moshtag B. cloned her phone, allowing him to read along with her messages on social media among others. He also reportedly forbade her from associating with other men and required her to take a lie detector test. Shortly after she had ultimately ended the relationship, the devastating explosion took place at the bridal fashion shop on Tarwekamp. Months of contact: That the main suspect felt his honour was harmed and wanted to financially ruin her had already emerged earlier from a reconstruction by NOS. But how exactly that was to happen was long unclear to co-suspects Mourad B., his cousin Ilias B. and Adil A., as the trio stated in their interrogations today. Those interrogations revealed that they had been in contact with the main suspect for months before the eventual explosion on 7 December. They explained how for a long time they did not know exactly what they were supposed to do, and on whose orders. They stated that since August they had met several times in various combinations to discuss plans. Mourad B. was the first to be involved by the main suspect, whom he knew from Roosendaal. Moshtag B. reportedly explained that he wanted to carry out an attack on a bridal fashion shop on behalf of an organisation. From stealing dresses to arson: But what kind of damage they were to cause exactly remained uncertain for a long time and was regularly a topic of conversation among the suspects. For example, Mourad B. claimed that initially it would be about stealing bridal dresses from the shop to then sell them. Suspects also said they would cause damage in the bridal shop by smashing tiles or applying paint to the walls. In the autumn the preparations took off and they bought items for starting a fire. The suspects also researched via ChatGPT which substance burns best and bought jerrycans. There was much discussion about how much petrol was exactly needed. In addition, they searched for torches that would spread the fire and the suspects talked about acquiring Cobra's, heavily illegal fireworks. These were ultimately reportedly bought by Ilias B. Sets of black clothing were also purchased which the suspects could wear during the attack. 170 litres of petrol: They first put on that clothing on 30 November. Then police by chance found a white Ford Transit van at a shopping centre in Oosterhout, with Mourad B. and Ilias B. dressed in black. They were waiting there for Adil A., who had dropped out of the job. Police found the men there with fourteen jerrycans containing 170 litres of petrol. Despite suspicions of an attempted attack, they were released the next day. A week later Mourad B. and Ilias B. went to Tarwekamp with new clothing and jerrycans of petrol, where they caused the explosion in the early morning. According to Moshtag B. he did not know they would use so much petrol. He himself was in London at that time. He had followed his ex-girlfriend there. At the end of the interrogation he told how he learned of the attack. "I woke up and the first thing I thought was: 'is this Tarwekamp?'. Only when I saw her car and the aerial photo did I know it was there."

title: Ukrainian honour for Melania Trump for mediating a ceasefire in Olesjky
lead: Ukrainian President Zelensky has awarded the American first lady Melania Trump Ukraine's highest honour for women. The reason is her mediating role in bringing about the ceasefire in the Russian-occupied city of Olesjky. The Ukrainian presidential decree refers to Trump's "considerable personal contribution" to humanitarian aid for Ukraine and her commitment to Ukrainian children, including children who have been deported or forcibly displaced from Russian-occupied areas. Longest local pause Trump receives the highest rank of the Order of Princess Olha, an honour specifically intended for women. Previous recipients include former Speaker of the US House of Representatives Nancy Pelosi and EU foreign policy chief Kaja Kallas. During the six-day ceasefire, weapons were laid down in the South Ukrainian city and food, medicine and other aid supplies were able to reach the city. This was the longest local pause in the fighting since the large-scale Russian invasion of Ukraine in 2022. Most people had already fled the city, but around 1700 people who could not leave were still in the city. Before the ceasefire began, famine threatened them. According to Trump, nearly 800 people were evacuated during the ceasefire. Residents of Olesjky were glad and visibly moved by the evacuation: After she sent a personal letter to Russian President Putin in August 2025, talks got under way about the return of the children, according to The Kyiv Independent. In it she urged him to make peace, with the children affected by the war in mind. Both the Russian and Ukrainian authorities have thanked Melania Trump for bringing about the ceasefire, although they gave no further details about the nature and extent of her involvement. According to the White House, Melania Trump acted as the "exclusive mediator" and her representatives worked directly with the Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set out the terms for a local ceasefire. Nearly five years of war The honour comes at a time when Russian attacks on Kyiv today caused power and water outages lasting hours in the Ukrainian capital. The Kyiv Independent also reports today that it has become the target of a Russian cyberattack. The site can still be reached. The death toll after a major attack on Zaporizhzhia on Monday has risen to 40. This makes it one of the deadliest attacks since the start of the war, which is now nearing five years. Nine bombs were dropped that day on the building in Komysjoevacha, in the Zaporizhzhia region, where humanitarian aid was being distributed. The building also served as a shelter. The village lies close to the front. Ukrainian and Russian delegations travel to the White House tomorrow. Melania Trump will give a speech about Olesjky in the afternoon.

title: Up to 30 percent fewer livestock farms expected as a result of nitrogen plans
lead: More animals per farm, 10 to 30 percent fewer livestock farms in the Netherlands, and an agricultural sector better in balance with what our country can bear. This is what the nitrogen plans of <entity id="person:jaimi-van-essen">minister Van Essen</entity> of Agriculture will lead to, according to Wageningen researchers. They also state that the plans do not endanger food security. "The nitrogen package is very far-reaching for the farming families involved," emphasises lead researcher Petra Berkhout of Wageningen University directly. "At the same time, shrinking the livestock sector is necessary to meet nature and environmental goals, and it is crucial that governments can grant permits again. If part of the livestock farmers stop, that also creates space and opportunities for the farmers who continue." Berkhout and colleagues carried out the research on commission from the ministry of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-landbouw-visserij-voedselzekerheid-en-natuur">Landbouw, Visserij, Voedselzekerheid en Natuur</entity>, as often happens with far-reaching cabinet plans. The Wageningen University study is a first, rough analysis of the economic impact on farm businesses of the nitrogen plans as Van Essen presented them in June. Many details had not been worked out in those plans and there were still many uncertainties. In the nitrogen bill that Van Essen presented yesterday, he deviated from his earlier plans on a few points - after a summer of demonstrations by farmers and intensive talks with the agricultural sector - but the bulk is unchanged. Substantial investments For dairy farmers, the targets they must meet in the future are the most concrete. These concern, for example, the amount of ammonia they may emit and requirements for the amount of grassland per cow. In a sample of dairy farmers, the researchers found that less than 5 percent of dairy farms already meet the requirements of <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity>. That means many livestock farmers must invest heavily to meet what the cabinet asks of them. There is admittedly a nitrogen fund to help livestock farmers with this, but Berkhout expects that even with that support a considerable share of livestock farms will not survive, including in sectors other than dairy farming. "If we look at all sectors of livestock farming, we expect even without the nitrogen plans that about 10 percent of all farms will stop between now and 2035," says Berkhout. "As a result of the nitrogen plans, we expect 10 to 30 percent additional farms to stop in that period." In total, this is expected to mean 20 to 40 percent fewer livestock farms in 2035. Scale enlargement "Whether you can continue depends on how much fat you have on the bones," says Berkhout. She expects that large farms will more easily stay afloat, because they can usually invest more. "Compare it to making your home more sustainable. Someone with a higher income can more easily buy a heat pump than someone who earns less." The nitrogen plans therefore further encourage scale enlargement, the researchers expect. "In 2000, a dairy farm had an average of 51 cows, now it has 114," says Berkhout. "An average pig farm has 3,900 pigs and an average poultry farm has 45,000 laying hens. Those numbers will increase." Berkhout does not necessarily see scale enlargement as something negative. "The most important thing is that livestock farms comply with the law and produce our food as cleanly as possible. Costs for extra environmental investments often land on the farm rather than in the price of products. So it is quite logical that farmers want more animals to earn back the costs." At the same time, this does not mean that all small or medium-sized farms will disappear. "There is always a diversity of farms and that will remain so," Berkhout expects. "Small farms are often already less intensive or have additional sources of income, such as a farm shop. If they meet the standards, such farms can also continue to exist in the future." More than we eat ourselves The researchers conclude that food security is not endangered by the nitrogen plans. "The plans mainly affect the number of animals we keep in the Netherlands. We do import some beef, but for all other animal products we produce much more than we eat ourselves," says Berkhout. With the presentation of the nitrogen plans yesterday, in which not all details have been worked out and there are therefore still uncertainties, this research is not outdated according to Berkhout. "Things may still change, especially in the zones around nature areas, but the overall task for agriculture to reduce ammonia emissions by 42 to 46 percent has not changed. In broad terms, our conclusions therefore still hold."

title: Three men jailed for multi-million fraud with fake returns at Amazon
lead: Two men aged 30 and 32 from Hoogeveen and a man aged 34 from Emmer-Compascuum have been sentenced by the court in Assen to prison terms for defrauding the web shop Amazon. The three made millions with fake returns. They did this by ordering expensive items such as phones, smartwatches and other electronics and then sending the parcels back empty. They filled the boxes with worthless materials that matched the weight of the original shipment. As a result, Amazon processed it as a return and refunded the purchase amount. By chance The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> came across the three by chance. The 30-year-old main suspect was arrested in Hoogeveen in early 2023 after a shooting. In a warehouse, officers then found drugs and shelves full of luxury goods. Not long after, it became clear that a great many shipments were being sent back to Amazon from the man's address. The police soon discovered that he was not acting alone. In the house of a fellow resident they found more evidence of so-called 'refund fraud' in the form of cash, goods still packed in boxes, phones, computers and shipping labels. The man from Emmer-Compascuum also turned out to have accounts with the web shop through which many items were ordered and returned. In addition, he had money counting machines, shipping codes, empty envelopes, set squares and a barcode scanner at home. Demand of 2,5 million The man from Hoogeveen was sentenced to almost three years (35 months) in prison. His 32-year-old fellow resident must serve 20 months behind bars. The man from Emmer-Compascuum received a sentence of 10 months, of which 5 are suspended. In addition, he must perform 480 hours of community service. Amazon is also claiming total damages of around 2,5 million dollars from the three fraudsters, RTV Drenthe reports. The multinational can still take the matter to the civil court for that.

title: 'Human rights organisations are breaking off cooperation with the Court under American pressure'
lead: At least twenty human rights organisations have since last year significantly restricted or completely halted their cooperation with the International Criminal Court (ICC), based in The Hague. That is what emerges from a survey by investigative platform Investico and German medium Süddeutsche Zeitung of one hundred non-profit organisations, in cooperation with weekly De Groene Amsterdammer. Many NGOs no longer dare to work with the Court as a result of the sanctions the United States imposed on the Court in February last year. For example, several human rights organisations have stopped cooperating because their contracts with American funders forbid it. Several organisations have quietly stopped their work, Investico writes. This includes large organisations such as Human Rights Watch. Restrictive sanctions The Court is being hit hard by the sanctions, as research by news agency AP also showed earlier. US President Trump introduced those penalties by decree, after the Court issued arrest warrants against, among others, Israeli Prime Minister Netanyahu, for war crimes and crimes against humanity. That sanctions package consists of financial penalties and visa restrictions for people who help the ICC with its investigation into American nationals and allies of the US, such as Israel. Because of the sanctions, staff no longer have access to their property and assets in the US, such as money they hold in an American bank account. They also may no longer buy anything from American companies or use their services. Recently <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity>-Trump added to that with new financial measures that will largely take effect next year. In a video message, foreign minister Rubio said the US will prohibit "transactions with this rogue court". No evidence, no investigations The organisations with strong local networks are indispensable in preparing criminal cases, because they provide, among other things, evidence, eyewitness accounts and new forms of evidence with which the Court can proceed. They are also often the first on the ground and can share specialist expertise on local legislation. "They are a very important part of our work", says former chief prosecutor Fatou Bensouda to Investico. "They do not investigate for us, but they do provide us with tips, which allows us to find ways to substantiate evidence." Bensouda worked for the ICC until 2021 and was herself hit by American sanctions when she was placed on a blacklist in 2020. What does the International Criminal Court do? The International Criminal Court investigates, prosecutes and tries persons accused of human rights violations and serves as a complement to the national courts of member states. The Court investigates, among other things, genocide, war crimes and crimes against humanity. All countries in the European Union are obliged to carry out decisions of the Court, because of the Rome Statute. The Court is not recognised by all countries in the world. For example, the United States, Israel, Russia and Iran do not recognise the Court. The number of organisations that have halted cooperation may be higher. According to Investico, many NGOs refuse to speak openly with journalists about the consequences of the sanctions. A number of organisations did so. Save the Children Netherlands says it is having difficulty finding a new form of cooperation. The platform Forensic Architecture says it is reconsidering its working relationship with the ICC. Fear of more sanctions Investigations that at first glance have nothing to do with the United States or Israel are also being affected. "For example, a European organisation that conducts investigations in East Africa, the Middle East and Ukraine was forbidden by an American donor to use its money for the Court", Investico writes. European organisations that do not fall directly under the sanctions have also halted cooperation. "We cannot accept the risk of being sanctioned ourselves, and of all our other work being endangered as a result", a German NGO tells the researchers.

title: From Ukraine to Iran: Democrats' victory will have worldwide impact
lead: The resounding election victory of the Democrats in the midterm Congressional elections will have a major impact not only in the US but also abroad. Such a drastic reversal of the balance of power in Washington cannot go unnoticed in countries such as Ukraine, Iran and Israel. The difference will only become clear once the newly elected American members of Congress actually begin their work. That happens on 3 January. Then the election winners in the Capitol will take up powerful positions: the House of Representatives, <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Senaat</entity> and also the influential foreign affairs and intelligence committees in Congress are all expected to get Democratic chairs. That is why Trump will become what Americans call a lame duck: a crippled president. He will no longer have the comfortable relationship with a cooperative Republican majority in Congress. The Democrats will likely block his domestic political agenda and vice versa. A political stalemate looms. Still a lot of power. It is a well-known pattern in American politics that a lame-duck president shifts his attention to foreign policy. This is often seen as an attempt by the president to build his political legacy during his last two years in the White House. The American constitution gives the president a great deal of power in the area of foreign policy, a power Trump has already used extensively, for example by attacking Iran and imposing high trade tariffs on many countries. What can Congress do about that? And what will the rest of the world notice? Ukraine and Russia. This spring Trump stopped virtually all financial and military aid to Ukraine, leaving the country unable to defend itself against the Russian missiles and drones that claim victims there daily. And last month Trump lifted US sanctions on Russian diesel, by his own account to do something about high fuel prices in the US. The move went very much against Ukraine's wishes, because diesel sales fill the Russian war chest. Many members of Congress, including many Republicans, are angry about Trump's course toward Moscow and Kyiv. Congress could resume aid to Ukraine with a new law and stop imports of Russian fuel. Several Republicans in the current Congress are also outspoken supporters of that. Republicans in the new parliament will probably join them as well, if only to distance themselves from Trump's warm ties with Putin. If supporters of such a law secure a two-thirds majority in both the House and the Senate, Trump cannot even block the resumption of aid to Ukraine with a veto. Iran. "We must stop the war in Iran immediately," said the presumed Democratic chair of the new Congress, Hakeem Jeffries, to CNN. Trump did not ask Congress for permission to start the war in Iran, even though that is formally required. In the months that followed, the Democratic minority in Congress submitted several resolutions to force him to back down. One of them was adopted with the support of some Republicans, but was subsequently ignored by Trump. The new Democratic majority in both chambers has the power to restrict defense spending. With that, they could gain some grip on the war against Iran. Despite Democrat Jeffries' firm language, Congress cannot end the war on its own. However, the Democrats can prevent Trump from escalating on a large scale by simply not allocating money for it. The question is whether the Democrats will do that. Because Iran seems determined to keep the Strait of Hormuz in its grip and thereby keep gas and oil prices high on the world market. Some members of Congress may think that argues for continuing the war. An American capitulation there could also turn against the Democrats. So there is a chance Trump can still win Congress over on this point. Israel. Mainly because of the genocidal violence in Gaza and the close ties between Trump and Prime Minister Netanyahu, support for Israel among Democrats has fallen sharply. Under their leadership, Congress could halt the billions in American military aid to Israel. Just before the elections, Trump himself promised to do that, starting early next year. He said Israel does not need that aid and can henceforth pay for American weapons itself. It was a last-minute attempt to take the wind out of the Democrats' sails and came too late to make a difference. But with that statement in hand, it may become even easier in Congress to restrict direct aid to Israel. On the other hand, the Democrats remain deeply divided over Israel. When Democrats in Congress proposed halting aid to Israel last summer, less than half of their own representatives voted in favor. Even after the elections, there will be Democrats in Congress who want to spare Israel. The Democrats may reach a compromise among themselves and adopt a less far-reaching measure, such as halting the supply of heavy bombs to Israel or imposing sanctions on the country for the expansion of Jewish settlements on the West Bank. Humanitarian aid programs. Last year Trump stopped about 5 billion dollars in aid via USAID, which forced large foreign aid programs against hunger and for the prevention of diseases such as Ebola and AIDS to be shut down. Although the Democrats cannot undo those actions by Trump and cannot revive USAID, they can use laws to resume part of the foreign aid.

title: World Health Organization allows use of two new Ebola vaccines
lead: The World Health Organization (WHO) has approved two new Ebola vaccines, which can now be used in the large-scale Ebola outbreak in the Democratic Republic of Congo. Green light has been given to test the vaccinations within the infection hotspots in the country. The two vaccines are the first treatments specifically developed for the deadly Bundibugyo variant of the virus, which has been spreading in the country since May. The first vaccine is called 'ChAdOx1' and was developed by the University of Oxford and the Serum Institute of India. The second vaccine, called 'mRNA-1469', was developed by the pharmaceutical company Moderna. Strict protocols The vaccines have passed animal tests and trial phases on small groups of people. These mainly tested safety and possible side effects; it has not yet become clear whether the vaccines can stop an epidemic. Independent experts have reviewed the first test results and advised the WHO to test the treatments in Congo. This should make clear whether the vaccines are also effective on a large scale. The vaccines have not yet completed all the tests required to be placed on the market. The treatments may now be tested on the basis of strict international protocols. Vaccine for another variant Another vaccine is already widely used to combat the Ebola virus in Congo. The Ervebo vaccine is fully approved, but was developed for a different Ebola variant: the Zaire ebolavirus. It is still uncertain whether Ervebo offers sufficient protection against the new variant. Even so, Ervebo may be used because there is an emergency situation. This is the second-largest Ebola outbreak ever. It has so far cost 5000 people their lives in Congo. More than 10,000 people have been infected to date. The WHO has allocated thousands of doses of the new vaccines to Congo. Healthcare workers and direct contacts of patients are being vaccinated in the hope of slowing the spread. Ring vaccination strategy The country is using a so-called ring vaccination strategy, a method to contain the spread of a virus without having to vaccinate an entire population. The idea is that all people in the social circle of an Ebola patient are identified, as well as the contacts of these people. Both groups (rings) are vaccinated. If someone from the so-called first ring becomes infected, that person cannot spread the virus further because the people around them, the so-called second ring, are already immune. In addition to vaccinations, various other treatments and medicines are also being tested. For example, the drug 'MBP134' has proven effective against all Ebola variants, and virus inhibitors that may increase patients' chances of survival are also being examined. Not yet in view Figures on infections show that only a quarter of the new cases had contact with other patients. This means that the vast majority of new patients were infected by people who were not yet known to healthcare workers. Although concerns are great, the number of cases is not increasing exponentially. Recently, around 400 to 500 new infections have been registered each week.

title: Hungary makes public the names of informants who spied on citizens
lead: Hungary has made public tens of thousands of documents from the secret police of the communist era. The documents include, among other things, names, aliases and other details of nearly 60,000 former informants who spied on citizens during the regime. By making the documents public, the Hungarian government hopes the country will come to terms with its past. Between 1945 and 1989, the secret police in Hungary used informants to keep watch over the population. The informants had to seek out dissidents or others who resisted the regime and report them. These could also be family members, friends or colleagues. Intellectuals and athletes Some informants were blackmailed into spying on their surroundings, for example because the secret police had sensitive information about them. Others were persuaded with promises to do the work, such as receiving certain medical care or admission to a university. The secret police recruited, among others, people who had contacts abroad, but also hospitality staff, taxi drivers, intellectuals and athletes. Trauma The government has launched a website on which all Hungarians can look up information about informants from today. Prime Minister Magyar has asked his fellow countrymen to deal with the released documents "with dignity and humanity". "Many families will be confronted with painful information, often about a family member who has since passed away," Magyar said at a press conference. "It is impossible to process a trauma without engaging in dialogue and asking questions." The digitised documents in the database list, besides the real name and code name of an informant, among other things the date of birth, the address and the name of the mother. It also describes why, according to the secret service, an informant was recruited. Not all information is public. Some parts have been blacked out because they are privacy-sensitive. These include, for example, descriptions by the secret service of someone's state of health and sexual orientation. The database is not complete. Some documents were lost or destroyed during the Hungarian Revolution of 1956 against the communist regime and in the 1980s. Election promise By making the documents public, Magyar has fulfilled one of his promises half a year after his election victory. After the fall of communism in 1989, there was for a long time a lack of political will to publish the records. Next February, the details of some 25,000 recruited people are expected to be made public.

title: Finding a majority for the tax plan remains a complex puzzle for the minority cabinet
lead: It is still uncertain whether <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> will succeed in getting the tax plan for next year through parliament. Tonight in <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">de Tweede Kamer</entity> it appeared that many political maneuvers are probably needed to find a way out. Because the minority cabinet did not succeed in finding a majority in advance, the parliamentary groups now have the lead. Governing party D66 wants to talk with opposition parties Pro and Volt about their proposal to change the plans so that the tax on wealth goes up, in order to be able to lower the tax for workers. With the support of these parties, a majority for the tax plan in both the Tweede and <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Eerste Kamer</entity> is within reach. "I understand the direction," said D66 MP Oosterhuis about the proposal from Pro and Volt. But according to coalition partner VVD, such an amendment to the tax plan is in conflict with the coalition agreement. "It is unthinkable that this proposal in this form would be supported by one of the coalition parties," said VVD MP Van Eijk about it. Besides conflicting with the coalition agreement, such a 'millionaires tax' is according to her bad for the investment climate and therefore bad for the Netherlands. The CDA considers the opposition parties' proposal "going too far". MP Van Dijk also sees "that there are a number of points in it that touch on what we agreed in the coalition agreement". She could not yet say whether her party could support it. But her <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">fractievoorzitter Bontenbal</entity> said yesterday that he is not happy that the cabinet is "gambling" on a majority for the tax plan. He accused the VVD of an overly rigid attitude on taxing wealth. In the Tweede Kamer a small majority can still be found, but in the Senate it is still far away. Business transfer In total, Pro and Volt want to shift 1.5 billion euros from the tax on labour to the tax on wealth. Part of that, 180 million euros, must come from abolishing a tax-favorable scheme for transferring a business. The minority cabinet's coalition agreement states precisely that this scheme should be left untouched. Pro-<entity id="person:jesse-feras-klaver">leider Klaver</entity> made clear that he has "gone deep" with his proposal. He accepts that income tax for workers goes up, but with his amendment proposal it is somewhat less. "It is an attempt to make it fairer. Everyone must contribute, not only workers." He is willing to negotiate the precise details. Divided votes If the proposal from Pro and Volt is amended so that it no longer conflicts with the coalition agreement, it could still be the key to a solution. The coalition parties do not rule out that they will vote in a divided way, although CDA MP Van Dijk said that this is "certainly not the intention". During the votes, the amendments proposed by the MPs are voted on first. If such an amendment is adopted, it immediately becomes part of the tax plan. Only after that is the entire plan voted on. It is possible that parties vote against an amendment but still support the final tax plan. In the corridors a scenario is circulating that the VVD votes against the part of the tax plan on the higher wealth tax, but accepts that the proposal gets a majority with the support of D66 and CDA anyway. That would save the tax plan and the coalition. In the debate, the coalition parties did not respond to questions about this. In the coming days much can still be negotiated and therefore the plans can still change. The votes on the tax plan are scheduled for next week Thursday, 12 November.

title: Conductor Herbert Blomstedt (99) has died
lead: The Swedish conductor Herbert Blomstedt has died at the age of 99. His management announced this. Blomstedt led the Concertgebouw Orchestra dozens of times between 1983 and 2023. "We will miss his modesty, his great musical dedication and his warm personality", the Concertgebouw Orchestra writes about the conductor, who was born in 1927 in the United States to Swedish parents. Blomstedt made his debut in 1954 with the Royal Stockholm Philharmonic Orchestra. He led various orchestras in Sweden, Norway and Denmark before moving to Germany in the 1970s. There Blomstedt became conductor of the Staatskapelle Dresden. Later he was also chief conductor of the Gewandhausorchester Leipzig and the San Francisco Symphony Orchestra. For his work and albums he received, among other awards, two Grammys, the British Gramophone Classical Music Award and the French Grand Prix du Disque. In an interview the Swede once said that his mission is "to let as many people as possible enjoy good music. It makes you think differently. You get a sharper sense of proportion and beauty from it." Final performance Blomstedt died on Wednesday at his home in the Swedish city of Gothenburg. He last performed in May. He then led the San Francisco Symphony Orchestra, although it was difficult. Blomstedt came onto the stage in a wheelchair and had difficulty bringing Gustav Mahler's Ninth Symphony (composed between 1909 and 1910 and his last completed symphony) to a good conclusion.
