If they make use of it, that can, together with costs for an unplanned landing, such as extra fuel, port fees and handling, run into the tens of thousands of euros." Unrest among passengers For airlines, a bomb threat therefore costs extra money, while they are already struggling with high fuel prices and restrictions, such as the closure of airspace above Russia and Ukraine. Aviation expert Joris Melkert considers the damage to airlines still manageable for now. "Financially this is annoying for the airlines, but in terms of total revenue it is still manageable for now." Any costs may ultimately also be passed on in ticket prices. Melkert also points out that only a limited number of flights were affected by a bomb threat. "Schiphol alone has more than a thousand aircraft movements every day." However, according to the aviation expert, it may lead to unrest among people who are considering booking a flight. Assessing the threat Bart van den Berg, security and defence expert at the Clingendael Institute, says the same. "The biggest consequence of these bomb threats is social unrest. Such a bomb threat has a psychological effect. It naturally also gets a lot of media attention, and that gives people a sense of insecurity." Van den Berg points out that it is difficult for airlines to assess the threat. "There are many reports now, but they all turn out to be false. Airlines now have to judge which reports may be real and which are false. It would be just your luck if there were thirty false reports and the next one was real, while you had not assessed it that way."

title: US carries out first attack on Iran since elections
lead: The American military carried out an attack on Iran last night, the first since the midterm elections in the US last Tuesday. President Trump has confirmed the action. According to him, it was "a small attack". Iranian state media report, based on witnesses, that two projectiles hit the Suza area on the island of Qeshm. That island is in a strategic position in the Strait of Hormuz and houses important military bases. Before the impacts, according to the witnesses, the sound of an aircraft could be heard above the island. Nothing is known yet about damage. The Iranian military does state that it shot down an American MQ-9 Reaper, a drone, above Qeshm. 'Within a quarter of an hour' For some time it has been assumed that President Trump is preparing a large, multi-day attack on Iran. He reportedly postponed it until after the elections, hoping not to be held accountable by American voters. Nevertheless, his Republican party suffered a major defeat on Tuesday. About the "small" attack last night, Trump told reporters that Iranian anti-aircraft guns had been destroyed. That happened, according to him, quickly, "within about fifteen minutes, maybe five". He gave no further details. Earlier in the day he said that diplomatic talks are still ongoing about an end to the war. According to him, those talks with representatives of the Iranian regime are going "very well". 20 million dollar reward Meanwhile, Central Command, which oversees American military operations in the Middle East, has offered a million-dollar reward for tips about Iran's nuclear programme. The money will be paid for valuable information about, for example, "facilities, equipment and personnel involved, such as scientists", according to a post on X. The reward can rise to 20 million dollars. The tipster is also offered "possible relocation".

title: Billions of euros for CO2 storage, but success is not yet assured
lead: The sustainability transition of industry is moving more slowly than it should in order to meet the climate targets. To keep those targets from disappearing even further out of sight, <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> is putting extra money into capturing and storing greenhouse gas. The first project in the Netherlands for CO2 storage is Porthos, which is due to start next year in Rotterdam. With 1.3 billion euros in extra government support, much more CO2 must still be stored. This concerns the larger Aramis project, in which CO2 from the Netherlands, Germany and Belgium disappears under the North Sea. Despite the extra subsidy, success is not yet assured, because companies are hesitating. Technical delay The former gas production platform P18-A lies 20 kilometres off the coast of Rotterdam. It is currently being converted into an injection platform for CO2 for Porthos. Initially the first CO2 was to disappear beneath the seabed by the end of this year, but the project is being delayed by several technical causes. Part of the CO2 from, among others, the oil refineries of Shell and ExxonMobil will soon be captured. These greenhouse gases will then no longer go into the atmosphere through chimneys, but through a 30 kilometre long pipeline to the very tip of the Maasvlakte. There the CO2 is pumped under high pressure at a compressor station into a subsea pipeline to the injection platform, where it is stored permanently in a largely empty gas field 3.5 kilometres under the seabed. Ten percent captured Each year Porthos can capture 2.5 megatonnes of CO2, which is about ten percent of all emissions in the Rotterdam port. Most of it comes from Shell's oil refinery in Pernis, which can thereby reduce its emissions by 20 percent. The remaining CO2 comes from Exxon Mobil, Air Products and Air Liquide. Watch here the report we made on the injection platform in the North Sea: it is called CCS; the English abbreviation of Carbon Capture and Storage . Opposition from the environmental movement The environmental movement long saw it as an expensive government measure with which fossil fuel companies could postpone real sustainability. Necessary for climate Scientists call CO2 capture necessary, especially now that many other measures are lagging behind and the temperature on Earth is rising faster than expected. Porthos is not the only CCS project in Europe. For example, fertiliser factory Yara in Sluiskil in Zeeland captures CO2, which goes by ship to Norway and is stored there under the seabed. There is also a number of smaller commercial CCS initiatives. In the Netherlands, attention is now focused mainly on the Aramis project, the major successor to Porthos. Waste incineration plants, Tata Steel, cement factories and the chemical industry could limit their CO2 emissions with it. Industry is responsible for roughly a third of the total emissions in the Netherlands. Despite subsidy schemes, companies currently show little appetite for participating in Aramis. It involves enormous investments, the returns of which are uncertain. Polluting is cheaper Companies that emit a lot of CO2 must buy rights through the European ETS system. The available emission rights and their price determine the cost of emissions for industry. These rights are currently priced too low to make costly sustainability measures commercially attractive. As a result, it is now cheaper to emit than to capture CO2 and store it. Last year Shell and TotalEnergies withdrew from building the transport infrastructure for Aramis, which will have a much longer underground pipeline than Porthos. The costs of building Aramis must now be fully borne by the state-owned companies <entity id="org:zbo-economie-bedrijven-en-nationale-rekeningen">EBN</entity> and Gasunie. Large customers sought With the extra subsidy of 1.3 billion euros, construction of Aramis can start with fewer participants. Even so, the business model with this subsidy is still not settled. A number of large customers will still need to come on board in order to take a final investment decision next year. Those companies must not only participate in the Aramis project, but also ensure that their CO2 is captured and arrives in Rotterdam. That can be done with pipelines or ships. All in all, it is an expensive investment. An investment that requires not only money, but also long-term certainty. Certainty about CO2 prices and stability of government policy.

title: Wake-up call 7/11: CDA holds party congress • European cyclocross championships in Zeddam
lead: Good morning! CDA <entity id="person:hendrik-bontenbal">leider Bontenbal</entity> addresses his party at a precarious moment for his minority coalition, and the women ride the European cyclocross championships in Zeddam. First the weather: The day starts locally with fog. It is variable cloudiness and mostly dry in most places. With little wind it will be 7 to 10 degrees. In the east of the country it stays fairly sunny for a long time. Elsewhere more cloud occurs and in the north fog is also possible at first. Depending on the amount of sun it will be 6 to 10 degrees. The wind is weak and blows from the south. The outlook for the coming days; watch the NOS Weather from last night here again: Are you going out today? Here you can find an overview of traffic jams and roadworks, and here you can see the situation on the rail network. What can you expect today? What did you miss? The American army carried out an attack on Iran overnight. It was the first since the interim elections last Tuesday. President Trump confirmed the attack. According to him it was "a small attack". Iranian state media report, based on witnesses, that two projectiles hit the Suza area on the island of Qeshm. That island has a strategic position in the Strait of Hormuz and houses important military bases. Before the impacts, according to the witnesses, the sound of an aircraft could be heard above the island. Other news from the night: And then just this: Pope Leo has arrived for a tour of several South American countries. In his second homeland of Peru he can encounter himself magnified: in the capital Lima a 14-metre-high statue of him has been placed, according to the artist the largest of this pope worldwide. Have a nice day!

title: Seven burglars taken off a roof in Groningen by cherry picker
lead: Seven burglars were arrested on the roof of a company in Groningen. The suspects were brought down with a cherry picker from the fire service, local media report. All suspects were taken to the police station. Their identities are not known. It is also not known whether any suspects fled. After the arrest of the seven, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> still searched the premises, but no one else was found there.

title: Mexican police shoot girl (7) dead at protest against arrest of drug criminal
lead: During an action against drug crime in Mexico, police shot and killed a 7-year-old girl. This happened in the city of Matamoros, which lies on the American border with Texas. The murdered girl held American nationality. Parts of the city had been unrest for days. Last week police arrested a local drug criminal, and in protest armed men blocked roads. To break those blockades, police went into action yesterday. According to justice authorities, officers in helicopters were fired upon from the ground and fired back. The girl, who was sitting in a car, did not survive that. Chase: The mother of the victim tells Mexican media that she was in the car with her family when a helicopter began to chase them. Her husband reportedly got out to make clear they were civilians and that there were children in the car, but shots were nonetheless fired. An investigation has been launched into the officers involved. They have not been detained.

title: More people with confused behaviour, putting pressure on care and the judiciary
lead: The nuisance caused by people with confused behaviour increases every year. Where the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> still had to act just over 66,000 times in 2015, last year it was already nearly 170,000 times. This year too, looking at the figures up to September, the number of reports is rising again, with an interim total of 149,519 incidents. Criminal judges Elmy Elderman and Joyce de Ruiter of the <entity id="org:rechtbank-overijssel">rechtbank Overijssel</entity> are concerned about this growing problem in society. "We cannot solve it. Administrators think: lock them up, then they're off the street. But afterwards they come back onto the street, untreated and without care", De Ruiter explains. It concerns a small group of people with serious psychiatric problems, often combined with an addiction. The umbrella organisation Council for the Judiciary endorses what the two criminal judges raise. Naked on the street Often it involves minor offences, from shoplifting to walking naked on the street, shouting and tearing down the door of the night shelter, but the pressure on care and the legal system is great because of this. Criminal judge Elderman: "With this kind of incident the entire criminal chain is under pressure: police, justice, probation and finally the prisons. And we often see these people come back." Both the criminal judges and the Council for the Judiciary think that intervention should happen earlier, and not by a judge. "Criminal law as an intervention is not always suitable or effective. By reaching non-criminal interventions at an earlier stage, it can be prevented that people end up in the criminal chain. That also contributes to preventing unnecessary victimhood and also unnecessary perpetration. The whole of society benefits from that", according to a spokesperson for the council. Psychiatrist Josephine Lenssen, medical director at mental health provider Dimence Groep in Overijssel, also shares the concerns about these people, who do not get the right help. "Our care workers spend days calling around the country for suitable housing. You can imagine that time could be spent differently." These vulnerable people often become homeless again as soon as they leave detention, and then the problems start all over again. Protected housing Protected housing offers these people the support that seems necessary to avoid falling into a negative spiral, says Lenssen. "If they have more continuity in housing, that relapse does not happen. There they get the protection that is needed, so that they don't keep falling off the wagon." The law offers possibilities to impose protected housing as part of the sentence, but often there is no place for it. In many cases it concerns intensive long-term care, where people may stay for their whole lives. 't Kastheel in Kampen is such a location, where people can live under supervision for the rest of their lives. Founder Bas de Greef compares it to wearing a corset. "When someone is doing well, we loosen the strings a bit; if someone relapses, we pull the strings tighter. But the corset stays on, and this group of people benefits from that." Housing groups needed De Greef is in talks with the ministries of Health and <entity id="org:ministerie-van-justitie-en-veiligheid">Justitie en Veiligheid</entity>. According to him, there is also an awareness there that such housing groups are needed to offer shelter to the growing group of people with confused behaviour causing nuisance. At present the locations are still scarce, Elderman and De Ruiter also see. "Very worrying, we see this group of confused people appearing before the court more and more. And new groups are also joining, which you actually want to prevent." Listen to our podcast Aid organisations already warned in March that pressure on care, shelter and the police from people with confused behaviour is increasing. Listen to the episode of the podcast De Dag on this via <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> Or listen via another podcast channel.

title: Former Middle East correspondent Thomas Loudon (56) has died
lead: Journalist and former correspondent Thomas Loudon has died. He suffered from neuroendocrine tumours (NET), a slow-growing form of cancer. He was diagnosed last year and this week he died from it. He was 56 years old. In 2001 Loudon became the first Dutch (video) journalist to settle in Iran after the Islamic Revolution. He reported in various languages on developments in Iran, Afghanistan and northern Iraq for, among others, the NOS, Trouw and Elsevier, but also for foreign media such as CNN, Chile's Canal 13 and Asia TV in Singapore. Egypt and Jordan In 2003 he moved to the Egyptian capital Cairo, where he became Middle East correspondent for the NOS. After that he worked from Jordan. He made, among other things, reports on the American war in Iraq. He remained a correspondent until early 2007, after which he returned to the Netherlands. In the years that followed he was active as a journalism teacher in Groningen and Rotterdam. He also founded his own organisation to support journalists in countries where press freedom is under pressure. In addition, Loudon developed platforms for video journalists and for political cartoons. In recent years Loudon was active as a documentary maker. He focused on themes such as economic growth, waste and sustainability. Loudon was also an actor. He played roles in, among others, the series De Joodse Raad , Flikken Maastricht, Gooische Vrouwen and The Spectacular .

title: Democratic sheriffs, prosecutors and regional officials also elected, what do they do?
lead: "Blue, blue, blue, blue," colored the US map with the results of the midterm elections. The Democrats not only won seats from the Republicans in Congress, but also defeated their opponents at the local level. Midterm elections always also include votes for administrative positions in the American states. Governors, sheriffs, chief prosecutors and, for example, chairs of the <entity id="org:onderwijsraad">onderwijsraad</entity> are elected this way. In this way the Democrats have penetrated to the very core of America. Executive power In Texas, Nevada, Iowa, Ohio and Georgia the Democrats took the governorship from the Republicans, and the deep-red states Alaska and Kansas may follow. Governors have a lot of power. They are a kind of president in their state, and each of them also has its own House of Representatives and Senate. A governor is in charge of budgets and can both introduce and veto bills. An important theme in the Democratic campaign in Texas, Georgia and Ohio was the arrival of data centers. The new Democratic governors in Georgia and Ohio want to introduce restrictions on data centers. And Gina Hinojosa, who was elected as the first Latina governor in Texas, promised there will be a moratorium on developing data centers in her state. Texas in particular has shown in recent years how far a governor's power reaches. For twelve years Republican Greg Abbott called the shots there. He was one of the most important partners of President Trump in the hard-line immigration policy and often went a step further. Abbott launched Operation Lone Star State, a border operation for which he allocated billions and deployed thousands of National Guard soldiers. As a form of protest, he also sent buses with tens of thousands of immigrants to Democratic cities such as New York and Washington. Sheriffs and judges In many states the Democrats also won the races for lieutenant governor (a kind of vice president), minister of Finance and sheriff. For example, in a district in Maryland a Democratic sheriff was elected for the first time in two decades. Republican Chuck Jenkins had been chief of police there since 2006 and was known for his anti-immigration policy. Jenkins worked closely with the immigration agency ICE. His Democratic opponent has said she will no longer do that. The judiciary at the local level is also elected. The Supreme Court is the highest judicial body in each state. It decides on matters such as abortion, the death penalty and who may marry whom. For example, the Texas Supreme Court blocked attempts to broaden the abortion law. At the moment, abortion may only be performed when the mother's life is in danger. In Texas, the Democrats on Tuesday won seats on the Supreme Court for the first time since 1994. As a result, four of the nine seats are now in Democratic hands. New chief prosecutor This victory may have a sequel. Republican judge James Sullivan lost to a Democrat and is losing his position on the Texas Supreme Court. According to news agency Reuters, President Trump may want to quickly appoint him as a federal judge, a position Sullivan may hold for life. Chief prosecutor Ken Paxton, who ran for a Senate seat but lost to James Talarico, is also leaving a vacancy. He will be succeeded by a Democrat. Trump loyalist Paxton sued the states Georgia, Michigan, Pennsylvania and Wisconsin in 2020, after Joe Biden had won the presidential elections. He claimed there had been electoral fraud, a claim for which he never provided convincing evidence. Education and culture war Texas also led the culture war between conservatives and progressives. Together with Florida, Texas formed ground zero of the battle of ideas in education. In these elections, at least four seats on the education department went to the Democrats. That department sets policy for public schools in Texas. The members of the education council decide what is taught in schools, which teaching materials are approved, and what requirements students must meet for a diploma. The Republicans had long held the majority in the education department. They allowed mandatory Bible readings for all students in public schools and approved teaching methods that trivialise American slavery. Banned books Last year, more than 8,000 books were also banned in public schools in the state. On that list of banned books is the biography of Michelle Obama and also, for example, the Harry Potter series. It was said to promote witchcraft. The Democrats are already hinting at a change of course in the classroom. For example, religion must again move further into the background, and they prefer to focus on funding for education. High on the wish list: more money for public schools and teachers.

title: Judge reverses tariff increase on Amsterdam canal boat tax
lead: A judge has reversed a tariff increase on the canal boat tax in Amsterdam. Shipping company Stromma will now once again pay the city 1.50 euros per canal boat passenger instead of 2.70 euros. The court points out that it is unclear what the city provided in return for the additional tax. According to local broadcaster AT5, part of the revenue was also spent on things that a canal boat company gets no benefit from, such as free public transport for children. Retribution Since January 2020, Amsterdam has levied a tax on all events that take place 'on' the water, the so-called entertainment retribution. The city argued that maintaining the canals and other waterways costs a lot of money and initially charged 1.50 euros per canal boat passenger or visitor to a (large) party on a vessel. In 2024, the college of mayor and aldermen wanted to raise the rate to 2.00 euros. The city council decided to add 50 cents on top of that. Later the rate went to 2.60 euros, and this year it is 2.70 euros. The levy is mostly passed on to passengers. Not substantiated After the tax for the years 2024 and 2025 had been paid, shipping company Stromma objected to the tariff increase. According to Stromma, the city did not justify the purpose of the additional levy. The city defended the increase, saying it would lead to a "fairer contribution from visitors to the city". Because the number of visitors is rising rapidly, Amsterdam also has much more to pay for maintaining facilities that operators benefit from, the levy official argued at court. Extra money But the court now states, just like Stromma, that the city does not substantiate how much (additional) money is needed for that exactly. The judge is particularly critical of the fact that part of the tax revenue is not spent on maintaining the canals. It goes to, for example, free public transport for children, greening of public space and a teachers' grant. "Facilities from which the entertainment involved in the levy derives no benefit at all", the court said. Repayment The tariff increase is reversed retroactively to the third quarter of 2024. Amsterdam must therefore repay the overpaid money to Stromma. The judge leaves open what the ruling means for the other canal boat companies and organisers of parties on vessels in Amsterdam. But given the court's reasoning, it is plausible that they too will revert to the rate of 1.50 euros per passenger.

title: New Zealand election neck-and-neck race, possible key role for newcomer
lead: The parliamentary elections in New Zealand have ended in a neck-and-neck race. The centre-right National Party of Prime Minister Chris Luxon is level with the largest opposition party, Labour under Chris Hipkins. With just over 95 percent of the votes counted, both parties are hovering just below 30 percent. A few thousand votes separate the two. "New Zealand has spoken, but it may take a little longer to work out exactly what it said," Hipkins joked in his speech on election night. According to the Labour leader, it is clear that parties must cooperate. Luxon also said it was "too close to call". He congratulated opposition leader Hipkins on a "hard-fought election campaign" and did not yet want to anticipate negotiations on a coalition. Cooperation between the two parties is in any case ruled out: that has never happened before. That is why one of the two parties will have to form a coalition with other parties. The election result means that smaller and newer parties will probably get a key role in this. It may therefore take days before it is clear who can form a government. Desire for change One thing is certain: a man named Chris will become prime minister of New Zealand. Yet the results are historically poor for both parties. For example, the National Party has lost around 10 percentage points compared with three years ago, and Labour also disappointed. It is clear that many Kiwis want change. The sitting conservative coalition government came to power three years ago with the promise to pull the economy out of the doldrums, but that has not succeeded. New Zealanders are frustrated by the extremely high cost of living, stubbornly high unemployment and a stagnating economy. There is also a housing crisis. "The cost of living is extremely high, and that is the most important issue for most people," says economist and professor Robert MacCulloch of the University of Auckland. "The current government has not been able to improve the economy. But there is also little confidence in Labour, which left the country in a very bad economic position after the coronavirus pandemic. People are simply not very impressed by the two traditional governing parties." The sluggish economy is leading many young, highly educated people to decide to leave the country. Last year a record number of New Zealanders moved abroad in search of a better life. That was nearly 68,000 people, more than 185 per day. More than 60 percent move to Australia, where they often earn thousands of dollars more than for the same work at home. The small, relatively new Opportunity party, led by 38-year-old Qiulae Wong, heard this discontent among young people and gave it a voice. For the first time the party has reached the 5 percent threshold needed for a seat in parliament. "New Zealanders are done with the status quo. They have made their voices heard, and they are saying it can be better," Wong said on election night to an elated crowd. She was welcomed as a heroine. "We believe we can change the way we do politics, with a focus on the future and the next generation." The new party in parliament will probably play an important role in the coalition talks, whether these turn out to be left or right. Notably, rights for the Maori, the indigenous population, were not an important theme for most political parties in the election campaign. Only the Maori party Te Pati Maori put the position of the original inhabitants high on the agenda. Recent research by Ipsos showed that nearly 80 percent of New Zealanders think it is important to protect Maori culture. Yet only 3 percent of respondents said these themes were the most important to them. The final allocation of seats in parliament will not be announced until the end of this month by the electoral commission. The final result is probably not clear until three weeks from now. Forming a coalition government may also take a long time.

title: Motorist assaults trucker after failed overtaking attempt in Breda
lead: A motorist (44) is suspected of assaulting the driver of a truck after a failed overtaking attempt this morning in Breda. The motorist, who was himself injured in the manoeuvre, was arrested shortly afterwards at his home in Breda, reports Omroep Brabant. The accident happened around 09.00 on the Westerhagelaan, close to the A16 motorway. According to the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity>, the motorist wanted to overtake the truck driving in front of him. In doing so he left the road, drove over the pavement and through the verge, and then his car overturned. Threatened The police state that the motorist then got out and threatened and assaulted the trucker. The man fled, but could be tracked down quickly. After his arrest he was taken to hospital by ambulance. Besides assault and threats, he is also suspected of leaving the scene of an accident and refusing a breath test. The police have not disclosed whether the truck driver was injured in the assault.

title: CDA leader Bontenbal: crucial moment for minority coalition
lead: CDA leader Bontenbal wants to do "everything" in the coming week to help the tax plan get a majority. He said so at a CDA congress in Almere, on the eve of what is set to be a tense week for the minority coalition. Without enough support in the Eerste and <entity id="org:tweede-kamer">Tweede Kamer</entity>, <entity id="org:kabinet">het kabinet</entity> can do nothing, according to Bontenbal. He repeated that he finds it irresponsible to send the tax plan to <entity id="org:eerste-kamer">de Eerste Kamer</entity> in that case, and he called on all parties to cooperate. He spoke of a crucial moment for the minority coalition. The CDA leader said this at the congress: This week the cabinet sent the tax plan to the Chamber after months of difficult negotiations with the opposition, again with some adjustments. The hope was that a debate would produce a majority. After a debate lasting hours, it turned out that parliament could not agree either. A majority in the Tweede Kamer may seem to be in sight, but in the Eerste Kamer it is far from it. That requires support from either left-wing parties such as Pro and Volt, or right-wing parties such as BBB, JA21 and SGP. The demands these parties make in exchange for their support divide the coalition: the VVD prefers to lean right, while D66 and the CDA lean left. Bontenbal does not name the VVD now. Still, CDA leader Bontenbal hopes for a deal. Today at the congress he praised 50Plus and the ChristenUnie for their constructive attitude. Earlier this week he said on the talk show Eva that the VVD should move on taxing the wealthy and should not block the route with Pro. Now he did not name the VVD. Bontenbal's call for cooperation was accompanied by concerns about democracy worldwide, in which he cited, among other things, the situation in France. According to him, the riots and unrest there show that political division is making it increasingly difficult to take political responsibility. "We cannot defeat political division with even more division." Whether the coalition in our country itself manages to really bridge its internal divisions will become clear in the coming days. In a last-ditch attempt to solve the problems, faction leaders are separately contacting opposition parties. Chaos looms Pro and Volt want to support the tax plan if 1.5 billion euros is shifted from the tax on workers to the tax on the wealthy. The VVD considers the plan to be in conflict with the coalition agreement and bad for businesses and entrepreneurs. The CDA and D66 do see merit in the direction of the plan. It was agreed last week that the parties may vote separately, but the VVD said afterwards that it is unthinkable that the coalition supports the plan "in this form". In the coming days it will become clear whether and how the opposition and coalition can still reach a "form" with which they can get through. The call for cooperation applies to all parties, Bontenbal said. Without going into the substance of negotiations, "perhaps the CDA base will not be happy either" with "deals that I may conclude in the coming days". The tax plan will be voted on Thursday. Without a majority, chaos may arise. The Eerste Kamer votes on the tax plan at the end of this month. If it is then rejected, provisional assessments for millions of taxpayers will no longer be correct, with enormous consequences for both citizens and the <entity id="org:belastingdienst">Belastingdienst</entity>.

title: Cohen and Van Aartsen join Red Line: 'We must call it genocide'
lead: Former politicians Job Cohen and Jozias van Aartsen will join the Red Line protest in <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity> tomorrow. That is what the two veterans of the PvdA and the VVD say in an extensive interview in de Volkskrant. At the protest, demonstrators demand action from the Dutch <entity id="org:kabinet">kabinet</entity> against Israel "to definitively end the illegal occupation of Palestine". It is the fourth time the protest is being held. Both Cohen and Van Aartsen are joining for the first time. The two speak of a genocide in Gaza. "You cannot avoid calling it that," says the 79-year-old Cohen. Disagreeing with own party: In the current cabinet, the VVD rarely criticises Israel. Van Aartsen, among others former <entity id="pos:minister-van-buitenlandse-zaken">minister van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> on behalf of the party, says he completely disagrees with that party line. "It would become a party that says it is liberal to defend core values such as humanity and international law. But they stand by and watch." Jetten currently shows no leadership, says the former mayor of <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity>. He also finds it not courageous that Jetten, as prime minister, does not keep what he promised, according to him. Jetten marched with the protest last year, then as a member of the House of Representatives. On social media he spoke of goosebumps and said: "Do everything in your power to stop Israel from starving and killing innocent Palestinians." Yesterday Jetten still said that the Netherlands is not going to take additional measures against Israel. According to the prime minister, the Netherlands is already sticking its neck out, and pressure on the Israeli government works better if it comes from a broad front from Europe. According to the prime minister, the Netherlands is conducting bilateral talks with Israel, among other things, and the cabinet has stepped up humanitarian aid in recent months. Van Aartsen advocates taking measures independently of Europe. "The Netherlands can take these measures independently. And consequences must also be attached to them." Struggling with the situation: Last year Cohen still opposed his party's proposal to impose a full arms embargo on Israel. Now the former <entity id="pos:burgemeester-amsterdam">burgemeester van Amsterdam</entity> says that since Hamas's attacks on 7 October 2023 he has been struggling greatly with the situation. "As a Jewish man, I find the existence of Israel important, but at the same time I saw that the Israeli government kept going and slowly moved towards genocide", a term that for him is linked to the Holocaust in the Second World War. "The Holocaust is the most terrible thing we have experienced in the last century. And what was it about? That certain people no longer belonged because of who they were. The same is now happening to the Arabs," said Cohen in the interview. Letter: Yesterday Cohen and Van Aartsen, together with 279 former cabinet members, former diplomats, former civil servants and civil servants, sent a letter to Jetten calling for firm measures against Israel. The cabinet has not yet responded to the letter.

title: EU investigation into possible fraud with subsidies for rail maintenance in Spain after accident
lead: The European Public Prosecutor's Office (EOM) has opened a second investigation into possible fraud with EU subsidies, which were intended for the renovation and modernisation of the safety, signalling and communication systems on the Madrid-Seville high-speed line. On this route, a high-speed train collided at full speed with a stationary train near the village of Urda, 140 kilometres south of Madrid, last week. 69 people died and dozens were injured. The accident happened after trains had come to a standstill due to a malfunction on the high-speed line from Madrid to Andalusia. Air traffic control then gave the trains permission to continue at normal speed, including the rear one. The agreements normally state that driving must then take place at a maximum of 40 km/h, but that did not happen. Meanwhile, the driver of the front train, who had also been told he could proceed, did not manage to start his vehicle. He therefore remained stationary, after which the collision followed. The investigation focuses on the rail infrastructure manager (ADIF), the Spanish state agency for railway safety (AESF) and the Spanish Court of Audit. The investigation was started on the EOM's own initiative and is supported by the Spanish Guardia Civil. The EOM says it will only make the start of the investigation public because of the great public interest, but will not share any further details. Earlier investigation There was already an investigation into possible fraud with EU funds that were intended for rail maintenance on the high-speed line. The EOM started this in March, after a train accident near the village of Adamuz in January this year. Two high-speed trains derailed on the same route. 46 people died and more than 120 people were injured. Spanish Minister of Transport Puente resigned this week. Because of the two fatal train disasters this year, his position as Minister of Transport came under pressure. There was great anger and fear among the Spanish after the accident. There was a question of whether residents could travel safely by train. Politics The number of serious accidents on the Spanish railways has increased over the past ten years, with the most fatal accidents in recent history in the past four years. There were already concerns for some time about the state of the rail network. Ahead of the Spanish elections on 29 November, politicians appear to be seizing on the problems on the railways to campaign. Far-right leader Santiago Abascal called transport minister Puente "minister of death". Alberto Núñez Feijóo, prime ministerial candidate for the largest opposition party, said that residents have "the right" to be informed about the "state of the railways and safety systems, which warnings have been received, which measures have been taken and which actions have been undertaken".

title: Ships collide in thick fog on the Maas near Den Bosch
lead: Two cargo ships collided this morning in thick fog on the Maas, not far from Den Bosch. There are no reports of injuries. One of the two ships was badly damaged. The collision happened around 11.15 am, reports Omroep Brabant. A container ship with an estimated ninety containers hit the side of a smaller cargo ship that, according to unconfirmed reports, was carrying dredging sludge. Dent A dent of about one and a half metres formed in the hull of the ship carrying the sludge. The covers used to seal the cargo were also damaged. The container ship is said to have suffered considerably less damage. After the collision, the ships sailed under their own power to a side branch of the Maas and moored there. The water police are now launching an investigation into the cause of the collision. Because the ships are no longer on the main shipping route, shipping traffic is not experiencing any disruption from the accident.

title: Wind turbines forced through by the province will often be switched off
lead: The wind turbines that will be built against the wishes of municipalities, on orders from the <entity id="org:provincie-utrecht">provincie Utrecht</entity>, will most likely stand still for hours on end. That is due to the overloaded power grid. According to grid operator Stedin, the problem mainly occurs on sunny and windy days. Then so much electricity is generated by solar panels that the grid cannot handle the extra power from wind turbines, RTV Utrecht reports. The province of Utrecht has been fiercely debating the construction of wind turbines for years. Almost three years ago, the province designated 27 locations that would be suitable for generating a lot of wind energy. But many municipalities and residents are opposed. Breeding birds "Of course we are not cooperating with this provincial project in any way," alderman Dick Polman of the <entity id="org:gemeente-stichtse-vecht">gemeente Stichtse Vecht</entity> responded immediately. In <entity id="org:gemeente-oudewater">Oudewater</entity>, residents protested against the construction of wind turbines because they would disturb breeding birds and cause (noise) nuisance. The <entity id="org:gemeenteraad-montfoort">gemeenteraad van Montfoort</entity> reluctantly agreed last week to the construction of two wind turbines. In <entity id="org:gemeente-amersfoort">Amersfoort</entity>, the decision-making was not moving fast enough for the province. While the municipal council was still hesitating, the province decided this week to build two wind turbines there as well. Under conditions That haste is remarkable. Because, regional grid operator Stedin says, new solar fields and wind turbines can only be connected to the power grid under certain conditions. One of those conditions is that the wind turbines are switched off at peak moments. At peak moments, especially on summer days when the sun shines and the wind blows, the already busy grid quickly fills up with electricity from solar panels. No more power can be added then. Solar peak It is impossible to predict how often those peak moments will occur, says a spokesperson for Stedin. "The 'solar peak' in May, June and July is much higher and longer than in March", he expects. But whether and for how long a wind turbine has to be 'off' cannot be said. That differs from place to place. Quickly switching a wind turbine on and off is in any case impossible, according to the spokesperson. Once a wind turbine is turning, it must be able to run for a few hours. The spokesperson: "if we expect it to be a sunny and windy day, the output of the wind turbine will be limited for several hours. When the sun then goes away, the wind turbines can run at full capacity again." Solution A solution to the overloaded power grid is a long time coming. National grid operator Tennet says that this first requires the expansion and construction of several high-voltage substations. But those substations are also controversial. For example, municipalities and nearby residents are joining forces against the construction of what they call a "colossal high-voltage substation" of just over 20 hectares near the small river the Gein at Abcoude (also in the province of Utrecht) and <entity id="org:gemeente-amsterdam">Amsterdam</entity>-Zuidoost.

title: 'Top executive of chip giant Nvidia had intimate relationship with Chinese spy'
lead: The top executive of chip giant Nvidia reportedly had an intimate relationship with a Chinese spy, according to suspicions held by American intelligence services. That is what sources tell the British business newspaper Financial Times, after The New York Times first reported on it last week. The affair revolves around Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang and Alice Huang, also known as Huang Le, an executive at Megaspeed. That is a Singaporean customer of the American chipmaker. With a market value of almost 5 trillion dollars (12 zeros), Nvidia is one of the most valuable companies in the world. American intelligence services suspect that Alice Huang was recruited by the Chinese secret services, presumably to get closer to chip secrets. The American secret services have been keeping an eye on her for at least a year. The findings of the secret services were shared in a memo with a small group of American government officials, just before President Trump traveled to Beijing in May for a meeting with his Chinese counterpart Xi, the Financial Times reports. The White House and the CIA refuse to comment. Nvidia says it sees nothing unusual in the relationship and says that Jensen Huang "meets thousands of customers every year". Photos and videos of the two are circulating on social media. They show the two drinking whisky together in June 2024. And in May 2025 they were spotted in a restaurant in the Taiwanese capital Taipei. The revelation about the memo comes two days after influential Republican members of the House of Representatives called on the Nvidia boss to answer questions behind closed doors about the reporting. What makes the matter even more striking is that Megaspeed was targeted by the United States last year for allegedly smuggling advanced Nvidia chips to China. That would be a violation of export rules. An employee of the Department of Commerce visited a Megaspeed data center in Malaysia and came across a situation he considered suspicious. The Nvidia equipment was still packed in boxes, which could indicate that it was not going to be installed but diverted. Nvidia conducted an internal investigation into the matter but concluded that there was no evidence of wrongdoing. An investigation by the American Department of Justice is still ongoing. According to The New York Times, it is unclear when Alice Huang began gathering information about the Nvidia top executive and which secrets she might have passed on to Beijing. Chip struggle between the US and China The United States is concerned about the possibility that advanced chips could end up in Chinese hands, allowing China to modernize its military faster and develop AI models better. The US has been trying for years to prevent this, including by imposing export restrictions. With its chips, Nvidia plays an important role in the global AI race. This year Jensen Huang tried to persuade Trump to grant permission for the export of the advanced H200 chip to China, which, according to the Financial Times, was a sore point for American national security officials. Precisely because of the tension between China and the US, Huang's relationship set off alarm bells within the White House, The New York Times reports. The newspaper writes that Trump was also informed by security services a year ago but decided to do nothing with the information. Trump wanted to prevent Nvidia's chip sales from being jeopardized. The company is an important engine of the American economy and the stock market.

title: Pinkpop pleased with Limburg plans for heritage list: 'Declaration of love'
lead: A decades-old pop festival on the Dutch and the international Unesco list of intangible cultural heritage. If it is up to the <entity id="org:provincie-limburg">provincie Limburg</entity>, Pinkpop in <entity id="org:gemeente-landgraaf">Landgraaf</entity> will receive this status. The Limburg Provincial States voted for this yesterday with a two-thirds majority. In the motion the VVD faction asked the provincial executive to "investigate the feasibility and support for including Pinkpop culture in the Dutch Intangible Heritage Inventory and a possible future Unesco nomination". A great honour, says festival director Tirsa Creusen of the plan. "We are proud of our roots in Limburg, it is wonderful to see that the love is mutual. We see it as a symbolic declaration of love." That the love is mutual can be read in the motion. "Pinkpop is more than music. It is a Limburg success story that connects generations, offers opportunities to entrepreneurs and gives our province international appeal. A tradition that originated here deserves to be preserved, passed on and brought to the world's attention." Pinkpop was first organised in 1970 and has been on the Guinness World Records list since 2012 as the longest-running annual festival. "How do we keep it going? We book the relevant acts of the moment and look at who the potential headliners of the future are. We try to give them a place on the stage in the early years so they can grow", Creusen says. Associations pour beer. She also grew up there herself: Creusen was born and raised near the festival site and has worked there for 15 years. Since last year she shares the management with Ide Koffeman, after co-founder Jan Smeets said goodbye in 2022. Many people from Landgraaf and other Limburgers are involved in the festival. "All bars are run by local associations. Here people aged 18 gain work experience for the first time, and people aged 70 roll up their sleeves and pour beers." Breakthrough in the Netherlands. And sometimes a band or artist who performed before returns. Such as Nothing But Thieves, who will perform in Landgraaf again next year after four shows. And Sting, who performed there in 1979 with The Police. It marked the band's breakthrough in the Netherlands. "Sting wanted to come back and for us this is very special. After almost 50 years he is still relevant." To become intangible heritage, the festival must first be placed on the inventory of the Kenniscentrum Immaterieel Erfgoed Nederland. That inventory contains over 400 forms of intangible heritage. Then the minister of <entity id="org:ministerie-van-onderwijs-cultuur-en-wetenschap">Onderwijs, Cultuur en Wetenschap</entity> (OCW) can, after advice from the Raad voor Cultuur, nominate it for the international list. The process takes years, so for festival-goers, artists and staff nothing changes for the coming editions. Which Dutch heritage is already on the Unesco list? Dutch intangible heritage on the international Unesco list: (Source: Unesco) The minister of OCW may nominate these forms of intangible heritage for the list: (Source: Raad voor Cultuur)

title: Man opens fire from car on central square in Krakow: 6 dead, 15 injured
lead: A shooting in the historic centre of the Polish city of Krakow has left six people shot dead, four women and two men. Fifteen people were also injured, including three police officers. The shooter was shot by officers and taken to a hospital, the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> reports. One of the officers was hit three times and is in critical condition, said Minister Kierwiński of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity>. Shots were fired around 15:00 from a black car driving on the city's central market square. The man wore military clothing and used a military firearm. Reports that he is a former soldier have been contradicted by the <entity id="pos:minister-van-defensie">minister van Defensie</entity>. A large number of weapons and ammunition were also found in his car, which have been seized. There was one perpetrator, a 24-year-old man from the Świętokrzyskie province in south-eastern Poland, according to the police. No motive is known yet. According to the Polish medium Onet, the perpetrator drove a car registered in the name of his 52-year-old father. The father is also said to hold a firearms permit and a total of eleven firearms. Onet writes that neither the perpetrator nor the father has a criminal record. Correspondent Christiaan Paauwe from Krakow: "This seems to be an attack on one of the most popular tourist destinations in Poland. I was on my way with my family to the old market of Krakow when we saw the trauma helicopter flying over. The square had just been cordoned off because the shooting had taken place shortly before. During the shooting people sought refuge in the hotels and restaurants around the square. Now the old market has been cleared, still with a large police presence. According to witnesses the man opened fire from a passenger car, which looks random. But residents suspect the location is not random. The Old Market is packed with tourists and day-trippers on a Saturday afternoon." A witness tells the Polish news channel Polsat News that he suddenly heard shots. "I thought it was fireworks. Suddenly people were running in all directions. Then my friend and I quickly fled into the bar." From the bar the witness could see what was happening. "We saw him shooting at people from the car." According to the witness the perpetrator shot randomly around him. He also says the shooter was wearing a helmet and that the police arrived quickly. "He fired a few more shots and then drove away." Many shops around the square were also hit, as was a tram. The driver's cabin window was shattered in the process. Nobody was injured. The perpetrator was eventually shot in a firefight with the police at an intersection close to the historic market square. Just before that he crashed his car into another white car. Footage shows the shooter lying on the ground in military gear, after which an officer kneels down beside him. Both are injured. Polish media suspect that this is the officer who is in hospital with serious injuries and is undergoing surgery. Footage of the arrest: At the time of the attack, according to Polish media, a demonstration by right-wing activists was taking place close to the Main Market Square. They were protesting against the crisis at the Constitutional Court of the country. Whether there is a connection is not yet known. The square and some surrounding streets have been cordoned off. The police are present in large numbers. The emergency services are urging residents of Krakow and tourists not to go to the square. "The police are investigating the background and all circumstances of the attack", writes Prime Minister Donald Tusk on social media. He also extends his sympathy to the families of the victims. "My greatest praise goes to the heroic police officers who risked their lives", he adds. He is on his way to Krakow and will join local authorities there this evening for a crisis meeting. The mayor of Krakow has declared a period of mourning until and including 11 November. The <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> in <entity id="org:gemeente-s-gravenhage">Den Haag</entity> says it is working with the embassy in Warsaw to determine whether there are any Dutch victims.

title: Detained protesters at Amsterdam data center protest released
lead: The more than 200 people arrested yesterday at a protest against a Microsoft data center in Amsterdam have been released. One of them had to spend a night in a police cell due to theft. That person was also allowed home during the course of today, a police spokesperson says. Two activist groups were involved in the protest in Amsterdam-West. Fossielvrij protested at the construction site against the arrival of data centers, because they use a lot of energy and some run on gas. Another group of activists from the pro-Palestinian Geef Tegengas was also there. They oppose Microsoft because the American company provides services to Israel and therefore, in their view, is co-responsible for genocide. According to the police, the activists forcibly entered the construction site and had, among other things, an angle grinder and climbing equipment with them. Despite multiple calls, they refused to hand over the items, after which the police decided to intervene. Confrontations with the mobile unit arose during this. Afterwards the demonstrators did manage to get onto the construction site, where they reportedly destroyed items and took items away. The data center is filing reports for trespassing, vandalism and burglary.

title: Police find ten thousand pieces of illegal fireworks in garage unit in Dinteloord
lead: In a garage unit in a residential area in the Brabant village of Dinteloord, police this week found 750 kilograms of heavy, illegal fireworks. This includes almost 10,000 cobras, avalanche arrows and mortar bombs. Drugs, jewellery and an alarm pistol were also seized. As for the drugs, this involved 90 grams of cannabis, 800 grams of hashish and more than 250 pills. On Wednesday a 25-year-old man from Dinteloord was arrested, and on Friday another man, aged 42, from Steenbergen. Dangerous flash powder. Following a report, the police had already been investigating the possible storage and trade in illegal fireworks for some time. The fireworks found contain large quantities of explosive flash powder. A possible explosion could have had disastrous consequences for the surrounding streets. Specialists have removed the fireworks. The police warn that fireworks are regularly stored under unsafe conditions, placing not only those involved but also residents and passers-by at serious risk. Since 1 August this year, possessing, selling and setting off fireworks has been prohibited for private individuals, including over New Year's Eve. It causes too many victims and too much nuisance for the emergency services. Check the figures for 'the last years of bangs' here: With the tracking down and seizure of illegal fireworks, the police aim to contribute to a safe New Year's Eve. People who suspect that dangerous fireworks are present somewhere are asked to report this to the police. This can also be done anonymously. Catch in Breda. In North Brabant, more illegal fireworks were found this week. According to Omroep Brabant, during a house search in Breda on Thursday the police came across 710 cobras, 37 mortar bombs and cash. Two men were also arrested in connection with this: a 26-year-old man from Breda and a 21-year-old from Roosendaal.

title: First regional yellow code from KNMI: warning for fog
lead: The KNMI has issued a regional yellow code for the first time. Dense fog is present in a narrowly defined area in the south of the <entity id="org:provincie-utrecht">provincie Utrecht</entity>, the north of <entity id="org:provincie-noord-brabant">Noord-Brabant</entity> and small parts of <entity id="org:provincie-gelderland">Gelderland</entity> and <entity id="org:provincie-zuid-holland">Zuid-Holland</entity>. According to the KNMI the fog can lead to dangerous situations and delays on the road. Until 1 November weather codes were always issued per province. For example, if it was slippery at the tip of <entity id="org:provincie-noord-holland">Noord-Holland</entity>, the KNMI issued a yellow, orange or red code for the whole province. In heavy rainfall or storms, sometimes four or five provinces were warned. Outdoor festivals As a result, a warning sometimes applied to large parts of the Netherlands, while meteorologists considered this unnecessary. Organisers of sporting events and outdoor festivals did not know where they stood. Given the large area covered by the code, safety regions could prepare poorly. The new regional weather alarm that has now been issued describes precisely where the dense fog could cause problems: indeed in <entity id="org:gemeente-wijk-bij-duurstede">Wijk bij Duurstede</entity>, not in <entity id="org:gemeente-rhenen">Rhenen</entity> or <entity id="org:gemeente-dordrecht">Dordrecht</entity>. The area around Den Bosch, where two ships collided this morning in dense fog, also falls under the regional weather alarm. On both the website and the app of the KNMI, anyone can zoom in on or search for their place of residence. Anyone who wants to can download the data and process it in their own maps or applications, RTV Utrecht reports. NOS weatherman Peter Kuipers Munneke responds enthusiastically. "This is exactly the purpose of a regional weather alarm like this. I myself live in the area where the yellow code now applies. It has been foggy all day and only three degrees", he says. "When I drove to <entity id="org:gemeente-hilversum">Hilversum</entity> for work this afternoon, the sky broke open around Utrecht. Exactly as shown on the KNMI map." Kuipers Munneke stresses that in the 'old situation' a yellow code would have been issued for the same fog bank for a total of four provinces. "While in very large parts there is absolutely nothing going on", the weatherman says. "This specific regional alarm benefits credibility."

title: At least 25 people killed in airstrike near Yemen's capital
lead: Airstrikes near the Yemeni capital Sanaa have killed at least 25 people, mainly women and children. A spokesperson for the Ministry of Public Health, which is led by the Houthis, reports this. The spokesperson said Saudi Arabia is behind the attacks. That country has not claimed responsibility. Images on social media show the aftermath of the attacks. Medical staff carry bodies of mainly young children out of ambulances at a local hospital. Other children lie on stretchers, bloodied and bandaged, while staff care for them. According to the ministry spokesperson, civilians are still lying under the rubble of houses hit by the airstrikes. He tells news agency AP that later attacks targeted rescuers trying to pull survivors from the rubble. Rapid advance: A civil war has been raging in Yemen since 2014 between the Houthis and the Yemeni government army, which is supported by Saudi Arabia. Four years ago the Houthis and Saudi Arabia signed a ceasefire, but it proved fragile. Since July this year, fighting between the Houthis and Saudi Arabia has flared up. The relative calm was broken when the Houthis began new offensives this summer. They made a rapid advance and captured a large part of the Yemeni Red Sea coast and strategic islands in the Bab el-Mandeb strait. At the same time they stepped up their attacks on Saudi Arabia, including on airports and oil depots . Systematic starvation Meanwhile the coalition led by Saudi Arabia is carrying out airstrikes in Houthi territory. The fiercest ground fighting is taking place around the strategic city of Taiz, which is held by <entity id="org:regering">de regering</entity> and has been surrounded by the Houthis. The southwestern city has been cut off from supplies of water, food, medicine and fuel. People in Taiz recently told NOS that there is already systematic starvation . According to the human rights organisation Human Rights Watch, the Houthis may be guilty of a war crime.

title: State of emergency on Canary Island El Hierro: 3000 migrants in one week
lead: The Spanish island of El Hierro has declared a state of emergency. The island council says it cannot cope with the influx of migrants and is asking the national government and the regional government for help. With 3000 new migrants in one week and 8000 since the end of summer, public services on the island are under pressure. The island council is also warning about the future. Migration pressure is expected to keep increasing in the coming months. For now, measures have been taken: sanitary conditions have been improved and temporary emergency shelter is to ease the pressure on existing reception centres. El Hierro is the southwesternmost and smallest of the inhabited Canary Islands; around 11,000 people live there. Due to its location, the currents and the weather, many migrants arrive. Autumn is often the busiest period, because conditions on the ocean are then most favourable. Yet not everyone survives the crossing from the African west coast. Volunteers on El Hierro provide a dignified farewell. According to the Red Cross, about 5 to 8 percent of people who board a boat in Africa bound for the Canary Islands die. In recent months eight deaths have been registered, but there could be more, because sometimes boats also disappear. Volunteers on El Hierro take care of deceased migrants: The director of the local hospital tells the local television channel Televisión Canaria that the emergency department is full. Extra camp beds have been set up, but the hospital wants a field hospital to be built near the harbour where the migrants arrive. The hospital director fears that if the migrant crisis continues, a shortage of care staff will arise that endangers healthcare on the island. Most people who have reached El Hierro in recent weeks come from Senegal and Gambia. Those are also the countries from which most boats depart. People smugglers are paid to bring migrants to the Canary Islands. Spanish minister in Senegal. The Spanish Minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> was in Senegal this week. In Dakar he met with the Senegalese ministers of Interior and of Public Security. He called on the country to do more to curb migration: "We must find a joint solution to tackle this complex situation and prevent more people from risking their lives by making the dangerous crossing", a press release states. Minister Grande-Marlaska acknowledges that Senegal has done more and says that this year 64 boats and more than 4000 people on their way to the Canary Islands have been intercepted. Nevertheless, he calls for more action. The regional president of the Canary Islands, Fernando Clavijo, sent a letter to Spanish prime minister Sánchez this week. He wants him to convene an emergency meeting to discuss new measures.

title: Heavy rain hits tent camps in Gaza, demand for aid grows
lead: Heavy rainfall has left tens of thousands of tents for displaced people in Gaza waterlogged. The expectation is that the situation will worsen further, as the rainy season has just begun. Jonathan Veitch, the Unicef representative for Palestine, tells the BBC that the "desperate" situation is being made worse by Israeli restrictions on the import of heavy machinery, for example. Gaza's civil defence agency reports that in just ten hours it received about 1,500 emergency calls after the rain began. The water level rose by 40 centimetres at various shelters. According to Hamas, 70,000 tents have been flooded. Many walls have also collapsed, and buildings damaged in the war threaten to collapse. Veitch says the situation is worse due to cuts to the UN budget. As a result, fewer tarpaulins, plastic sheeting and tents can be supplied to the Gaza Strip. "We have to be much more selective in which projects we support," he says. "Unfortunately, the heavy flooding this morning means that nearly everyone needs help." About 90 percent of Gaza's residents have been displaced by the war, with limited access to clean water and sanitation. A 34-year-old woman who lives with her children in Deir al-Balah in central Gaza tells the French news agency AFP that she no longer knows how to protect her children. "My children ask me where we will sleep tonight and I have no answer," she says. A 41-year-old man tells AFP he is also worried about his children, "not only because of the flooding of the tents, but also because of the cold and the diseases going around everywhere." Ceasefire violated almost daily: since October last year a ceasefire has been in effect between Israel and Hamas, but in practice Israel violates it almost daily. Since then more than 1,500 people have been killed, the Hamas-led Gaza Ministry of Health has reported. The ministry's figures are considered reliable by the UN. Israel says it targets Hamas, but civilians often also lose their lives. Since the start of the war, according to the Gaza Ministry of Health, 74,594 people have been killed in the area.

title: In Liechtenstein, the public broadcaster has been replaced by cheaper AI radio
lead: It is almost like at so many other radio stations in Europe and the rest of the world: every hour or half hour a jingle sounds and a presenter reads the radio news. So too in the small Alpine country of Liechtenstein. "Eleven o'clock, now with the news", sounds on Radio Vaterland. But the first sentence of the radio bulletin already gives it away: "This is the voice of Nicky Stettler with artificial intelligence". The texts of the radio bulletin are entirely written by AI and then spoken by cloned voices of editors. The music mix is also determined without human intervention. And this is what it looks like: in the capital Vaduz, initiator Daniel Bargetze jokingly shows the radio studio: his laptop. "We are a radio station without a studio, everything is in the cloud." The AI model uses articles from his newspaper, the Liechtensteiner Vaterland, which are produced daily by dozens of people. "The basis therefore remains the human." But presenters and weather presenters are no longer needed. "At first we still checked the texts, but by now everything works well enough", Bargetze continues. Small mistakes remain, such as the pronunciation of foreign politicians and bands such as U2 and Lynyrd Skynyrd. And although the population speaks among themselves a dialect of German, the AI model can at this moment only speak Standard German. Radio Vaterland has filled the gap that arose when the public broadcaster in the microstate with around 41,000 inhabitants was shut down. In 2024 a small majority voted in a referendum for privatisation of the broadcaster. That proved financially unfeasible, after which the Liechtenstein broadcaster stopped. In one blow 25 broadcast employees were left on the street. "Our AI station is 10 to 20 times cheaper than the former broadcaster", says Bargetze proudly. Against this, the market share of Radio Vaterland is much smaller than that of the dissolved, human-driven public broadcaster. The technology behind Radio Vaterland was first used on Helgoland, an island in the German North Sea. Founder Thore Laufenber of Radio Helgoland now sells that software for a fee to radio stations that want to use AI. Emotion: Former employee of the Liechtenstein public broadcaster Michel Erismann thinks that an AI station can never offer the same emotion as a "human" station. Therefore, after the public broadcaster disappeared, he started a Liechtenstein version of Radio2go, an existing Swiss station. Dutch AI radio: In the Netherlands, TalkRadio started this summer, an AI-driven radio station with, among other things, news from the ANP. "It is a big ambition to renew a 105-year-old medium", says initiator Richard Otto. He is still tinkering with his station, including the voices. "I expect that in four months it will sound better again than it does now." The <entity id="org:zbo-nederlandse-publieke-omroep">NPO</entity> has no plans to do that on its radio station NPO Radio 1 too. "Radio is about human connection", media director Jurre Bosman says in a written response. "When it comes to making the programmes and our podcasts, I don't see AI simply taking over the role of the human maker." "An AI station is nice, but can never offer the same as real radio", Erismann tells in his home studio. "Radio is about human contact and conveying emotions", he continues. "When it snows here in the Alps, you want to hear someone say: guys, watch out, it's snowing like crazy!" His wish is to build a full-fledged station, with independent journalistic programmes. "But there is a lack of money", sighs Erismann. The Liechtenstein <entity id="org:regering">regering</entity> has been asked for funding, but so far rejects that request. AI radio is then a lot cheaper. Editor-in-chief Bargetze sees AI as a tool, not as a replacement for his work. "It works for us because we are already a newspaper editorial office. Without these journalists no input for AI."

title: Shooting in Schiedam residential area: one dead, manhunt for shooters
lead: In Schiedam, one person has died following a shooting in the front garden of a house. He died on the spot. A second man was hit in the leg. The <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> has launched a manhunt for three suspects, Rijnmond reports. According to the police, three young men were doing work in the front garden of the home, next to a shed. They came under fire around 17:00 when three other men of roughly the same age approached. It is unclear which of them fired. The second victim is not in life-threatening danger and has been taken to hospital. The third man who came under fire fled and has since been tracked down by the police, Rijnmond reports. A doorbell camera belonging to a neighbour filmed the suspects approaching and running back after the shooting in the direction they came from. The shooting itself is not visible. The footage has been handed over to the police. Emotions run high A news photographer who was quickly on the scene tells Rijnmond that shortly after the fatal shooting, many family members of the victims were outside. They were informed a street away about what had happened. Emotions ran high. People were shouting loudly, according to the photographer. The family members have been taken care of at the police station.

title: Opposition leader Eisenkot may form Israeli government, but faces a difficult puzzle
lead: In Israel, opposition leader Gadi Eisenkot (Yashar) may be the first to try to form a new government. President Herzog has appointed him as the first formateur. Netanyahu's Likud party was the largest in the election, but Eisenkot received more recommendations from the parties. There are several routes that could lead to a government, but it will not be easy. The Arab parties, the United Arab List (Ra'am) and the Joint List, have won a record nineteen seats in this election. They could help Eisenkot form a government, but several leaders in the opposition bloc rule out such cooperation. Four conditions Eisenkot himself says he can work with anyone who meets his four conditions: recognising Israel as a Jewish and democratic state, upholding the values of the Declaration of Independence, military or civilian national service for everyone, recognising that Hamas is a terrorist organisation, and committing to dismantle the group's military and administrative capacity. Mansour Abbas's United Arab List has repeatedly indicated that it wants to govern and takes a pragmatic stance. Although Abbas condemns Hamas's terrorist attack of 7 October 2023, he does not explicitly label Hamas a terrorist organisation. The Joint List, a partnership of three smaller parties, says it does not feel bound by Eisenkot's conditions. However, the List says it is willing to support a government under his leadership. Eisenkot therefore has the option of forming a minority government with the Arab parties, but partners within the opposition bloc, including Bennett and Lieberman, rule out a government that depends on support from Arab parties. Netanyahu: 'Election fraud' Current prime minister Netanyahu meanwhile is trying to stir up fear among the population of a government with Arab parties. On Wednesday he still warned of a government dependent on "Islamist parties that support terrorism". Netanyahu and his Likud party also accuse the Arab parties of election fraud and speak of foreign interference in the election. Investigations have been launched, but the election committee and the police say there is no evidence of large-scale election fraud. Before the weekend, another possibility suddenly emerged for Eisenkot: a government with the ultra-Orthodox parties. United Torah Judaism (UTJ) was always an ally of Netanyahu, but this time the party did not make a recommendation for prime minister to the president. This seems to signal that UTJ is distancing itself from Netanyahu. National service for everyone? Exemption from military service for ultra-Orthodox men is an important demand for the ultra-Orthodox parties. In recent years UTJ has become increasingly frustrated under Netanyahu, because he has not managed to regulate this by law. Still, cooperation with Eisenkot's bloc, a bloc that ran a campaign strongly favouring national service for everyone, does not seem logical. Even so, opposition leader Lieberman suddenly said on Thursday that he was willing to compromise on national service, if that would allow a coalition to be formed without Netanyahu. It remains to be seen whether the other opposition leaders, and above all Eisenkot himself, will agree. A day later Eisenkot posted a message on X restating his four conditions for cooperation, including military and civilian national service for everyone. Finally, a government of national unity is also on the table, in which Eisenkot and Netanyahu would work together. Netanyahu called for this again last night, but Eisenkot rules out any cooperation with Netanyahu, as do the other opposition leaders. A new war with Iran could possibly change that. The threat of a new attack by America and Israel has been hanging in the air for weeks. If an attack happens, the call for national unity could grow. That could increase the pressure on Eisenkot to cooperate with Netanyahu after all. Breaking election promises Israel's political landscape has thus become entangled in election promises and red lines. In the coming weeks it will become clear which parties are willing to adjust their positions. Eisenkot faces a complicated political puzzle, and it looks like election promises will have to be broken. He has 28 days to reach a coalition, with an extension of 14 days. If Eisenkot does not succeed within that time, the turn may pass to Netanyahu.

title: Two women and a man found dead in house of Krakau shooter, presumably family
lead: In the house of the 24-year-old man who shot six people dead in Krakau on Saturday afternoon, two women and a man were found dead. Polish Prime Minister Tusk announced this at a press conference with the security services in Krakau. The victims are probably the man's immediate family members. According to Polish media, the victims are the perpetrator's father, mother and sister. Tusk said he was convinced that the <entity id="org:politie">politie</entity> would quickly arrest the shooter's "accomplices". The motive is still unclear. The <entity id="pos:minister-van-defensie">minister van Defensie</entity> speaks of "a terrorist act against the residents of Krakau". The minister of <entity id="org:tweede-kamer-commissie-biza">Binnenlandse Zaken</entity> says the shooter was presumably inspired by far-right ideologies. Firearms and ammunition were found in the man's car. The weapons were registered in the name of his father. It was also announced that one of the six people shot dead in the centre of Krakau holds British nationality. Fifteen people were injured in the attack. Among them are two police officers and five foreigners. After a firefight with the police, the shooter himself was taken to hospital; his condition is said to be critical. In Krakau, an investigation is underway at the spot where the shooter was shot. It is being checked whether the car could explode, and residents have been evacuated. The shooting minute by minute: Minister Kierwinski of Binnenlandse Zaken praised the quick action of the police; according to him, a "much greater bloodbath has been prevented". The man wore military clothing and a bulletproof vest during the attack, and used a military firearm. This fuelled reports that he was a former soldier, but this has been contradicted by the minister of Defensie. 'The square will be ours again' The mayor of Krakau, Lukaz Gibala, has announced that the city will be in mourning until Wednesday. He also promised that Krakau will remain open to visitors despite the tragedy. "The square will be ours again," he said on social media. The Dutch <entity id="org:ministerie-van-buitenlandse-zaken">ministerie van Buitenlandse Zaken</entity> reports that, according to the police in Krakau, there are no Dutch nationals among the victims. The shock in Poland is great. Eyewitness Konrad looks back on the day for the Polish news site Interia.
